teile.einleitung: The quadratic formula is a recipe with which you can solve any quadratic equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0. You simply put in the numbers a, b and c and get the solutions. Because you are supposedly meant to be able to recite it even when woken up at midnight, in Germany it is jokingly called the midnight formula.
wichtigste: The quadratic formula is x = (-b ± √(b²−4ac)) / (2a).
It works for all quadratic equations ax² + bx + c = 0 with a not equal to 0.
The expression b²−4ac is called the discriminant.
If the discriminant is positive, there are two real solutions.
If it is zero, there is exactly one solution; if it is negative, there is no real solution.
The sign ± means that you calculate once with plus and once with minus.
In Germany it is jokingly called the midnight formula.

abschnitte.text: A **quadratic equation** contains the unknown x squared, for example 2x² − 5x − 3 = 0. In general it is written as ax² + bx + c = 0, where a must not be 0. The **quadratic formula** tells you directly which values of x satisfy the equation. It is x = (-b ± √(b²−4ac)) / (2a). The sign **±** means that you calculate once with plus and once with minus and so get up to two solutions.

The part under the square root, b²−4ac, is called the **discriminant**, which means something like the one that tells things apart. It reveals how many solutions there are even before you have finished calculating. If it is greater than 0, there are two different real solutions. If it is exactly 0, there is exactly one solution. If it is less than 0, there is no real solution, because you cannot take a real square root of a negative number.

In 2x² − 5x − 3 = 0, a = 2, b = -5 and c = -3. The discriminant is 25 + 24 = 49, its square root is 7, so x = (5 ± 7) / 4. That gives x = 3 or x = -0.5. For x² − 6x − 16 = 0 you get x = 8 or x = -2. For x² − 2x − 1 = 0 the solutions are even irrational: x = 1 + √2 or x = 1 − √2.

Sometimes you have to find out when an equation has exactly one solution. Then the discriminant must be 0. For x² + kx + 9 = 0 that means k² − 36 = 0. This is true for k = 6 or k = -6. Geometrically it means that the **parabola** touches the x-axis at only one point.

About 4000 years ago, the **Babylonians** were already solving problems that lead to quadratic equations. The Persian scholar **al-Khwarizmi** described methods of solving them around 820, and the word algorithm comes from his name. Today's formula with letters only developed from the 16th and 17th centuries. Quadratic equations are needed, for example, to calculate the path of a thrown ball or areas. Besides the midnight formula there is the related **pq formula** for equations of the form x² + px + q = 0.

begriffe.erklaerung: An equation in which the unknown appears at most squared.
The expression b²−4ac, which tells you how many solutions there are.
The curve that belongs to a quadratic function; it looks like a U.
A number in front of a variable, such as a, b and c in the quadratic formula.

gewusst: With complex numbers, even an equation with a negative discriminant has two solutions.
There are also formulas for equations of the third and fourth degree, but for the fifth degree there is no general one.
The word algebra comes from the title of a book by al-Khwarizmi.

teile.einleitung: Transforming a term changes the look of a mathematical expression without changing its value. For example, you simplify 3x + 5x − 2x to 6x or expand brackets. Transforming terms is the basic tool of algebra and helps when solving equations.
wichtigste: When a term is transformed, its value stays the same for all numbers.
Like terms have the same variables with the same exponents and may be combined.
3x + 5x − 2x can be simplified to 6x.
According to the distributive law, a(b + c) = ab + ac.
If there is a minus in front of a bracket, all the signs inside the bracket change when it is expanded.
When multiplying, numbers are multiplied and the exponents of the same variables are added.
Transforming terms is needed for solving equations and in many formulas.

abschnitte.text: A **term** is a mathematical expression made of numbers, **variables** such as x or a, and operation signs. Examples are 3x + 5, 2(a + 3) or 4x². If you substitute numbers for the variables, you get a value. When **transforming a term**, you write it differently, but for every number you put in, the same result comes out.

**Like terms** have the same variables with the same exponents. You can add them like apples: 3 apples plus 5 apples minus 2 apples are 6 apples, so 3x + 5x − 2x = 6x. In 5a²b − 2ab² + 3a²b only 5a²b and 3a²b belong together, and the result is 8a²b − 2ab². Unlike terms such as a²b and ab² must not be combined, just as you do not add apples and pears together.

According to the **distributive law**, you multiply the number in front of the bracket by each term inside the bracket, so a(b + c) = ab + ac. So 2(a + 3) becomes 2a + 6. If there is a minus in front of the bracket, you reverse all the signs: -(a − 4) becomes -a + 4. That is why 2(a + 3) − (a − 4) together gives a + 10, and -(2x − 5) + 3(x − 1) gives x + 2.

When multiplying, you multiply the numbers together and combine the same variables into powers. So 4x · 3x gives the product 12x², because 4 times 3 is 12 and x times x is x². When dividing, you cancel: (12x²y) : (4xy) gives 3x, provided x and y are not zero. You may never divide by zero, which is why this condition is needed.

The word **algebra** comes from the title of a book by the Persian scholar al-Khwarizmi, who lived in Baghdad in the 9th century. Writing letters for unknown numbers only became common much later, partly thanks to the Frenchman François Viète in the 16th century. Today transforming terms is needed to solve equations and rearrange formulas. Engineers, programmers and physicists use it every day.

begriffe.erklaerung: An expression made of numbers, variables and operation signs.
A letter that stands for a number, for example x.
The rule for multiplying a number by a bracket.
The raised number that shows how many times a number is multiplied by itself.

gewusst: The name “algorithm” also goes back to al-Khwarizmi; in Latin his name became “Algorismi”.
Computer programs for mathematics can transform and simplify terms automatically; this is called computer algebra.

teile.einleitung: Two straight lines are parallel if they are the same distance apart everywhere and therefore never cross. You know this from railway tracks, the lines of a musical stave or the stripes of a zebra crossing. Parallelism is one of the most important basic ideas in geometry.
wichtigste: Parallel lines are the same distance apart everywhere.
Two different parallel lines have no point where they cross.
That two lines are parallel is written with the sign ∥.
If g is parallel to h and h is parallel to k, then g is also parallel to k.
If a line cuts two parallels, it forms equal corresponding angles and alternate angles.
Parallels are easiest to draw with a set square (Geodreieck).
The Greek Euclid described parallels more than 2000 years ago.

abschnitte.text: Two **straight lines** in a plane are parallel if they run in the same direction and are the same distance apart everywhere. That is why they never meet, even if you extend them for ever. So two different parallels have **no point of intersection**. You write g ∥ h and read “g is parallel to h”. The opposite is lines that cross, for example perpendicularly at a right angle.

With a **set square** (Geodreieck) parallels are easy to draw. You place the centre line or one of the guide lines on the given line and draw the new line along the long edge. The fine parallel lines on the set square help you keep to a certain distance. The **distance** between two parallels is always measured perpendicularly from one line to the other. You can also draw parallels with two set squares slid along each other.

If g is parallel to h and h is parallel to k, then g is also parallel to k. If two lines are perpendicular to the same third line, they are parallel to each other. Through a point that does not lie on a line there is exactly one parallel to that line. This statement goes back to the famous **parallel postulate** of the Greek Euclid. Around 300 BC Euclid wrote the textbook “Elements”, which was the basis of geometry teaching for almost 2000 years.

If a third line cuts two parallels, four angles form at each of the two crossing points. Angles in the same position at both crossing points are called **corresponding angles** and are equal. Angles that lie diagonally opposite on different sides are called **alternate angles** and are also equal. With these rules you can prove that the angles in every triangle add up to 180 degrees. The reverse is also true: if corresponding angles are equal, the lines are parallel.

Parallels are everywhere: railway tracks, the lines of an exercise book, the five lines of a **musical stave** or the stripes of a zebra crossing. In shapes such as the rectangle, the square and the **parallelogram**, opposite sides are parallel. The strings of a guitar and the rungs of a ladder run parallel too. If you look along long railway tracks, they seem to meet in the distance, but that is only a trick of perspective. Painters use this effect to make pictures look three-dimensional.

On a curved surface such as the globe, different rules apply than on a flat sheet. The lines of longitude are all perpendicular to the equator and still meet at the poles. In the 19th century, mathematicians such as Carl Friedrich Gauss, János Bolyai and Nikolai Lobachevsky discovered geometries in which the parallel postulate does not hold. They are called **non-Euclidean geometries**. Today they are important for navigation and for Einstein's theory of relativity.

begriffe.erklaerung: A straight line with no beginning and no end.
The same distance apart everywhere, without ever crossing.
Equal angles in the same position where a line cuts two parallels.
Equal angles lying diagonally opposite where a line cuts two parallels.
A see-through triangle (Geodreieck) for measuring angles and drawing lines.

gewusst: The word parallel comes from Greek and means “beside one another”.
The circles of latitude on the globe are also called parallels, because they run parallel to the equator.
For almost 2000 years mathematicians tried in vain to prove Euclid's parallel postulate from other rules.

teile.einleitung: A number wall is a number puzzle that looks like a wall made of bricks. Two neighbouring bricks add up to the number in the brick above them. In this way the wall grows from the bottom up until there is a single brick at the very top.
wichtigste: A number wall consists of number bricks stacked on top of each other like real bricks.
The number in a brick is the sum of the two bricks directly below it.
If 3 and 5 are at the bottom, 8 goes above them.
You can also work backwards and find missing bricks using subtraction.
Number walls are a popular type of exercise in Swiss primary schools.
They train addition and subtraction and logical thinking at the same time.

abschnitte.text: A number wall looks like a small **pyramid** of bricks. There are the most bricks at the bottom, and fewer and fewer towards the top. Each brick sits on two bricks in the row below. The number in the upper brick is the **sum** of the two lower numbers. If 6 and 7 are at the bottom, the brick above contains 13.

If you know the bottom bricks, you simply calculate row by row upwards. With the bricks 1, 2 and 3, the second row gives 3 and 5, and at the very top comes 8. With the bricks 2, 4 and 1 you first get 6 and 5 and then 11 at the top. If there are three 5s at the bottom, there are two 10s in the middle and 20 at the top.

It gets exciting when bricks are missing. If the top is 10 and the bottom left is 4, the bottom right must be 6, because 4 + 6 = 10. If the top is 15 and the bottom right is 9, you work out 15 minus 9 and get 6. In this way you practise the **inverse operation**, subtraction as the opposite of addition.

With bigger walls you sometimes have to guess and try things out. A little trick: in a three-storey wall, the middle brick of the bottom row counts twice towards the **top brick**. That is why the wall 1, 2, 3 gives 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 at the top. If you discover patterns like this, you can solve number walls much faster.

Number walls are among the typical exercises in primary school maths books, in Switzerland too. They are sometimes also called **number pyramids**. Children first practise with small numbers and later with tens such as 20 and 30, which add up to 50. Instead of addition you can also use other operations, such as multiplication.

begriffe.erklaerung: The result of an addition.
A calculation that undoes another one, like subtraction for addition.
The highest brick of a number wall.
Another name for a number wall.

gewusst: If you change a brick in the bottom row by 1, the top brick can change by more than 1.
Number walls with four or five rows can be tricky even for adults.
The shape is reminiscent of the pyramids in Egypt, which also get narrower towards the top.

teile.einleitung: A tally chart is a simple way of counting things by making a mark for each one. To keep track, the marks are grouped into bundles of five. Tally charts are used by children at school, but also by researchers, athletes and waiters.
wichtigste: A tally chart is used for counting.
For each thing counted you make a vertical line.
The fifth line is drawn across the other four and makes a bundle of five.
2 bundles of five and 3 single lines make the number 13.
The number 9 is shown with 1 bundle and 4 lines.
Tally charts help to evaluate surveys and compare results.
Even in the Stone Age people scratched tally marks into bones and wood.

abschnitte.text: A **tally chart** is a table in which you make a mark for each thing you count. On the left are the things you are counting, for example animals or colours. On the right you collect the marks. At the end you add up the marks and write down the number.

You make four lines vertically next to each other. The fifth line is drawn across the other four, making a **bundle of five**. The bundles are reminiscent of a hand with five fingers. This makes counting quick: 4 bundles are 20, and 2 bundles with 3 single lines are 13.

With a tally chart a class can carry out a **survey**, for example about favourite colours or the morning snack (in Swiss German “Znüni”). If blue has 8 marks, red 6 and green 5, blue is the most popular. If there are 4 marks for apple, 6 for banana and 9 for bread, 19 children were counted altogether. If “dog” has 7 marks and “cat” 4, “dog” has 3 marks more.

Tally marks are among the oldest ways of recording numbers. Archaeologists have found bones with notches carved into them that are many thousands of years old, for example the **Ishango bone** from Africa. In the Middle Ages debts were cut as notches into a piece of wood, the **tally stick**. That is where the German saying “etwas auf dem Kerbholz haben” (“to have something on the tally stick”) comes from.

Tally marks do not look the same everywhere. In China, Japan and Korea people write the character 正 stroke by stroke; it has exactly five strokes. In South America people sometimes count with a square and a diagonal. Tally charts are often turned into a **column chart** so that the results can be compared at a glance.

begriffe.erklaerung: Five lines in which the fifth goes across the other four.
You ask many people the same thing and count the answers.
A wooden stick into which notches were cut in the past to count debts.
A picture that shows amounts with columns of different heights.

gewusst: The Ishango bone is about 20,000 years old and was found in what is now Congo.
The Roman numerals I, II and III are actually little tally charts too.

teile.einleitung: The dot product is a way of multiplying two vectors together. The special thing is that the result is not a new vector but a single real number. With the dot product you can calculate angles, check whether two directions are perpendicular to each other and, in physics, work out the work done.
wichtigste: The dot product of two vectors gives a real number, not a vector.
You calculate it by multiplying the matching coordinates and adding the products.
If the dot product is zero, the vectors are perpendicular to each other.
If it is negative, the angle between the vectors is obtuse.
The dot product of a vector with itself gives the square of its length.
In physics, work is the dot product of force and distance.

abschnitte.text: A **vector** is an arrow with a direction and a length, for example (3, -2, 4) in space. The **dot product** combines two such vectors into a number. It is often written with a dot, as a · b. Because the result is a simple number, it is also called the inner product or scalar product.

You multiply the first coordinates, then the second and then the third, and add everything together. For (3, -2, 4) and (1, 5, 2) this gives 3 times 1 plus -2 times 5 plus 4 times 2, that is 3 − 10 + 8 = 1. For (2, k, 1) and (3, -1, 4) you get 6 − k + 4, and that is zero for k = 10. There is also a second formula: the length of a times the length of b times the **cosine** of the angle between them.

From the two formulas you can work out the angle between two vectors. For (1, 1, 0) and (0, 1, 1) the dot product is 1 and each length is the square root of 2, which gives an angle of 60 degrees. If the dot product is zero, the vectors are **orthogonal**, that is perpendicular, to each other, like (2, 1, -2) and (1, 0, 1). A positive result means an acute angle, a negative one an obtuse angle.

If you multiply a vector by itself, you get the square of its **length**. For (3, 4) this gives 9 + 16 = 25, so the length is 5. This is really Pythagoras’ theorem in a new form. In this way you can also calculate distances between points in space.

In physics, **work** is calculated as the dot product of force and distance. If you pull a sledge at an angle upwards, only the part of the force that points in the direction of travel counts. In computer games and 3D graphics, the dot product is used to work out how brightly a surface is lit by a lamp. It also comes up all the time in statistics and machine learning.

begriffe.erklaerung: An arrow with a direction and a length, described by coordinates.
A simple number without a direction, for example a temperature.
Perpendicular to each other, that is at a right angle of 90 degrees.
A trigonometric function that gives a value between -1 and 1 for every angle.

gewusst: Someone carrying a suitcase horizontally through a station does no work on the suitcase in the physics sense, because force and distance are perpendicular to each other.
The word “scalar” comes from the Latin “scala”, meaning ladder or staircase, so a number on a scale.

teile.einleitung: Left and right are the two sides that we tell apart as seen from ourselves. They help us when giving directions, in traffic, and when reading and writing. Because left and right depend on which way you are facing, you sometimes have to be very careful.
wichtigste: Left and right always depend on which direction you are facing.
If you turn right twice, you are then facing backwards.
Switzerland drives on the right; cars drive on the right-hand side.
Before crossing a road in Switzerland, you look left first.
Most people write with their right hand.
German is read and written from left to right.
In most people the heart lies slightly more to the left in the chest.

abschnitte.titel: What is left, what is right
abschnitte.text: **Left** and **right** describe the two sides of the body. Many children remember: the right hand is usually the writing hand, and on the left hand the thumb and index finger form an L. Left and right are relative; they turn with you. If you turn right twice, you have turned halfway round and are facing backwards.

If a child stands opposite you and raises their right hand, you see it on your left side. That is why people in PE often mix up the sides when the teacher demonstrates at the front. In a mirror, left and right seem to be swapped, but really it is front and back that are swapped. With a **compass** it is easier: if you walk north and turn left, you are walking west.

In Switzerland and most countries, traffic **drives on the right**. That is why cars on the near side of the road come from the left, and when crossing you look left first, then right and then left again. In Britain, Ireland, Japan, Australia and India, on the other hand, traffic **drives on the left**. Sweden switched from driving on the left to driving on the right on 3 September 1967.

About 9 out of 10 people prefer to write with their right hand. Roughly one person in ten is **left-handed**. In the past, left-handed children were often forced to write with their right hand; today they may use their favourite hand. There are special scissors, fountain pens and rulers for them. Amazingly, the left half of the brain mainly controls the right side of the body, and the other way round.

German, French and Italian are written from left to right. Arabic and Hebrew, on the other hand, are written from right to left. On ships, people say **port** instead of left and starboard instead of right, so that there are no misunderstandings. In politics people also talk about left and right, because in the French National Assembly around 1789 the groups sat on different sides of the hall.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rule that vehicles drive on the right-hand side of the road.
A person who is more skilful with the left hand.
The left side of a ship when you are facing forwards.
The right side of a ship when you are facing forwards.

gewusst: Many animals also have a favourite side; parrots, for example, often prefer to grip with a particular foot.
In Switzerland trains usually run on the left, although traffic on the roads drives on the right.
Ships have a red navigation light on the left and a green one on the right, so that at night you can tell which way they are going.

teile.einleitung: Probability theory is the branch of mathematics that describes chance with numbers. It explains how to calculate chances in dice games, medical tests or weather forecasts. Together with statistics it forms stochastics.
wichtigste: Probability theory studies random processes with mathematical rules.
For independent events you multiply the probabilities, so 0.3 times 0.5 gives exactly 0.15.
The probability of rolling at least one six in two throws is 11/36.
The expected value of a fair die is 3.5.
From just 23 people, there is a more than 50 per cent chance that two share a birthday.
Positive tests for rare diseases often mean only a small probability of having the disease.
The foundations were laid by Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat in 1654.

abschnitte.text: Probability theory arose from questions about **games of chance**. In 1654 the French mathematicians Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat wrote each other letters about how to share out a stake fairly. The Basel mathematician **Jakob Bernoulli** wrote the important work “Ars Conjectandi”, which appeared in 1713 after his death. It contains the law of large numbers. In 1933 the Russian Andrei Kolmogorov laid down the basic rules, the axioms, that are valid today.

If two events are **independent**, you multiply their probabilities. With P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5, the probability of both together is 0.15. For “at least one six in two throws” it is best to calculate with the opposite: no six has 5/6 times 5/6, that is 25/36. That leaves 11/36 for at least one six. With three coin tosses there are 3 of 8 ways of getting exactly two heads, so 3/8.

An urn contains 3 red and 2 blue balls. If you draw two balls without putting the first one back, the contents change after the first draw. The first ball is red with 3/5, the second then only with 2/4. Both together give 3/5 times 2/4, that is 3/10. Such multi-stage experiments are often drawn as a **tree diagram**.

The **expected value** is the result you get on average in the long run. For a fair die you add 1 to 6 and divide by 6, which gives 3.5. You can never actually roll a 3.5, but after many throws the average gets closer to this value. This is described by the **law of large numbers**. Casinos and lotteries are set up so that the expected value is negative for the players.

In the **birthday problem**, just 23 people are enough for there to be a more than 50 per cent chance that two share a birthday. This is because there are very many possible pairs. Another example is medical tests: if only 1 per cent of a population has a disease, you are often still healthy even with a positive test. In the example mentioned, the chance of really being ill is only about 9 per cent. Questions like this are solved with **Bayes’ theorem**.

Insurance companies use it to calculate premiums and risks. In medicine it is used to test whether a new medicine really works. Weather services such as MeteoSwiss give probabilities of rain. It also plays a big role in physics, genetics and artificial intelligence. It helps you make sensible decisions under **uncertainty**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The umbrella term for probability theory and statistics.
Two events do not influence each other.
A drawing that shows multi-stage random experiments with branches.
The average you expect over very many trials.
A test reports something that is not actually there.

gewusst: The Bernoulli family from Basel produced several famous mathematicians.
In a school class of 30 children the chance of a shared birthday is already about 70 per cent.
The expected value of a die, 3.5, is a number you can never roll.

teile.einleitung: A pyramid is a geometric solid with a flat base and triangular side faces that meet at a point at the top. The best known is the pyramid with a square base, like the famous pyramids in Egypt. Pyramids are very stable and are among the oldest building shapes made by humans.
wichtigste: A pyramid has a base and triangles as side faces.
All the side faces meet at a shared apex.
A pyramid with a square base has 5 vertices.
There are 4 triangles on the sides of a square pyramid.
The square pyramid has 5 faces and 8 edges.
The volume is one third of base area times height.
The triangular pyramid is also called a tetrahedron.

abschnitte.text: A **pyramid** consists of a **base**, which is a polygon, for example a triangle or a square. From each side of the base a triangle rises upwards. All these triangles meet at one point, the **apex**. So how many side faces a pyramid has depends on the shape of its base. A pyramid with a hexagon as its base, for example, has six triangles on its sides.

On a pyramid with a square base you count 4 vertices at the bottom and 1 at the top, so **5 vertices** altogether. It has 4 edges around the base and 4 edges leading to the apex, so 8 edges. Then there are 5 faces: the square at the bottom and 4 triangles on the sides. The mathematician Leonhard Euler from Basel discovered a rule for this: vertices minus edges plus faces always equals 2. It works for the pyramid: 5 minus 8 plus 5 equals 2.

If you unfold a square pyramid, you get a **net** made of a square with four triangles attached. It looks a little like a star. You calculate the **volume** as base area times height divided by 3. So a pyramid holds only a third as much as a cuboid with the same base and height. As with the cone and the cylinder, an experiment with sand or water helps here.

The simplest pyramid has a triangle as its base and four triangular faces. If all four triangles are the same size, it is called a **tetrahedron**. The tetrahedron is one of the five Platonic solids, which are especially regular. If the apex is exactly above the centre of the base, it is called a right pyramid. If the apex is shifted to one side, the pyramid is oblique.

The most famous pyramids stand at **Giza** near Cairo in Egypt. The largest of them is the Great Pyramid of Khufu, built about 4500 years ago as a tomb for a pharaoh. It was originally about 146 metres high and remained the tallest building in the world for almost 4000 years. The Maya in Central America also built step pyramids for their temples. In Paris a modern glass pyramid has stood in front of the Louvre museum since 1989.

begriffe.erklaerung: The face on which the pyramid stands.
A pyramid made of four triangles of the same size.
A line where two faces meet.
A solid spread out flat, from which it can be folded.

gewusst: The first milk carton made by the company Tetra Pak had the shape of a tetrahedron, a triangular pyramid.
The Great Pyramid of Giza is made of more than two million stone blocks.

teile.einleitung: The sine function is one of the most important functions in mathematics. Its graph is a regular wavy line that repeats again and again. It is used to describe vibrations and waves, from the sound of a guitar to the electricity from a socket.
wichtigste: The sine function is written f(x) = sin(x).
Its graph is a wave, the sine curve.
The function repeats after 2π; that is its period.
Its values always lie between minus 1 and 1.
Its zeros lie at all whole-number multiples of π.
If you shift the sine curve π/2 to the left, you get the cosine curve.
Many vibrations in nature and technology follow a sine shape.

abschnitte.text: You can explain the sine using the **unit circle**, a circle with radius 1. A point moves anticlockwise round the circle. The sine of the angle is the height of this point above the horizontal axis. Because the point never goes higher than 1 or lower than minus 1, all sine values lie between minus 1 and 1. After a quarter circle, that is π/2, the point is right at the top and sin(π/2) = 1.

If you plot the height against the angle, you get the **sine curve**. After one full turn, that is 2π or 360 degrees, everything starts again, which is why 2π is the **period**. The curve crosses the x-axis at 0, π, 2π and all other multiples of π. The graph has point symmetry about the origin, because sin(minus x) equals minus sin(x).

With numbers in front of and inside the function you can change the wave. For f(x) = 3·sin(x) the curve swings up to 3 and down to minus 3, so the **amplitude** is 3. For f(x) = sin(2x) the wave swings twice as fast and the period is only π. If you shift the curve π/2 to the left, you get the cosine function.

Many processes follow a sine curve, for example a swinging pendulum or a tuning fork. The **alternating voltage** from a socket is sinusoidal too. The Swiss electricity grid has a **frequency** of 50 hertz, which means 50 oscillations per second. A single period therefore lasts 20 milliseconds. Even the height of a car on a big wheel follows a sine curve.

The Greek astronomer **Hipparchus** calculated tables of chords of circles in the 2nd century BC, forerunners of sine tables. Indian mathematicians such as Aryabhata developed the sine as we know it today around the year 500. The word sine comes from Latin and means bay or curve. It arose in the Middle Ages when Arabic texts were translated into Latin.

begriffe.erklaerung: The length after which a function repeats itself.
The largest distance of an oscillation from the centre line.
A circle with radius 1 around the origin.
A point where the graph crosses the x-axis.
The number of oscillations per second, measured in hertz.

gewusst: Every sound can be made up of many individual sine waves.
Calculators do not look up the sine in a table but work it out in a flash with a formula.
In the USA the electricity grid runs at 60 hertz instead of 50 hertz as in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Estimating means giving an approximate size or amount without measuring or counting it exactly. If you are good at estimating, you notice straight away whether a result can be right at all. For this you mainly need reference sizes from everyday life.
wichtigste: An estimate is an approximate value, not an exact one.
Good estimates are based on known reference sizes.
A pencil is about 18 cm long, a room door about 2 m high.
An apple weighs about 150 g, a child in Year 2 about 25 kg.
A football pitch is about 100 m long.
In Switzerland a school lesson usually lasts 45 minutes.
Estimating lets you check your own results.

abschnitte.text: With an **estimate** you give a number that is roughly right. You do not measure exactly but think it through using experience and common sense. A good estimate is close to the correct value. People often say “roughly”, “about” or “around”.

For lengths, **reference sizes** help. A pencil is about 18 cm long, a room door about 2 m high and a football pitch about 100 m long. Your own body is a measuring tool too: a child’s hand span is about 15 cm, a big step about half a metre to a metre. With such reference sizes you can estimate almost anything.

An apple weighs about 150 g, a bar of chocolate often 100 g. A large carton of milk contains about 1 litre, which also weighs about 1 kg. A child in Year 2 weighs about 25 kg. If you know such **reference values**, you can easily judge whether a rucksack is too heavy.

Time is hard to estimate, because it feels long or short depending on your mood. Brushing your teeth should take about 3 minutes. In Switzerland a **school lesson** usually lasts 45 minutes. With an hourglass or a timer you can practise judging time better.

When **estimating a calculation**, you round the numbers and work it out roughly in your head. This shows you quickly whether an exact result is plausible. If something costs 19.80 francs and you buy 3 of them, that is about 60 francs. If the calculator shows 594, you have probably mistyped.

Experts estimate all the time too, for example the number of animals in a forest or the number of visitors at a festival. The physicist Enrico Fermi was famous for tricky estimation questions, which are now called **Fermi questions**. One example is: how many bikes are there in Switzerland? You break the question down into small steps that are easier to estimate.

begriffe.erklaerung: An approximate value that you find by thinking rather than measuring exactly.
A known size that you compare other things with.
A quick calculation with rounded numbers.
Believable and reasonable, so that it could be right.

gewusst: In estimation competitions, the average of all the estimates of a large group is often astonishingly close to the correct value.
A litre of water weighs almost exactly a kilogram, which makes estimating in the kitchen easy.
People can take in small amounts of up to about four objects at a glance without counting.

teile.einleitung: Tens numbers are numbers such as 10, 20, 30 or 90 that end in zero. You can calculate with them almost as easily as with the numbers from 1 to 9. If you know that 3 + 4 = 7, you can also work out 30 + 40 = 70.
wichtigste: Tens numbers are multiples of 10, for example 20, 50 or 80.
When calculating with tens numbers, you treat the tens like ones.
30 + 40 is the same as 3 tens plus 4 tens, so 7 tens or 70.
Multiplying and dividing work like this too: 4 times 20 is 80.
Ten tens make a hundred.
Calculating with tens helps with mental arithmetic and estimating.

abschnitte.text: **Tens numbers** are the numbers 10, 20, 30 and so on, which you reach by counting in steps of ten. They always have a 0 in the units place. The number 70, for example, is made up of 7 tens and 0 units. Our number system is called the **decimal system**, because ten units are always grouped into a bigger unit.

For 30 + 40 you think of 3 + 4 = 7 and add the zero back on. In this way 90 minus 60 becomes 9 minus 6, so 30. For 80 + 60 you get 14 tens, which is 140, more than a **hundred**. For 300 minus 80 you can first take away 100 and then add 20 back, getting 220.

The same idea helps with multiplication: 3 times 30 is like 3 times 3, just with a zero, so 90. For 4 times 20 you work out 4 times 2 = 8 and get 80. Division works the same way: 60 divided by 3 is 20, because 6 divided by 3 is 2. If you divide a tens number by 10, the zero simply disappears, so 80 divided by 10 becomes 8.

Ten tens make 100. If you want to know how many tens are missing from 40 to 100, you work out 10 minus 4 and get 6. Such **completing exercises** are important for calculating later up to 1000 and beyond. At school a hundred square or wooden tens rods are often used for this.

We often come across tens numbers, for example with money: there are notes of 10, 20 and 50 francs. When **estimating**, too, you round to tens to get a rough idea of a result. If one thing costs 29 francs and another 41 francs, that is roughly 30 + 40, so about 70 francs. With this estimate you can quickly tell whether an exact result can be right.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bundle of ten units.
The place on the far right of a number.
Our number system, in which ten units are always grouped into a bigger one.
Roughly working out a result by calculating with rounded numbers.

gewusst: The fact that we count in tens probably has to do with our ten fingers.
An abacus with beads in rows of ten has been used for calculating for centuries.
If you are confident calculating with tens, you can also solve 3000 + 4000 straight away.

teile.einleitung: Long division is a method for dividing large numbers on paper. You divide place by place from left to right. With this method you can also solve problems that would be far too difficult in your head.
wichtigste: In division you divide the dividend by the divisor.
The result of a division is called the quotient.
You work place by place from left to right.
If something is left over at the end, it is called the remainder: 1000 : 7 = 142 remainder 6.
0 divided by a number always gives 0, but you may not divide by 0.
You check with multiplication: 729 · 8 = 5832.
Long division helps, for example, when sharing out costs.

abschnitte.text: In **long division** you divide a large number by a smaller one on paper. The number being divided is called the **dividend**, and the number you divide by is called the divisor. The result is called the **quotient**. In 5832 : 8, 5832 is the dividend, 8 the divisor and 729 the quotient.

You start on the left and ask: how many times does the divisor go into the first digit or digits? In 5832 : 8, 8 does not go into 5, so you take 58. 8 goes into 58 7 times, with 2 left over. Then you bring down the next digit, 3, and carry on with 23. In this way the result 729 is built up place by place.

You can also divide by two-digit numbers in writing. 9156 : 12 gives 763, and 4725 : 25 gives 189. Here it helps to write out the **times table** of the divisor first, that is 12, 24, 36 and so on. If a 0 comes up in an intermediate step, you must not forget it in the result, as in 63,504 : 6 = 10,584.

Not every division works out exactly. For 1000 : 7 you get 142 with 6 left over, so you write 142 **remainder** 6. You can also carry on calculating with decimal places, and then you get a decimal number. If you divide 0 by 5, the result is 0. Dividing by 0, however, is not allowed, because there is no sensible result.

With a **check** you test the result: you multiply the quotient by the divisor and add any remainder. For 142 remainder 6: 142 · 7 + 6 = 1000. In everyday life division is needed, for example, to share out costs. If a class trip costs 3456 francs and 24 children go, each child pays 144 francs.

People could divide even in ancient times, but with Roman numerals it was very laborious. Only with the **place value system** and the Hindu-Arabic numerals did long division become easy. These numerals came to Europe in the Middle Ages, among other things through Leonardo Fibonacci’s arithmetic book of 1202. Today the method is used in schools all over the world, even though the way it is written looks a little different from country to country.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number that is divided.
The number you divide by.
The result of a division.
What is left over when a division does not work out exactly.
A control calculation to test whether a result is correct.

gewusst: In English-speaking countries long division is written with a completely different sign that looks like half a bracket with a roof.
The sign ÷ for division is hardly used in Switzerland; a colon is usually written instead.
Calculators also divide step by step inside, only much faster than a person.

teile.einleitung: A square is a quadrilateral with four sides of equal length and four right angles. It is one of the simplest and most regular shapes in geometry. You find squares everywhere, for example on a chessboard, on tiles or on squared paper.
wichtigste: In a square all four sides are the same length.
All four angles of a square are right angles.
Every square is also a rectangle.
The perimeter is calculated as 4 times the side length, so 8 cm for a side of 2 cm.
The area is calculated as side length times side length.
4 small squares with a side of 1 cm fit into a square with a side of 2 cm.
A square on a chessboard usually has the shape of a square.

abschnitte.text: A **square** is a quadrilateral in which all four sides are the same length and all four corners form a **right angle**. Opposite sides are parallel. The word comes from the Latin quadratus and means four-cornered. Because a square has four right angles, every square is also a **rectangle**. But the other way round, not every rectangle is a square.

The **perimeter** is the length of all four sides together, so 4 times the side length. A square with a side of 2 centimetres therefore has a perimeter of 8 centimetres. The **area** is side times side, so 4 square centimetres for 2 centimetres. That is why exactly 4 small squares with a side of 1 centimetre fit inside it. A square metre is a square with a side length of 1 metre.

If you join opposite corners, you get the two **diagonals**. They are the same length, are perpendicular to each other and cut each other in half. A square has four lines of symmetry: two through the midpoints of the sides and two along the diagonals. If you turn it by 90 degrees about its centre, it looks exactly the same again. Hardly any other shape is so regular.

When you multiply a number by itself, the result is called a **square number**. The first square numbers are 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25. The name comes from the fact that you can lay that many dots out exactly as a square, for example 9 dots in 3 rows of 3. You write 3 to the power of 2 and say three squared. The reverse is called the square root: the square root of 25 is 5.

A **chessboard** consists of 8 by 8, that is 64 square fields. Tiles, napkins, sticky notes and many windows are square as well. Squares fit together without gaps, which is why they are good for floors and walls. Squared paper helps with sums because each box is a small square. The pixels that make up a screen are often tiny squares, too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A shape with four corners and four sides.
A straight line joining two opposite corners.
The length of the whole edge around a shape.
The result of multiplying a number by itself, for example 16.

gewusst: A chessboard contains not just 64 but 204 squares altogether, if you count all sizes.
The square is the only quadrilateral that is both a rectangle and a rhombus.
The Swiss flag is one of the few square national flags in the world.

teile.einleitung: Pocket money is money that children and young people regularly receive from their parents and are allowed to manage themselves. With it they learn how to handle money: budgeting, saving and sometimes going without. With pocket money, maths becomes very practical, from adding up to working with percentages.
wichtigste: Pocket money is a fixed amount that children may decide about themselves.
Younger children often get it weekly, older ones more often monthly.
If you get 25 francs a month, you receive 300 francs in a year.
A savings goal helps you to fulfil a bigger wish.
With percentages you can work out spending and increases.
A budget shows how much money comes in and how much is spent.
Budgetberatung Schweiz gives parents recommendations on how much pocket money suits each age.

abschnitte.text: **Pocket money** is a regular amount of money that parents give their children. The child may decide for themselves what to spend the money on or whether to save it. In this way they learn that money is not unlimited and that you have to set priorities. Mistakes with small amounts are good practice for later.

How much pocket money a child gets is up to the parents. The advice service **Budgetberatung Schweiz** publishes guideline amounts that rise with age. Younger children often get a small amount every week, teenagers rather a larger amount once a month. Some families give older teenagers a **youth allowance**, with which they also pay for their own clothes or mobile phone contract.

If Lea gets 25 francs a month, that makes 300 francs in 12 months. Tim gets 6 francs a week and saves half of it, that is 3 francs; after 8 weeks he has 24 francs. Elin has received 35 francs and spent 28.40 francs, so she has 6.60 francs left. Jan has 50 francs and spends 7.50 francs every week; after 6 weeks he has only 5 francs left, and so for the first time less than 10 francs.

A **per cent** is one hundredth. If Noah spends 15 per cent of 40 francs on a comic, it costs 6 francs. If Sara saves 12 francs out of 30 francs and spends 9 francs on the cinema, 9 francs are left, which is 30 per cent. If Luca now gets 25 per cent more than his 20 francs, he receives 25 francs.

Write down in a **budget** how much money you get and what you spend it on. Set a savings goal and work out how long you need to save: for headphones costing 72 francs, at 8 francs a week, you need 9 weeks. Before every purchase, think about whether you really need the thing. Try not to borrow money, because **debts** have to be paid back.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plan that sets income against spending.
A larger amount with which teenagers also pay their own costs, such as clothes.
One hundredth of a whole, written with the sign %.
Money that you owe someone and have to pay back.

gewusst: Experts advise not to cut pocket money as a punishment or raise it as a reward, so that children can plan with it reliably.
If you save just 2 francs every week, after a year you already have 104 francs.

teile.einleitung: A school timetable is a table that shows when each school subject takes place. It arranges the week by days and lessons and helps everyone keep track. You can also do lots of maths with a timetable: counting lessons, calculating times and planning weeks.
wichtigste: A timetable shows the school subjects arranged by days of the week and times.
In Switzerland a lesson usually lasts 45 minutes.
Normally there is school on 5 days a week.
In many Swiss primary schools there is no school on Wednesday afternoon.
Two lessons in a row last 90 minutes together.
Between the lessons there are breaks, for example a long break in the morning.
The timetable follows the curriculum, which sets how many lessons a subject has.

abschnitte.text: A **timetable** is a table with the days of the week in the columns and the lessons in the rows. Each box says which subject takes place at that time and often also in which room. That way you always know which books and things you need to pack. Teachers, music schools and sports clubs also work with plans like this.

In Switzerland a school period is called a **lesson** (Lektion) and usually lasts 45 minutes. The school week has 5 school days from Monday to Friday. In many primary schools Wednesday afternoon is free. In German-speaking Switzerland the **Lehrplan 21** curriculum sets roughly how many lessons a subject gets per week, and the cantons decide the details.

If school starts at 8.00 and the first lesson lasts 45 minutes, it finishes at 8.45. Two PE lessons in a row last 90 minutes, that is an hour and a half. If the **break** lasts from 10.00 to 10.20, you have 20 minutes for your morning snack. To solve calculations like this, it is best to count on in minutes.

You can solve lots of problems with a timetable. If you have 4 lessons in the morning and 2 in the afternoon, that makes 6 lessons together. If you have PE every Tuesday and Friday, you have PE 4 times in 2 weeks. If there are 5 maths lessons and 1 music lesson in the timetable, there are 4 more maths lessons.

Making a timetable for a whole school is a difficult **puzzle**. Every class needs its lessons, every teacher can only be in one place at a time, and there is only one gym. In the past timetables were made by hand with large peg boards. Today **computer programs** often help by working through many possibilities.

begriffe.erklaerung: A school period, in Switzerland usually 45 minutes long.
A document that sets out what children should learn in each subject.
Two lessons of the same subject directly one after the other.
An interruption between lessons for resting and eating.

gewusst: Making a good timetable is such a difficult computing problem that computer scientists study it scientifically.
A school period hardly anywhere lasts a whole hour; it is usually 45 minutes.

teile.einleitung: Platonic solids are especially regular solids whose faces all consist of identical regular polygons. There are exactly five of them: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron. They are named after the Greek philosopher Plato.
wichtigste: There are exactly five Platonic solids.
All the faces are identical regular polygons, and the same number meet at every corner.
The tetrahedron, with 4 triangles, has the fewest faces.
The cube is also called a hexahedron and has 6 squares.
The octahedron consists of 8 and the icosahedron of 20 equilateral triangles.
The dodecahedron consists of 12 regular pentagons.
They are named after the philosopher Plato from Athens.

abschnitte.text: A **Platonic solid** is a solid whose faces are all identical **regular polygons**. In addition, the same number of faces meet at every corner. As a result the solid looks the same from every corner. Such solids are regarded as the most regular there are. Amazingly, there are only five of them.

The **tetrahedron** consists of 4 equilateral triangles and has the fewest faces. The cube, also called a **hexahedron**, has 6 squares. The octahedron consists of 8 equilateral triangles and looks like two pyramids placed base to base. The **dodecahedron** has 12 regular pentagons. Finally, the icosahedron consists of 20 equilateral triangles.

At least three faces must meet at a corner, and their angles must add up to **less than 360°**, otherwise the corner becomes flat. With triangles of 60° this works with 3, 4 or 5 faces, giving the tetrahedron, octahedron and icosahedron. Three squares of 90° make the cube, and three pentagons of 108° the dodecahedron. Three regular hexagons give exactly 360° and so lie **flat** in the plane. That is why there cannot be a Platonic solid made of hexagons or larger polygons.

The Greek philosopher **Plato** described the solids around 360 BC in his work Timaeus. He linked four of them to the elements: the tetrahedron to fire, the cube to earth, the octahedron to air and the icosahedron to water. The dodecahedron stood for the whole universe. The mathematician **Euclid** proved in his work Elements that there are exactly five such solids. In 1596 the astronomer Johannes Kepler also tried to explain the distances between the planets with them.

abschnitte.titel: In everyday life and in nature
abschnitte.text: In board games and role-playing games there are **dice** in the shape of all five Platonic solids, with 4, 6, 8, 12 or 20 sides. Some viruses and tiny sea creatures, the radiolarians, have the shape of an icosahedron. Some crystals, such as table salt, form cubes. For all Platonic solids **Euler's polyhedron formula** holds: corners minus edges plus faces gives 2. For the cube that is 8 minus 12 plus 6, so exactly 2.

begriffe.erklaerung: A flat shape with sides of equal length and angles of equal size.
A solid bounded only by flat polygons.
A solid made of four equilateral triangles, like a pyramid with a triangular base.
A solid made of twelve regular pentagons.
A solid made of twenty equilateral triangles.

gewusst: A classic football is not a Platonic solid, but it is made from an icosahedron whose corners have been cut off.
The cube and the octahedron are dual to each other: if you join the centres of the faces of a cube, you get an octahedron.
More than a hundred mysterious bronze dodecahedra from Roman times have been found, and their purpose is still unclear today.

teile.einleitung: Statistics is the art of making sense of lots of numbers. It collects data, sorts it and sums it up with a few key figures such as the mean or the median. This tells you, for example, how tall children are on average or how many people live in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Statistics deals with collecting, sorting and analysing data.
The arithmetic mean is the sum of all the values divided by how many there are.
The median is the value in the middle when all the values are put in order of size.
The mode is the value that occurs most often.
The range is the difference between the largest and the smallest value.
Variance and standard deviation show how widely the values are spread.
The median hardly reacts to single extreme outliers.
In Switzerland the Federal Statistical Office in Neuchâtel collects a lot of data about the country.

abschnitte.text: Statistics is a branch of mathematics. First, **data** is collected, for example through surveys, measurements or counts. Then it is sorted and shown in tables or **charts**. Finally you try to draw conclusions from the numbers. In this way you can find out, for example, which break-time snack is most popular in a class.

The **arithmetic mean** is also called the average in everyday life. For the values 4, 8, 6, 10 and 7 you work out 35 divided by 5 and get 7. The **median** is the middle value of an ordered list. With an even number of values you take the midpoint of the two middle numbers, so for 1, 3, 4, 8, 10 and 22 it is 6. The **mode** is the most frequent value; for 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 7, 7 and 9 it is 7.

Two classes can have the same average and still be completely different. The **range** measures the distance from the smallest to the largest value; for 12, 5, 19, 8 and 15 it is 19 minus 5, that is 14. More precise is the **variance**, the average of the squared distances from the mean. Its square root is called the **standard deviation**. For the values 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7 and 9 the mean is 5 and the standard deviation exactly 2.

An **outlier** is a value that lies far away from all the others. If one person in a group earns much more than everyone else, the average rises sharply. The median, on the other hand, stays almost the same, which is why it is often used for incomes. Charts can also be misleading if the axis does not start at zero. Anyone reading statistics should therefore always look carefully.

In Switzerland marks go from 1 to 6, with 6 being the best mark. If Lena has the marks 4.5, 5 and 5.5 and wants an average of 5.25 after four tests, she needs 21 points in total. She already has 15, so she still needs a 6. Calculations like this help you plan your own goals. The **average mark** is one of the best-known examples of a mean.

The **Federal Statistical Office** is based in Neuchâtel. It publishes figures on population, the economy, the environment, health and education. In the past the population was counted every ten years in a big census. Since 2010 mainly the data from population registers has been used, supplemented with samples. Weather services, hospitals and sports clubs also work with statistics every day.

begriffe.erklaerung: Collected information, usually numbers.
The value exactly in the middle of an ordered list.
A number that shows how far the values are, on average, from the mean.
A value that is much larger or smaller than all the others.
A small selection of people who are asked, instead of asking everyone.

gewusst: The word statistics comes from the Latin word for state, because in the past it was mainly states that counted their inhabitants and their wealth.
With a well-chosen sample of a few thousand people, you can estimate fairly accurately what a whole country thinks.
The variance is the square of the standard deviation.

teile.einleitung: An oblique drawing is a drawing that makes a three-dimensional solid such as a cube or cuboid look as if it has depth. To do this, the edges that run backwards are drawn at a slant and shortened. In this way you can show a solid on flat paper that seems to have depth.
wichtigste: An oblique drawing shows a three-dimensional solid on a flat surface.
The front face is drawn at its true size.
In school oblique drawings, the edges running backwards are usually drawn at 45°.
These depth edges are usually shortened to half their length.
Edges that you cannot actually see are drawn as dashed lines.
Parallel edges of the solid stay parallel in the oblique drawing too.
In the usual oblique drawing of a cube, 3 edges are hidden.

abschnitte.text: An **oblique drawing** is a special way of drawing solids. It shows the front, one side face and the top face at the same time. This makes the solid look three-dimensional, even though the paper is flat. At school this method is used mainly for cubes, cuboids and prisms.

The **front face** is drawn at its true size, that is exactly as big as it really is. The edges that lead backwards are called **depth edges**. They are drawn at an angle of 45° and shortened to half their length. So a cube with an edge length of 4 cm gets depth edges 2 cm long.

On a real cube you cannot see all the edges. In an oblique drawing the **hidden edges** are drawn anyway, but as dashed lines. In the usual oblique drawing of a cube there are 3 of them, meeting at the back bottom corner. This helps you understand how the whole solid is built.

Parallel edges stay **parallel** in an oblique drawing. That is why the square top face of a cube appears as a **parallelogram**, and so does the side face. Only the front and back faces keep their real shape. Because of the shortening, you cannot measure lengths going backwards directly with a ruler.

First you draw the front face, ideally on squared paper. Then from each corner you draw the depth edges at a slant towards the back; on squared paper this works well diagonally through the boxes. After that you join the back ends to make the back face. Finally the invisible edges are drawn in as dashed lines.

Experts distinguish between different **parallel projections**. If the depth is shortened to half, it is called cabinet projection; without shortening it is called cavalier projection. Architects and engineers also use plans and elevations, or central perspective, in which lines meet at a vanishing point. Today computer programs create such views at the touch of a button.

begriffe.erklaerung: A three-dimensional shape such as a cube, cuboid or sphere.
An edge that runs backwards in the drawing.
A quadrilateral in which opposite sides are parallel.
A way of drawing in which parallel lines stay parallel in the picture.

gewusst: A cube has 12 edges, 8 vertices and 6 faces, all of which can be found in the oblique drawing.
In old pictures from the Middle Ages, houses and tables often look strangely slanted, because the rules of perspective were not yet properly known.
Shortening the depth edges makes sure a cube does not look stretched out too long.

teile.einleitung: The metre is the most important unit for measuring length. With it you measure, for example, how tall a person is or how long a classroom is. It is shortened to m and is used in science all over the world.
wichtigste: The metre is the basic unit of length, shortened to m.
One metre has 100 centimetres, shortened to cm.
Half a metre is 50 centimetres.
1 metre and 20 centimetres together make 120 centimetres.
1000 metres make one kilometre.
The metre was introduced in France at the end of the 18th century.
Today the metre is defined using the speed of light.

abschnitte.text: The **metre** is the basic unit of length in the International System of Units. One metre is about as long as a big step taken by an adult. In metres you can easily measure things like the length of a classroom, the wall of a house or a running track. Small things are measured in centimetres, long distances in kilometres.

One metre has 10 decimetres, 100 **centimetres** or 1000 millimetres. So 3 metres are 300 centimetres, and 200 centimetres are 2 metres. 1000 metres make one **kilometre**. The prefixes come from Latin and Greek: “centi” means a hundredth, “kilo” means a thousand.

In the past every region had its own measures of length, such as the ell, the foot or the fathom, which caused a lot of confusion in trade. At the time of the French Revolution, in the 1790s, the metre was invented in France. It was meant to be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator. Later a **standard metre** made of metal was kept near Paris, and all other measuring rods were made to match it.

Since 1983 the metre has been defined using light. One metre is the distance that **light** travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. That sounds complicated, but it has an advantage: every well-equipped laboratory in the world can measure the metre exactly in this way. A metal rod, on the other hand, could change or be damaged.

Switzerland introduced the **metric system** in the 1870s. For measuring, people in Switzerland often use a folding ruler, the **Doppelmeter** (two-metre folding rule), or a tape measure. Signposts for hiking paths usually show times, road signs show kilometres. The height of mountains is given in metres above sea level; the Dufourspitze, for example, is 4634 metres high.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed quantity used for measuring, for example the metre or the kilogram.
One hundredth of a metre, shortened to cm.
1000 metres, shortened to km.
A former metal rod that was exactly one metre long and served as the model.

gewusst: The word metre comes from the Greek word “metron”, which means “measure”.
Only very few countries, including the USA, still mainly use feet and miles in everyday life.
Today a metre is defined more precisely than ever before, namely by the speed of light.

teile.einleitung: Calculating with hundreds means calculating with numbers such as 300, 600 or 900. The trick is simple: you calculate with small numbers and add two zeros at the end. This turns a big problem into an easy one, and you can count confidently up to 1000.
wichtigste: Hundreds numbers are whole hundreds such as 100, 200, 300 up to 1000.
For 600 + 200, the small sum 6 + 2 = 8 helps, so the result is 800.
For 900 − 500 you work out 9 − 5 = 4 and get 400.
10 hundreds together make a thousand: 400 + 600 = 1000.
From 700 to 1000, 300 are missing.
Hundreds help with shopping, estimating and calculating with money.

abschnitte.text: A **hundred** is a number with the value 100. Whole hundreds numbers such as 300 or 800 are made only of hundreds and therefore have a zero in the units and tens places. In the **place value chart**, the hundreds digit is on the far left in three-digit numbers. 10 hundreds make 1 **thousand**.

abschnitte.titel: The trick with the small sum
abschnitte.text: For 300 + 400 you think of 3 hundreds plus 4 hundreds. That is 7 hundreds, so 700. The **small sum** 3 + 4 = 7 helps here; you just have to add the two zeros back on. In the same way 900 − 500 gives the same as 9 − 5, only in hundreds, so 400.

The number 1000 is especially important. 400 + 600 gives exactly 1000, because 4 + 6 = 10. If you ask how much is missing from 700 to 1000, the answer is 300. This is called **completing** to the thousand. Backwards: 1000 − 200 = 800.

A bike for 400 francs and a helmet for 100 francs cost 500 francs together. You can add three numbers like this too: 200 + 300 + 100 = 600. In Switzerland there is even a **hundred-franc note** with 100 francs printed on it. When **estimating**, people often round prices to hundreds to see quickly whether they have enough money.

Materials such as hundred squares, showing 100 small cubes, help with learning. A **number line** up to 1000 also shows well how the hundreds follow one another. With play money you can count and exchange hundred-franc notes. If you are confident calculating with hundreds, you can easily go on later to thousands and millions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A quantity of exactly 100; the third place from the right.
The value of a digit, depending on the place where it stands.
Finding out how much is missing up to a certain number.
Calculating roughly and quickly to get an approximate result.

gewusst: The German word “hundert” is ancient and has relatives in many languages, such as “hundred” in English.
A hundred-franc note changed into 1-centime coins would be 10,000 coins, even though the 1-centime coin is no longer legal tender today.

teile.einleitung: In mathematics and physics a vector is a quantity that has not only a size but also a direction. It is drawn as an arrow: the length shows how big it is, and the tip shows where it points. Vectors are used to describe movements, forces, velocities and much more.
wichtigste: A vector has a length and a direction.
It is shown as an arrow or with coordinates, for example (2 | 3 | 6).
The length is calculated with Pythagoras’ theorem.
You get the vector from A to B by subtracting A from B.
If the dot product of two vectors is zero, they are perpendicular to each other.
The cross product is perpendicular to both original vectors.
In physics, force and velocity are typical vectors.

abschnitte.text: A **vector** describes a movement with a length and a direction. All arrows that are the same length, parallel and pointing the same way represent the same vector. In contrast, a **scalar** such as temperature or mass has only a numerical value. So a vector is more than a number; it also says where something is going.

In a coordinate system a vector is written with its **coordinates**, for example (3 | −4). The vector from A(1 | 2) to B(4 | −2) is (3 | −4), because you work out tip minus tail. You find the midpoint of a line segment by averaging the coordinates of the end points: between A(2 | 4) and B(6 | −2) it is at (4 | 1). Vectors such as (−3 | 6) and (2 | −4) are **collinear**, because one is a multiple of the other.

The **length** or **magnitude** of a vector is calculated with Pythagoras’ theorem. For (2 | 3 | 6) you work out the square root of 4 + 9 + 36 = 49 and get 7. The **dot product** multiplies the coordinates in pairs and adds them up; for (1 | 2 | 3) and (4 | −5 | 6) this gives 4 minus 10 plus 18 = 12. The dot product is also used to calculate angles; for example (1 | 0) and (1 | 1) enclose an angle of 45 degrees.

In three-dimensional space there is also the **cross product**, sometimes called the vector product. It gives a new vector that is perpendicular to both original vectors. Its length equals the area of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors. Physicists need it, for example, for rotational movements and magnetic fields.

Many physical quantities are vectors, such as **force**, velocity or acceleration. If two forces of 30 newtons and 40 newtons pull at right angles on a point, the result is a total force of 50 newtons. Wind also has a strength and a direction, which is why weather maps often show it as arrows. Vector calculation was developed in the 19th century by mathematicians such as Hermann Grassmann and William Rowan Hamilton.

begriffe.erklaerung: The length of a vector.
A quantity that consists only of a number, without a direction.
Numbers that say how far a vector goes in the direction of each axis.
A calculation with two vectors whose result is a number.
Two vectors are collinear if they are parallel.

gewusst: The word vector comes from the Latin “vehere” and means roughly carrier or driver.
Satnavs and computer games calculate with vectors all the time.
The zero vector is the only vector without a direction.

teile.einleitung: Doubling means taking a number twice; halving means dividing it into two equal parts. The two calculations are opposites: what you have doubled you can undo by halving. They are among the most important tricks in mental arithmetic.
wichtigste: Doubling means multiplying by 2.
Halving means dividing by 2.
Doubling and halving are inverse operations.
Double 7 is 14, and half of 18 is 9.
Large numbers are best doubled in parts, for example tens and units separately.
Only even numbers can be halved into two whole numbers without a remainder.
The ancient Egyptians multiplied by doubling.

abschnitte.text: When **doubling** you take a number twice, so you work out the number plus itself. Double 25 is 50, double 250 is 500. When **halving** you share an amount fairly into two equal parts. Half of 300 is 150, half of 70 is 35.

Doubling and halving undo each other; they are **inverse operations**. If you double 9, you get 18; if you halve 18 again, you are back at 9. That is why you can check any halving problem with a doubling. Mia has 12 francs, Tim has twice as much, so 24 francs, and half of Tim’s money is 12 again.

Larger numbers are doubled in parts: for 45 you work out 40 plus 40 = 80 and 5 plus 5 = 10, which makes 90 together. Halving works the same way: half of 70 is half of 60 plus half of 10, that is 30 + 5 = 35. This also helps with multiplication: 4 times a number is double the double. For 5 times, you first work out 10 times and then **halve** it.

Numbers that can be halved without a remainder are called **even numbers**, for example 2, 4, 6 and 8. With odd numbers such as 7 there is a remainder when halving, or you get a half number, namely 3.5. Double any whole number is always even. A cake with 8 slices can therefore be halved fairly, leaving 4 slices in each half.

More than 3500 years ago the ancient Egyptians multiplied only by doubling and adding, as the **Rhind Papyrus** shows. Computers calculate in the binary system, in which doubling is especially simple. In everyday life you halve a recipe for fewer people or double it for a party. When sharing between two brothers or sisters, too, you halve, so that both get the same amount.

begriffe.erklaerung: The result of multiplying a number by 2.
One of two equal parts.
A number that can be divided by 2 without a remainder.
A calculation that undoes another one.

gewusst: If you fold a sheet of paper, its thickness doubles with every fold.
After doubling ten times, 1 has already become 1024.
One grain of wheat on the first square of a chessboard, two on the second and so on would in the end give more grain than there is in the world.

teile.einleitung: In geometry a line is a stroke that has only length but no width. Lines can be straight or curved, open or closed. Letters, digits and all the shapes we draw are made of lines.
wichtigste: Lines can be straight or curved.
The letter E consists only of straight lines.
The letter C consists of only one curved line.
The digit 2 has straight and curved lines.
A semicircle consists of one straight and one curved line.
For a triangle you need at least 3 straight lines.
The line of a circle is closed; it has no beginning and no end.

abschnitte.text: A **line** is a stroke that you draw, for example, with a pencil. In mathematics you imagine that it has no width at all, only length. More than 2000 years ago the Greek mathematician Euclid described a line as “breadthless length”. Drawn lines are of course always a little wide, so that you can see them.

A **straight line** has the same direction everywhere and does not turn anywhere. It is best drawn with a ruler. In geometry a distinction is made between the line segment with two end points, the ray with only one starting point and the straight line that goes on infinitely in both directions. The letters E, H and T, as well as triangles and squares, are made of straight lines.

A **curved line** keeps changing its direction. The letter C and the letter O consist only of curves. A **wavy line** swings gently up and down; a zigzag line goes up and down with sharp corners. Some shapes mix both: the digit 2 has a curve at the top and a straight stroke at the bottom, and a semicircle has a curve and a straight side.

A line is **closed** if its end meets its beginning again, as with a circle or the edge of a triangle. A closed line surrounds an area that you can colour in. An open line has a beginning and an end that do not meet, as with the letter C or a wavy line. A triangle needs at least 3 straight lines; with 2 you cannot enclose an area.

On roads, white and yellow **markings** show where cars may drive and where the zebra crossing is. On maps, lines show borders, rivers and footpaths. In sport, lines mark out the pitch, for example in football or tennis. Exercise books have lines too, so that writing turns out nice and straight.

begriffe.erklaerung: A straight piece of line with a start point and an end point.
A straight line without beginning or end that goes on infinitely.
A line that bends gently up and down.
A line whose end arrives back at its beginning, as with a circle.

gewusst: You cannot draw the German puzzle figure “Haus vom Nikolaus” as a single closed line, but you can draw it in one go as an open line.
The yellow line on Swiss railway platforms shows where you must stay behind when a train comes in.
A line drawn with a sharpened pencil can be many kilometres long before the lead is used up.

teile.einleitung: “Multiplication and division before addition and subtraction” is one of the most important rules in arithmetic. It says that you multiply and divide before you add and subtract. Without this rule, the same calculation could give completely different results depending on who works it out.
wichtigste: Times (·) and divided by (:) are called “dot operations” in German, because their signs contain dots.
Plus (+) and minus (-) are called “line operations”, because their signs are made of lines.
Multiplication and division are done before addition and subtraction: 3 + 4 · 5 = 23.
Brackets are always worked out first: (3 + 4) · 5 = 35.
If there are only multiplications and divisions, or only additions and subtractions, you work from left to right.
The rule applies worldwide so that everyone understands the same calculation in the same way.
Modern calculators follow the rule automatically.

abschnitte.text: The rule says that **multiplication and division** come first. Only after that do you do **addition and subtraction**. So for 3 + 4 · 5 you first work out 4 · 5 = 20 and then 3 + 20 = 23. For 20 − 12 : 4 you first work out 12 : 4 = 3 and then 20 − 3 = 17.

If you want a different order, you use **brackets**. Whatever is in brackets is always calculated first. So (3 + 4) · 5 does not give 23 but 7 · 5 = 35. With 48 : (2 + 6), too, you work out the bracket first and get 48 : 8 = 6.

If there are only multiplications and divisions in a row, you work from **left to right**. That is why 60 : 5 · 2 first gives 12 and then 24, and not 60 : 10 = 6. The same applies to calculations with only addition and subtraction, such as 20 − 5 + 3, which gives 18. This rule prevents many mistakes.

With long problems you go step by step: first brackets, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. For 100 − 4 · (7 + 8) you work out 7 + 8 = 15, then 4 · 15 = 60 and finally 100 − 60 = 40. For 7 · 8 − 6 · 5 you work out both products, so 56 − 30 = 26. And 2 · (15 − 3 · 4) + 9 gives 2 · 3 + 9 = 15.

Mathematics is a language that should be understood the same way all over the world. Without a fixed order, 3 + 4 · 5 could give 35 one time and 23 another. The rule developed over centuries together with today’s **way of writing formulas**. Later it was added that **powers** such as 3² are calculated even before multiplication and division.

begriffe.erklaerung: Calculations with · or :, called “dot operations” in German.
Calculations with + or -, called “line operations” in German.
Signs that enclose part of a calculation, which is worked out first.
An expression made of numbers, operation signs and sometimes variables.

gewusst: In English there are memory words such as “PEMDAS” or “BODMAS” that describe the same order.
Simple calculators that only work from left to right give the wrong answer 35 for 3 + 4 · 5.
On the internet, puzzles involving the order of operations regularly cause heated arguments, because many people have forgotten the rule.

teile.einleitung: The Pythagorean theorem is one of the most famous theorems in mathematics. It says: in a right-angled triangle, a² + b² = c². With it you can calculate missing side lengths without measuring them.
wichtigste: The theorem only applies to right-angled triangles.
The longest side, opposite the right angle, is called the hypotenuse; the other two are the legs.
The formula is a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse.
With legs of 6 cm and 8 cm, the hypotenuse is 10 cm long.
Three whole numbers such as 3, 4, 5 or 8, 15, 17 are called a Pythagorean triple.
The theorem is used to calculate diagonals and distances in a coordinate system.
It is named after the Greek scholar Pythagoras of Samos.

abschnitte.text: In every **right-angled triangle** the longest side, the **hypotenuse** c, lies opposite the right angle. The two shorter sides a and b are called the **legs**. The theorem says: a² + b² = c². If you draw a square on each side, the two small squares together are exactly as big as the large one.

If the legs are 6 cm and 8 cm long, then 36 + 64 = 100, so the hypotenuse measures 10 cm. If you know the hypotenuse and one leg, you work backwards: with 13 cm and 5 cm, the other leg is √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12 cm. A 5 m ladder whose foot stands 1.4 m from the wall reaches 4.8 m high. Often you get square roots that are not whole numbers.

The diagonal divides a square into two right-angled triangles. With a side length of 5 cm it is √50 = 5√2 cm long, about 7.1 cm. In a cube with an edge of 3 cm, the **space diagonal** measures 3√3 cm. You can also find the distance between the points (1|2) and (4|6) in a coordinate system like this: 3² + 4² = 25, so the distance is 5.

Sometimes all three sides are whole numbers, for example 3, 4, 5, because 9 + 16 = 25. Such numbers are called **Pythagorean triples**. Other examples are 5, 12, 13 and 8, 15, 17. A Babylonian clay tablet called **Plimpton 322**, which is about 3800 years old, already lists numbers from such triples.

**Pythagoras** lived in the 6th century BC and came from the Greek island of Samos. Later he founded a community in southern Italy that studied numbers, music and philosophy. But the Babylonians and Indians knew the theorem long before him. Whether Pythagoras proved it himself is not certain, but it bears his name.

Craftspeople and builders use the triple 3, 4, 5 to check whether a corner is exactly a right angle. Screen sizes are given by the diagonal, which can be worked out with the Pythagorean theorem. Satnavs and computer games also use it to calculate distances. For triangles without a right angle there is an extension in the **law of cosines**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The longest side in a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.
One of the two sides that form the right angle.
An angle of exactly 90 degrees, like the corner of a room.
Three whole numbers that satisfy the equation a² + b² = c².

gewusst: Several hundred different proofs of the Pythagorean theorem are known.
