Even a US president, James Garfield, invented his own proof of it.
The followers of Pythagoras are said to have believed that the whole world could be explained with numbers.

teile.einleitung: A swap sum is made when you swap the two numbers in a calculation, for example 3 + 8 and 8 + 3. In addition and multiplication the result stays the same. This simple trick makes many calculations easier.
wichtigste: The swap sum of 3 + 8 is 8 + 3.
In addition the result stays the same if you swap the numbers.
This also applies to multiplication: 3 · 9 and 9 · 3 both give 27.
In subtraction and division you may not swap: 9 − 4 is not 4 − 9.
With swap sums you can calculate more cleverly, for example 49 + 2 instead of 2 + 49.
In mathematics this rule is called the commutative law.

abschnitte.text: In a **swap sum** you swap the two numbers in a calculation. 3 + 8 becomes 8 + 3, and 4 · 7 becomes 7 · 4. The two calculations form a pair, like 5 + 7 and 7 + 5. With plus and times, both sums always have the same result.

Whether you first put 3 apples and then 8 apples into a basket or the other way round, in the end there are always 11 apples. That is why, in **addition**, the result stays the same. This helps with calculating, because 49 + 2 is much easier than 2 + 49. It is best to start with the bigger number and add the smaller one.

You can also swap when **multiplying**. An egg box with 2 rows of 6 eggs contains 12 eggs. If you turn it round, you see 6 rows of 2 eggs; there are still 12, so 6 · 2 = 2 · 6. If you know 3 · 9 = 27, you therefore know straight away that 9 · 3 = 27 too, and you only have to learn half as many times tables by heart.

In **subtraction** and division you may not swap. 9 − 4 gives 5, but 4 − 9 gives -5, a negative number. 8 : 2 gives 4, but 2 : 8 gives only a quarter. So you always have to look carefully at which operation you are dealing with.

In mathematics the rule of swap sums is called the **commutative law**, from the Latin word “commutare” for to swap. It is written with letters as a + b = b + a and a · b = b · a. Together with other laws of arithmetic such as the associative law, it forms the basis of algebra. Children usually learn about swap sums in their first or second year at school.

begriffe.erklaerung: A calculation in which the two numbers have been swapped.
The rule that you may swap the numbers in addition and multiplication.
Plus sums, that is putting numbers together.
Times sums, that is adding a number to itself several times.

gewusst: In everyday life swapping does not always work: putting on socks and then shoes is something different from shoes first and then socks.
Thanks to swap sums you only really need to learn just over half of the 100 sums in the times tables by heart.

teile.einleitung: Ordinal numbers show the position of something in an order, for example first, second or third. You need them for rankings, dates, floors and queues. In German they are written with digits and a full stop after them, such as “3.” for “dritte” (third).
wichtigste: Ordinal numbers give a position in an order.
Cardinal numbers such as one, two, three, on the other hand, say how many there are.
In German ordinal numbers are written with a full stop, for example “1.” for “erste” (first).
March is the third month, December the twelfth.
In Switzerland Monday is the first day of the week.
If you stand behind three children in a queue, you are fourth.
After “der Neunte” (the ninth) comes “der Zehnte” (the tenth).

abschnitte.text: An **ordinal number** answers the question “which place?”. It shows where something stands, for example in a race: if Lena runs ahead of Sara and Sara ahead of Tom, Lena comes first, Sara second and Tom third. Experts also say **ordinal**. In contrast, **cardinal numbers** such as three or ten say how many things there are. Five children is an amount; the fifth child is a place in the line.

In German, ordinal numbers in digits are written with a full stop: “der 1. August” is read as “der erste August” (the first of August). Up to 19, most German ordinal numbers are formed with the ending “-te”, so “der vierte”, “der neunte”. From 20 onwards you add “-ste”, for example “der zwanzigste” or “der hundertste”. Irregular ones are “erste”, “dritte” and partly “siebte”. German ordinal numbers change their endings like adjectives, so “der zweite Platz” and “am zweiten Tag”. In English you write endings such as 1st, 2nd and 3rd instead of the full stop.

Months and days of the week have a fixed order. March is the third month, December the twelfth and last. According to the international standard, which also applies in Switzerland, **Monday** is the first day of the week. Centuries are also counted with ordinal numbers: we live in the 21st century. For dates you write, for example, “17 October”, which means the seventeenth day of October.

With rows it pays to think carefully. If 5 children stand in a row and Ella is second from the front, then she is fourth from the back. The rule is: place from the front plus place from the back equals the number of children plus 1. If 3 children are ahead of you at the till, you are fourth in the queue. In the alphabet, too, every letter has its place: D is the fourth letter.

Ordinal numbers are everywhere: for floors such as the 3rd floor, for rankings in sport and for **school years** such as the 5th class. In ski races and at the Federal Wrestling Festival (Eidgenössisches Schwingfest), the places are given with ordinal numbers. Kings and popes also have ordinal numbers in their names, such as Louis XIV, read as “the Fourteenth”.

In chemistry the German word Ordnungszahl has a meaning of its own: the atomic number. It shows how many **protons** an atom has in its nucleus and fixes its place in the periodic table. Hydrogen, for example, has the atomic number 1, carbon the atomic number 6. In higher mathematics, Georg Cantor even studied ordinal numbers beyond infinity. In everyday life, though, an ordinal number almost always means the number for a place.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that gives a place in an order.
A number that gives an amount, for example three apples.
A list showing who reached which place.
The technical term for ordinal number.

gewusst: On 1 August Switzerland celebrates its national day, written in German with an ordinal number as “1. August”.
In German “erste” (first) is irregular; you do not say “einte”.
Roman numerals in names such as Elizabeth II are read as an ordinal number, so “the Second”.

teile.einleitung: Modular arithmetic is calculating with remainders. Instead of counting on for ever, you start again from the beginning after a certain number, just like the hands of a clock. This “clock arithmetic” is found in calendars, check digits and encryption on the internet.
wichtigste: In modular arithmetic you calculate only with the remainders of a division.
17 mod 5 is 2, because 17 divided by 5 gives 3 remainder 2.
The clock is an example: after 24 hours the counting starts again at 0.
Days of the week also repeat with the modulus 7.
If the modulus is a prime number, every number from 1 to m−1 has a multiplicative inverse.
The check digits of an IBAN, including a Swiss IBAN, are calculated with the modulus 97.
In 1801 Carl Friedrich Gauss introduced the notation used today.

abschnitte.text: It is 9 o'clock, and you want to know what time it will be in 30 hours. 9 + 30 makes 39, but after 24 hours the day starts again. 39 minus 24 gives **15:00**. That is exactly modular arithmetic: you calculate modulo 24 and keep only the **remainder**. With a clock face you even calculate modulo 12.

The notation **a mod m** means: divide a by m and take the remainder. 17 mod 5 gives 2, because 17 = 3 · 5 + 2. The number m is called the **modulus**. Two numbers are called congruent modulo m if they leave the same remainder when divided by m, for example 17 and 2 modulo 5. You can add, subtract and multiply with remainders and still get correct remainders.

The week has 7 days, which is why you calculate modulo 7 with days of the week. Today is Monday, so what about in 100 days? 100 divided by 7 gives 14 remainder 2, so two days after Monday it is a **Wednesday**. Last digits are remainders too, namely modulo 10. Because 7 to the power 4 equals 2401 and ends in 1, 7 to the power 100 also ends in 1. You get the remainder when dividing by 9 from the digit sum: 123456 has the digit sum 21 and so leaves the remainder 3.

Scholars in ancient China and India were already calculating with remainders, for example in the **Chinese remainder theorem**. The modern form comes from **Carl Friedrich Gauss**, who published his famous book “Disquisitiones Arithmeticae” in 1801. In it he introduced the sign ≡ for “congruent”. Gauss was only 24 years old at the time. His ideas are still the foundation of number theory today.

The **IBAN**, the international bank account number, contains two check digits that are calculated with the modulus 97. That way a bank notices straight away if someone has mistyped a digit. There are similar check digits in barcodes and book numbers. Encryption on the internet, such as the **RSA** method, calculates with huge numbers modulo a number. Even the simple Caesar cipher shifts letters modulo 26.

In normal arithmetic every number except 0 has a reciprocal; for example, 1/3 is the reciprocal of 3. Modulo m you look instead for a number that, multiplied by 3, gives the remainder 1. Modulo 7 that is 5, because 3 · 5 = 15 leaves the remainder 1 when divided by 7. 5 is called the **multiplicative inverse** of 3 modulo 7. If the modulus is a prime number, there is such an inverse for every number from 1 to m−1.

begriffe.erklaerung: What is left over in a division with whole numbers.
The number after which you start again from the beginning when calculating.
Two numbers leave the same remainder when divided by the modulus.
An extra digit used to spot typing mistakes in numbers.

gewusst: You can tell whether a number can be divided by 9 from its digit sum; that is modular arithmetic.
The mileometer of an old car that jumps back to 0 after 99,999 calculates modulo 100,000.
The encryption in online banking is based on calculations with remainders of very large numbers.

teile.einleitung: Multiplying and dividing by 10 are among the simplest and most useful calculations there are. When you multiply by 10, you simply add a zero. When you divide by 10, you take away a zero or move the decimal point one place to the left.
wichtigste: Multiplying by 10 means a zero is added at the end: 7 becomes 70.
Dividing by 10 means a zero is taken away: 90 becomes 9.
Each digit moves one place to the left or right in the place value table.
Our number system is called the decimal system because 10 units always make a bigger one.
1 franc has 100 centimes, that is 10 ten-centime coins.
Multiplying and dividing by 10 are inverse calculations.
With decimals, you move the decimal point.

abschnitte.titel: What happens when you multiply by 10?
abschnitte.text: If you multiply a number **by 10**, it becomes ten times as big. With whole numbers this is very easy to see: a **zero** is added at the end. 6 becomes 60, 7 becomes 70 and 34 becomes 340. 25 times 10 is easy too; it gives 250. So you do not need to calculate for long; you just add the zero.

abschnitte.titel: What happens when you divide by 10?
abschnitte.text: If you divide a number **by 10**, it becomes ten times smaller. With numbers that end in zero, you simply take that zero away. 90 divided by 10 gives 9, and 500 divided by 10 gives 50. Multiplying and dividing by 10 are **inverse calculations**: what one does, the other undoes. So from 9 times 10 = 90 it follows at once that 90 divided by 10 = 9.

The trick works because we calculate in the **decimal system**. 10 ones make a ten, 10 tens a hundred and 10 hundreds a thousand. In the **place value table**, when multiplying by 10, each digit moves one place to the left. So 3 tens and 4 ones, that is 34, become 3 hundreds and 4 tens, that is 340. When dividing by 10, each digit moves one place to the right.

For 80 francs you need 8 ten-franc notes, because 80 divided by 10 is 8. If a pack has 10 coloured pencils, 6 packs contain 60 pencils. If you share 1 franc, that is 100 **centimes**, fairly among 10 children, each gets 10 centimes. It helps with units too: 1 centimetre is 10 millimetres, so 7 cm is exactly 70 mm. And 1 decilitre is 10 centilitres.

With decimals you do not add a zero; you move the **decimal point**. If you work out 2.5 times 10, the point moves one place to the right, and it gives 25. If you divide 7 by 10, you get 0.7, so the point moves to the left. It works the same way with 100 or 1000, only then it is two or three places. That way you can easily work out 4 times 100 = 400 and 3000 divided by 1000 = 3 in your head.

begriffe.erklaerung: A table with columns for ones, tens, hundreds and so on.
A number system in which 10 units always make one unit of the next level.
A calculation that undoes another, such as dividing by 10 after multiplying by 10.
The sign in a number that separates the whole parts from the tenths.

gewusst: We probably calculate in the decimal system because humans have ten fingers.
The number 1 followed by a hundred zeros is called a googol.
Adding a zero only works with whole numbers: 2.5 times 10 would not be 2.50.

teile.einleitung: “Doubles plus one” is a trick for mental arithmetic. For sums such as 6 + 7, where the numbers are right next to each other, you work out 6 + 6 and add 1 more. This makes difficult addition sums really easy.
wichtigste: The trick helps with sums of two neighbouring numbers such as 6 + 7.
You double the smaller number and add 1.
So 8 + 9 becomes 8 + 8 + 1 = 17.
You can also double the larger number and then subtract 1.
The trick also works with big numbers such as 50 + 51 = 101.
The strategy is also called near doubles.
If you know the doubles by heart, you can calculate especially fast with it.

abschnitte.text: Many children know doubles such as 6 + 6 = 12 very well by heart. These **doubles** are a great help for harder sums. If two numbers are right next to each other, such as 6 and 7, the sum is almost a double. You work out 6 + 6 + 1 and get 13.
First you find the smaller of the two numbers. Then you **double** it. Finally you add 1, because the other number is 1 bigger. For 8 + 9 this means: 8 + 8 = 16, plus 1 gives 17.
It also works the other way round. For 7 + 8 you can work out 8 + 8 = 16 and then **take away 1**, which gives 15. Both ways lead to the same result. Each child can choose the way they find easier.

The trick does not only work with numbers up to 20. For 25 + 26 you work out 25 + 25 = 50 plus 1, so 51. For 40 + 41, 40 + 40 helps, and 15 + 16 gives 31. 50 + 51 = 101 is also quickly solved this way.

Tricks like this are among the **calculation strategies** learned in primary school. They help you not to count laboriously but to build cleverly on sums you already know. This makes **mental arithmetic** faster and more reliable. There are similar tricks for sums such as 6 + 8, that is doubles plus two.

begriffe.erklaerung: Adding a number to itself, that is multiplying by 2.
Two numbers that differ by only 1, such as 7 and 8.
A clever way of solving a problem more easily.
Calculating without paper and without a calculator.

gewusst: The sum of two neighbouring numbers is always an odd number.
With the fingers of both hands you can see doubles up to 5 + 5 very well.
Many adults use this trick in mental arithmetic without consciously knowing it.

teile.einleitung: Thales’ theorem is one of the oldest theorems in geometry. It states: if the point C lies on a circle with the diameter AB, then the triangle ABC always has a right angle of 90° at C. It is named after the Greek scholar Thales of Miletus.
wichtigste: Every angle over a diameter of a circle whose vertex lies on the circle is a right angle.
The circle over the line segment AB is called the Thales circle.
The theorem is named after Thales of Miletus, who lived around 600 BC.
In a right-angled triangle the centre of the circumcircle lies at the midpoint of the hypotenuse.
The Thales circle is used to construct tangents from an outside point to a circle.
If C lies inside the circle, the angle at C is greater than 90°; if C lies outside, it is smaller.
The inscribed angle theorem extends Thales’ theorem to any chord.

abschnitte.text: If you draw a circle and a **diameter** AB inside it, you can choose any point C on the edge of the circle. If you join C to A and B, you get a triangle. The angle at C is then always exactly **90°**, no matter where C lies on the circle. If, for example, the angle at A is 35°, the angle at B must be 55°, because the angles in a triangle add up to 180°.

The proof is surprisingly simple. You join C to the **centre** M of the circle. MA, MB and MC are all the same length, namely the radius. This creates two isosceles triangles, each with two equal angles. Together the angles add up to 180°, and the angle at C is exactly half of that, so 90°.

If C does not lie on the circle but **inside** it, the angle ACB becomes greater than 90°, that is obtuse. If C lies outside the circle, it becomes smaller than 90°, that is acute. The reverse is also true: every right-angled triangle fits into a circle so that the longest side, the **hypotenuse**, is a diameter. That is why the centre of the circumcircle lies exactly at the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

With the Thales circle you can construct right angles using compasses and a ruler. It is very often used to draw **tangents** from a point outside a circle to that circle. A practical trick: if you place the right-angled corner of a set square on the edge of a round plate, the points where its sides cross the edge are joined by a diameter. In this way you can also find the centre of the plate.

**Thales** lived from about 624 to 546 BC in Miletus, a Greek city on the west coast of present-day Turkey. He is regarded as one of the first philosophers and mathematicians of Greece. According to tradition he predicted a solar eclipse and worked out the height of the pyramids using their shadows. Whether he proved the theorem himself is not certain; the Babylonians may have known it earlier.

Thales’ theorem is a special case of the **inscribed angle theorem**. This says that all angles over the same chord of a circle are equal if their vertex lies on the same arc. If the chord is a diameter, these angles are exactly 90°. Together with the Pythagorean theorem, Thales’ theorem is one of the basic building blocks of school geometry.

begriffe.erklaerung: A line through the centre that joins two points on the edge of the circle.
A circle drawn with a line segment as its diameter, on which all points form right angles.
The longest side in a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.
A straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point.

gewusst: Thales is regarded as one of the “Seven Sages” of ancient Greece.
You can use Thales’ theorem to mark out an exact right angle on a meadow with a piece of string and two pegs.
Miletus is no longer by the sea today, because over centuries the river Maeander filled the bay with mud.

teile.einleitung: A magic square is a square of numbers in which every row, every column and both diagonals add up to the same sum. That sounds like magic, but it is pure mathematics. For thousands of years people in China, India, Arabia and Europe have puzzled over such number riddles.
wichtigste: In a magic square the sum is the same in every row, every column and both diagonals.
This shared sum is called the magic number or magic constant.
A 3×3 square has 9 squares and is often filled with the numbers 1 to 9.
With the numbers 1 to 9 each row makes 15, and the 5 is always in the middle.
Every magic square has exactly 2 diagonals.
The oldest known magic square is the Chinese Lo Shu square.
In 1514 Albrecht Dürer hid a 4×4 square in his engraving “Melencolia I”.

abschnitte.text: A magic square has the same number of rows and columns, for example 3 by 3 or 4 by 4. A number goes into each square. If you add up the numbers in a row, a column or a **diagonal**, the same result always comes out. This sum is called the **magic number**. In a “normal” magic square, every number from 1 up to the number of squares appears exactly once.

The best-known magic square has 9 squares with the numbers 1 to 9. Because 1 + 2 + ... + 9 makes 45 altogether and this sum is shared among 3 rows, each row must make 15. The **5**, the middle number from 1 to 9, is always in the centre. One possible solution has the rows 2, 7, 6, then 9, 5, 1 and at the bottom 4, 3, 8. All the other 3×3 solutions come from this one by turning or reflecting, so there are exactly 8 versions.

The oldest known magic square is the **Lo Shu square** from China. According to legend, long ago a turtle climbed out of the river Lo with patterns of dots on its shell. These patterns made a 3×3 square with the sum 15. Later, scholars in India and in the Arab world also knew magic squares and wrote books about them.

In 1514 the German artist **Albrecht Dürer** made the famous engraving “Melencolia I”. In it, a 4×4 square with the numbers 1 to 16 and the magic number 34 hangs on a wall. In the bottom row, the middle numbers are 15 and 14, the year it was made, 1514. A number square can also be seen on the church of the **Sagrada Família** in Barcelona; there every row makes 33.

For a normal magic square with n rows there is a formula for the magic number: n times (n times n plus 1) divided by 2. For n = 3 this gives 15, for n = 4 it gives 34 and for n = 5 already 65. The bigger the square, the more solutions there are. For 4×4 there are already 880 different magic squares, if you do not count turned and reflected ones twice. If you are looking for a missing number yourself, you simply subtract the known numbers from the magic number.

Magic squares are popular puzzles in school books and magazines. If a row with the sum 15 is missing its third number next to 9 and 5, you work out 15 minus 14 and get 1. The famous number puzzle **sudoku** works in a similar way, but it does not ask for sums. Anyone who solves magic squares practises mental arithmetic and logical thinking.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sum that every row, column and diagonal makes in a magic square.
A slanting line from one corner of the square to the opposite corner.
An ancient Chinese magic square with the numbers 1 to 9.
A picture cut into a copper plate and then printed on paper.

gewusst: In the 3×3 square with 1 to 9, the even numbers 2, 4, 6 and 8 are always in the corners.
Benjamin Franklin, one of the founding fathers of the USA, invented his own magic squares to pass the time.
There are also magic cubes and magic stars, for which similar rules about sums apply.

teile.einleitung: In mathematics a matrix is a rectangular table of numbers arranged in rows and columns. With matrices you can solve many equations at once, rotate or reflect figures and process large amounts of data. They are a central tool of linear algebra and are found in every piece of computer graphics.
wichtigste: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns.
A matrix with 2 rows and 3 columns has the size 2×3.
A 2×3 matrix times a 3×4 matrix gives a 2×4 matrix.
With matrices, A·B is usually not equal to B·A.
The identity matrix has ones on the main diagonal and zeros everywhere else.
A square matrix has an inverse exactly when its determinant is not 0.
Rotations and reflections can be described with matrices.

abschnitte.text: A **matrix** looks like a table full of numbers. The horizontal lines are called **rows**, the vertical ones columns. If a matrix has 2 rows and 3 columns, it is called a 2×3 matrix. A matrix with as many rows as columns is called square. The plural of matrix is matrices.

In the **matrix product** you multiply each row of the first matrix by each column of the second. For the first entry of [[1, 2], [3, 4]] times [[5, 6], [7, 8]] you work out 1·5 + 2·7 = 19, and the whole result is [[19, 22], [43, 50]]. For this to work, the first matrix must have as many columns as the second has rows. That is why a 2×3 matrix times a 3×4 matrix gives a 2×4 matrix. Unlike with numbers, A·B is usually **not equal** to B·A.

Every square matrix can be given a number, the **determinant**. For a 2×2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] you work it out as a·d−b·c; for [[3, 8], [4, 6]] that gives 18 − 32 = -14. The **identity matrix**, with ones on the main diagonal and zeros everywhere else, behaves like the number 1. If the determinant is not 0, there is an **inverse matrix** that undoes the effect. The inverse of [[2, 1], [1, 1]], for example, is [[1, -1], [-1, 2]].

Matrices can move points in the plane. The matrix [[0, -1], [1, 0]] rotates every point through 90° **anticlockwise** about the origin. So the point (1, 0) becomes the point (0, 1). Other matrices reflect, stretch or distort figures. If you swap the rows and columns of a matrix, you get the **transposed** matrix; a 2×3 matrix becomes a 3×2 matrix.

In an old Chinese arithmetic book, The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, systems of equations were already being solved with tables of numbers. The name matrix was introduced by the English mathematician **James Joseph Sylvester** in 1850. A few years later Arthur Cayley developed the rules for calculating with matrices. Today graphics cards in computer games calculate millions of matrix products every second. Search engines, weather forecasts and **artificial intelligence** also work with huge matrices.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rows are the horizontal lines of a matrix, columns the vertical ones.
A number calculated from a square matrix that tells you a lot about it.
A matrix with ones on the diagonal and zeros everywhere else; it changes nothing.
A matrix that undoes the effect of another matrix.
The branch of mathematics that deals with vectors, matrices and linear equations.

gewusst: A digital photo is really a huge matrix in which each number gives the colour of a pixel.
The determinant of a matrix tells you how much an area is enlarged or reduced when it is transformed.
The 1999 science fiction film The Matrix takes its name from the same word, but the story has little to do with mathematics.

teile.einleitung: Euclid’s theorem states that there are infinitely many prime numbers. The Greek mathematician Euclid proved this around 300 BC with a short and brilliant line of reasoning. His proof is still regarded today as one of the most beautiful examples of mathematical thinking.
wichtigste: Euclid’s theorem says: there are infinitely many prime numbers.
Euclid lived around 300 BC and worked in Alexandria.
The proof appears in Euclid’s famous work, the “Elements”.
The proof is a proof by contradiction using the number N = p₁ · p₂ · … · pₙ + 1.
N leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by every prime number in the list.
N does not have to be a prime number itself: 30031, for example, is divisible by 59.
Leonhard Euler from Basel later found a completely different proof.

abschnitte.text: A **prime number** is a natural number greater than 1 that can only be divided by 1 and itself, such as 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and 13. The larger the numbers get, the rarer prime numbers become. You might therefore suspect that at some point they stop altogether. But **Euclid’s theorem** shows that there is no largest prime number and that the list never ends.

Euclid first assumes the opposite: that there are only finitely many prime numbers p₁, p₂ up to pₙ. Then he multiplies them all together and adds 1, giving the number N. If you divide N by any of these prime numbers, there is always a **remainder of 1**. But every number greater than 1 has at least one prime factor, and this cannot be in the list. That is a **contradiction**, so the assumption was wrong.

If you take the prime numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and 13, their product plus 1 gives the number 30031. This number is not itself a prime number, because 30031 = 59 · 509. Even so, the proof works, because 59 and 509 are new prime numbers missing from the original list. So what matters is not that N is prime, but that every **prime factor** of N is new.

**Euclid** lived around 300 BC in Alexandria in Egypt, which was then a centre of Greek science. Almost nothing is known about his life. His main work, the **“Elements”**, consists of 13 books on geometry and number theory. For more than 2000 years it was the most important maths textbook in the world, and the proof about prime numbers is in the ninth book.

In the 18th century the Basel mathematician **Leonhard Euler** found a completely different approach. He showed that the sum of the reciprocals of all prime numbers, that is 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/5 + 1/7 + ..., becomes infinitely large. That would be impossible if there were only finitely many prime numbers. Today dozens of different proofs of the theorem are known, and the search for ever larger prime numbers continues with computers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A natural number greater than 1 that can only be divided by 1 and itself.
You assume the opposite and show that something impossible follows from it.
A prime number by which another number can be divided without a remainder.
The flipped fraction of a number; for example 1/7 is the reciprocal of 7.

gewusst: The largest known prime numbers have many millions of digits and were found by computers.
Euclid’s “Elements” is one of the most frequently printed books in history.
Although there are infinitely many prime numbers, there are stretches between them of any length in which not a single one occurs.

teile.einleitung: A piggy bank is a money box shaped like a pig, into which you put coins and notes through a slot. Many children use one to save for a bigger wish for the first time. With a piggy bank you learn arithmetic along the way: adding, taking away and planning.
wichtigste: A piggy bank is a money box shaped like a pig with a slot for money.
In many countries the pig is a symbol of good luck, hence the German saying “Schwein haben” (to have a pig), meaning to be lucky.
If you put in the same amount every week, you can easily work out when you will reach a goal.
In Switzerland there are coins from 5 centimes to 5 francs.
100 centimes make 1 franc, so five 20-centime pieces make 1 franc.
Saving helps you to fulfil a bigger wish later.

abschnitte.text: A **piggy bank** is a container made of clay, porcelain, plastic or metal in the shape of a pig. It has a slot on top through which you put coins and folded notes. Some piggy banks have a stopper underneath; others have to be broken to get at the money. Money boxes also come in other shapes, such as little houses, animals or the Swiss “Kässeli”.

Clay money boxes were known many hundreds of years ago; very old animal figures for saving have been found, for example, on the island of Java. In the German-speaking world the pig is a **symbol of good luck** and a sign of wealth. Anyone who owned a pig had enough to eat. That is why people still say “Schwein gehabt” (“had a pig”) today when someone has been lucky.

Switzerland has the **Swiss franc**, and 1 franc has 100 centimes. There are coins of 5, 10 and 20 centimes and of half a franc, 1, 2 and 5 francs. Banknotes come in 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. Three 1-franc pieces and one 2-franc piece add up to 5 francs.

If there are 5 francs in the piggy bank and you add 2 francs, there are 7 francs. If you put in 5 francs every week for 3 weeks, you have saved 15 francs; that is a **multiplication**. If a ball costs 12 francs and there are 8 francs inside, 4 francs are still missing. If you take 6 francs out of 20 francs, 14 francs are left.

Set yourself a clear **savings goal**, for example a game or a book. Work out how long you need to save: with 2 francs a week you will have 10 francs after 5 weeks. Write down how much you have put in, so that you keep track. Larger amounts can later be taken to a **savings account** at a bank, where they are kept safe.

begriffe.erklaerung: A container with a slot in which you collect money.
The smaller unit of the Swiss franc; 100 centimes make 1 franc.
The amount or wish you are putting money aside for.
An account at a bank where you keep money safe.

gewusst: In Switzerland a money box is often called a “Kässeli”.
Many banks used to give money boxes to children so that they would later bring their savings to the bank.

teile.einleitung: Negative numbers are numbers that are smaller than zero, for example -3 or -15. In everyday life you meet them on the thermometer, with debts or with depths below sea level. Together with zero and the positive numbers they make up the integers.
wichtigste: Negative numbers are smaller than zero and have a minus sign.
The numbers ..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ... are called integers.
On the number line negative numbers lie to the left of zero.
The further left a number lies, the smaller it is, so -9 is smaller than -2.
Minus times minus gives plus, so -6 · (-4) = 24.
The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero; the absolute value of -15 is 15.
In India, rules for calculating with negative numbers were written down as early as the 7th century.

abschnitte.text: **Negative numbers** are smaller than zero and have a minus sign in front. They are best known from the **thermometer**: at -5 degrees it is 5 degrees colder than at freezing point. Depths are also given as negative numbers: a diver 12 m under water is at -12 m. If she rises 5 m, she is at -7 m. In a bank account a minus means that you have **debts**.

On the **number line** the negative numbers lie to the left of zero and the positive ones to the right. Together with zero they are called **integers**. The further left a number stands, the smaller it is. That is why -9 is smaller than -2, even though 9 is bigger than 2. Two numbers such as 5 and -5, which are the same distance from zero, are called opposite numbers.

If you add a positive number, you move to the right on the number line: -7 + 3 gives -4. If you subtract, you move to the left: 5 − 12 gives -7. You have to be especially careful when subtracting a negative number. Minus and minus then become plus, so 3 − (−5) = 3 + 5 = 8. You can imagine that taking away debts makes you richer.

For multiplying and dividing there are simple **sign rules**. Plus times minus gives minus, and minus times minus gives plus. That is why -6 · (-4) = 24, but -24 : 6 = -4. The **absolute value** of a number is its distance from zero and is always positive, so the absolute value of -15 is 15. It is written with two vertical lines, like this: |-15| = 15.

In China, more than 2000 years ago, people were already calculating with red and black counting rods for positive and negative values. In the 7th century the Indian mathematician **Brahmagupta** wrote down rules for calculating with debts and assets. In Europe negative numbers were long regarded as nonsensical and were only properly accepted from the 16th and 17th centuries. In Switzerland, La Brévine in the Neuchâtel Jura is known as a particularly cold place; -41.8 degrees was measured there in 1987. In winter the thermometer in the mountains often shows values well below zero.

begriffe.erklaerung: All positive and negative whole numbers, together with zero.
A line on which the numbers are arranged in order of size.
The plus or minus sign in front of a number.
The distance of a number from zero; it is never negative.
The number on the other side of zero at the same distance, like -5 for 5.

gewusst: The lowest point on land, the shore of the Dead Sea, lies more than 400 metres below sea level.
In bookkeeping, debts used to be written in red ink, which is where the expression “in the red” comes from.
Temperatures in kelvin have no negative values, because 0 kelvin is the lowest possible temperature.

teile.einleitung: The gradient tells you how steeply a line, a curve, a road or a railway rises or falls. In mathematics it is the ratio of the difference in height to the horizontal distance. In everyday life we come across it on road signs, on mountain railways and on every bike ride.
wichtigste: The gradient m is calculated with (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
A positive gradient means upwards, a negative one downwards, and zero means horizontal.
The line through (0|4) and (2|0) has the gradient -2.
With a 10 % gradient, a road rises 50 m over 500 m of horizontal distance.
A line with gradient 1 has an angle of inclination of 45 degrees.
A line perpendicular to one with gradient 2 has the gradient -1/2.
The Pilatus Railway, with up to 48 %, is the steepest cogwheel railway in the world.

abschnitte.text: The **gradient** tells you how much you go up or down when you take one step to the right. You divide the difference in height by the horizontal distance and get a number that is often called m. For a straight line the gradient is the same everywhere. For a curve it changes from point to point.

If you know two points (x₁|y₁) and (x₂|y₂), you work out m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). For (0|4) and (2|0) this gives (0 − 4)/(2 − 0) = -2, so the line falls. In the **equation of a straight line** y = mx + q, the gradient stands directly in front of the x. For 2y = 6x + 4 you first divide by 2 and get y = 3x + 2, so the gradient is 3.

The gradient is closely linked to the **angle of inclination**, because it is the tangent of this angle. A gradient of 1 corresponds to 45 degrees, a gradient of √3 to 60 degrees. Two lines are perpendicular to each other if the product of their gradients is -1. So a line with gradient -1/2 is perpendicular to a line with gradient 2.

On road signs the gradient is given as a **percentage**. 10 % means that the road rises by 10 m over 100 m of horizontal distance, so by 50 m over 500 m. 100 % corresponds to an angle of 45 degrees, not a vertical wall. Swiss mountain pass roads such as the Klausen or the Gotthard have gradients of around 10 % in places.

The **Pilatus Railway** near Lucerne has been running since 1889 and, with gradients of up to 48 %, is the steepest cogwheel railway in the world. That corresponds to an angle of inclination of about 26 degrees. Even steeper is the **Stoos funicular** in the canton of Schwyz, which has gradients of up to 110 % and opened in 2017. Its cabins are built like barrels that rotate so that passengers always stand level.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ratio of the difference in height to the horizontal distance.
The angle between a line and the horizontal.
An equation of the form y = mx + q that describes a straight line.
A railway that pulls itself up with a cogwheel on a toothed rack.

gewusst: A road with a 100 % gradient is not vertical but only 45 degrees steep.
On the Pilatus Railway two horizontal cogwheels grip the rack from the sides, so that the train does not jump off on the steep gradient.

teile.einleitung: A root, or zero, is a place where a function takes the value zero. In the picture of a function, it is the point where the graph meets the x-axis. Finding roots is one of the most common tasks in mathematics, from school to space travel.
wichtigste: A root of a function f is an x-value with f(x) = 0.
On the graph, a root is a point where it crosses or touches the x-axis.
The function f(x) = x² − 9 has the roots 3 and -3.
A product such as (x − 1)(x + 5) is zero when one of the factors is zero.
Some functions, such as f(x) = x² + 4, have no real roots.
At a double root the graph only touches the x-axis.
With the bisection method you can approach roots step by step.

abschnitte.text: A **function** gives every number x a value f(x). A **root** is an x-value for which f(x) is exactly 0. If you draw the function as a curve, there is a point on the x-axis there. A straight line such as f(x) = 2x − 6, for example, has the root 3, because 2 · 3 − 6 = 0. Roots help you understand the shape of a graph.

For simple functions you set f(x) = 0 and solve the **equation**. From x² − 9 = 0 it follows that x² = 9, so x = 3 or x = -3. For a product such as (x − 1)(x + 5) the **zero product rule** helps: it is zero when one factor is zero, so at 1 and -5. For quadratic equations such as x² − 8x + 15 = 0 there is a formula for the solutions, the quadratic formula, in Switzerland often called the “Mitternachtsformel” (midnight formula). Here the roots are 3 and 5.

Not every function has roots. The graph of f(x) = x² + 4 is a parabola that lies entirely above the x-axis, so there is no real root. With f(x) = (x − 4)² the parabola only touches the x-axis at x = 4 without crossing it. This is called a **double root**; the function values do not change sign there. Exponential functions have roots too: 2 to the power x minus 8 is zero at x = 3.

Many equations cannot be solved exactly. Then you approach the root step by step. In the **bisection method** you look for an interval in which the function changes sign and keep halving it. That way you get closer to the root with every step. Usually faster is **Newton's method**, which goes back to the physicist Isaac Newton and works with tangents.

Roots answer many practical questions. For a thrown ball, a function describes the height, and the root shows when it lands on the ground. In business, a root of the profit function shows from when a company stops making a loss. Calculators and computer programs work out roots in fractions of a second. The **fundamental theorem of algebra** says that a polynomial of degree n has at most n different roots.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rule that gives every number x exactly one value.
The drawn curve of a function in a coordinate system.
The U-shaped curve of a quadratic function.
The values change from positive to negative or the other way round.

gewusst: A parabola can have zero, one or two roots, but never three.
The sine function has infinitely many roots, because its wave keeps repeating.
Satnavs and satellites also calculate roots all the time to work out positions.

teile.einleitung: An inequality compares two expressions with the signs <, >, ≤ or ≥. Unlike an equation, it usually has not just one solution but a whole range of solutions. Inequalities are needed whenever something may be at most or at least a certain size.
wichtigste: An inequality links two sides with <, >, ≤ or ≥.
The solution of an inequality is usually a whole range of numbers.
Inequalities are solved almost like equations, step by step.
If you multiply or divide by a negative number, the sign is reversed.
From 2x + 3 < 11, for example, it follows that x < 4.
Solution sets are often written as an interval, such as [2; 5[.
In everyday life inequalities describe limits such as budgets or speed limits.

abschnitte.text: An **inequality** says that one side is smaller or larger than the other. The sign < means “less than”, > means “greater than”. With ≤ and ≥ equality is allowed too. So x ≤ 6 means that x may be at most 6.
As with an equation, you do the same to both sides. For 2x + 3 < 11 you first subtract 3 and get 2x < 8. Then you divide by 2 and get x < 4. For x/2 + 1 ≤ 4 you get x ≤ 6 in the same way.

There is an important rule: if you multiply or divide by a **negative number**, the inequality sign is reversed. For -3x > 12 you divide by -3 and get x < -4. You can easily see why with an example: 2 < 3 is true, but -2 is greater than -3. If you forget this rule, you get exactly the wrong numbers as the solution.

The solutions often form a section of the number line, an **interval**. The numbers x with 2 ≤ x < 5 are written as [2; 5[; the square bracket pointing outwards shows that 5 is not included. For |x| < 3, all the solutions lie between -3 and 3. For (x − 1)(x + 2) < 0 exactly one factor must be negative, so -2 < x < 1.

Lena has 50 francs, and a cinema ticket costs 14 francs. She is looking for the biggest number n with 14 · n ≤ 50; that is **3**, because four tickets would cost 56 francs. Speed limits, weight limits in lifts and age limits are inequalities too. In business and technology people plan with many inequalities at the same time to find the best solution.

begriffe.erklaerung: The signs <, >, ≤ and ≥ for comparing quantities.
All the numbers that satisfy an inequality.
A continuous section of the number line.
The distance of a number from zero, written |x|.

gewusst: The signs < and > were introduced in the 17th century by the Englishman Thomas Harriot.
A memory aid: the open side of the sign always points to the bigger number.
Many train timetables and school timetables are planned by computers that solve huge systems of inequalities.

teile.einleitung: Pythagoras of Samos was a Greek thinker who lived in the 6th century BC. The famous Pythagorean theorem, which schoolchildren learn all over the world, is named after him. His followers believed that the whole world could be explained with numbers.
wichtigste: Pythagoras was born around 570 BC on the Greek island of Samos.
In Croton in southern Italy he founded a community, the Pythagoreans.
The motto “All is number” is attributed to the Pythagoreans.
Pythagoras’ theorem states a² + b² = c² for right-angled triangles.
The smallest Pythagorean triple is 3, 4 and 5.
The Pythagoreans discovered numerical ratios in music.
No writings by Pythagoras himself have survived.

abschnitte.text: Pythagoras was born around 570 BC on **Samos**, an island in the Aegean Sea near present-day Turkey. He is regarded as a philosopher, mathematician and religious teacher all at once. Around 530 BC he moved to **Croton** in southern Italy, which is now called Crotone. He probably died in Metapontum, also in southern Italy. Because he wrote nothing down himself, we know him only from the accounts of later writers.

In Croton Pythagoras founded a community whose members are called **Pythagoreans**. They lived by strict rules and believed that the soul moves on into a new body. Their motto “All is number” means that behind everything in nature there are numbers and ratios. Many of the group’s discoveries were later simply credited to Pythagoras.

In a right-angled triangle, the two sides that form the right angle are called the **legs**, and the longest side opposite is called the **hypotenuse**. The theorem says: the squares of the two legs added together equal the square of the hypotenuse, so a² + b² = c². With legs of 6 cm and 8 cm, the hypotenuse is 10 cm long, because 36 + 64 = 100. A rectangle with sides of 5 m and 12 m has a diagonal of 13 m.

Three whole numbers that fit the theorem are called a **Pythagorean triple**. The smallest is 3, 4 and 5, because 9 + 16 = 25. With a rope divided into 3 plus 4 plus 5 equal pieces, you can mark out a right angle. Babylonian clay tablets show that such triples were known more than 1000 years before Pythagoras.

The Pythagoreans studied vibrating strings on an instrument called a **monochord**. If you halve the length of the string, the note sounds an **octave** higher. Other pleasant harmonies arise from simple ratios such as 2 to 3 for the fifth. For the Pythagoreans this was proof that numbers bring order to the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the two sides that form the right angle in a right-angled triangle.
The longest side in a right-angled triangle; it lies opposite the right angle.
A person who thinks about the big questions of life and the world.
An interval between two notes where the higher one vibrates twice as fast.

gewusst: Nobody knows for sure whether Pythagoras himself proved the theorem named after him.
The harbour town of Pythagoreio on Samos is named after him today.
Today there are hundreds of different proofs of Pythagoras’ theorem.

teile.einleitung: Rounding means replacing a number with a simpler number close to it. Instead of 4786, for example, you say about 4800. Rounded numbers are easier to remember, compare and work with in your head.
wichtigste: When rounding, you replace a number with an approximate value.
What matters is always the digit to the right of the rounding place.
If this digit is 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4, you round down; if it is 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9, you round up.
4786 rounded to the nearest hundred is 4800; 23,450 rounded to the nearest thousand is 23,000.
For rounded numbers the sign ≈ is used, meaning “approximately equal to”.
In Switzerland amounts of money are rounded to 5 centimes at the till.

abschnitte.text: When **rounding**, you replace an exact number with a rounder number nearby. You say which place you are rounding to, such as tens, hundreds or thousands. The result is an **approximate value** and no longer quite exact. That is why ≈ is often written instead of =; it means “approximately equal to”.

You always look at the digit directly to the right of the rounding place. When rounding to tens, the **units digit** decides. If it is 0 to 4, you **round down**; if it is 5 to 9, you **round up**. For 4786 to the nearest hundred, the tens digit is 8, so it is rounded up to 4800. For 23,450 to the nearest thousand, the hundreds digit is 4, so the result is 23,000.

Sometimes rounding up changes several places. 7950 rounded to the nearest hundred gives 8000, because 79 hundreds become 80 hundreds. 1,649,999 rounded to the nearest million gives 2,000,000, because the hundred-thousands digit is 6. On the other hand, many numbers can give the same result: 4512 rounded to the nearest thousand gives 5000, just like 4500 or 5499.

Decimal numbers can be rounded too, for example to **tenths** or hundredths. 2.47 rounded to tenths gives 2.5, because the hundredths digit is 7. 3.14159 rounded to hundredths gives 3.14. With measurements in the sciences, you often round so that you give no more digits than you have really measured accurately.

The smallest Swiss coin today is the 5-centime piece; the 1-centime coin was withdrawn as legal tender in 2007. That is why amounts are rounded to **5 centimes** when paying in cash. A purchase of Fr. 12.37 then costs Fr. 12.35, one of Fr. 12.38 costs Fr. 12.40. With card payments, however, the exact amount is often charged.

begriffe.erklaerung: Replacing a number with a simpler value close to it.
Going to the next larger round number when the deciding digit is 5 to 9.
Going to the next smaller round number when the deciding digit is 0 to 4.
A value that is not quite exact but close to the correct value.

gewusst: If you first round many numbers and then add them, the rounding error can become quite large in the end.
In statistics, rounded percentages sometimes add up to 99 % or 101 % instead of exactly 100 %.
Banks and computers sometimes use other rounding rules, for example so-called commercial or mathematical rounding.

teile.einleitung: Change is the money you get back at the till when you pay more than something costs. If you pay for an exercise book costing Fr. 3.40 with a 5-franc coin, you get Fr. 1.60 back. Working out and checking change is a practical maths exercise for everyday life.
wichtigste: Change is the difference between the amount paid and the price.
You work it out with a subtraction or by counting up to the amount paid.
In Switzerland there are coins of 5, 10, 20 and 50 centimes and of 1, 2 and 5 francs.
Changing money also means swapping it for smaller coins or notes.
Ten 10-centime coins are worth the same as one franc.
It is always worth counting your change.

abschnitte.text: If you pay with a larger amount than the price, you get **change** back. For an apple costing Fr. 1.00 that you pay for with Fr. 5.00, you get Fr. 4.00 back. A loaf of bread costs Fr. 4.50; if you pay with a 10-franc note, you get Fr. 5.50 back. The change is always the amount paid minus the price.

Many shop assistants count out the change by **counting up**. They start at the price and count up to the amount paid. For an exercise book costing Fr. 3.40 and a payment of Fr. 5.00, they give 10 centimes up to Fr. 3.50, then 50 centimes up to Fr. 4.00 and one franc up to Fr. 5.00. Together that makes Fr. 1.60, exactly as in the calculation 5.00 minus 3.40.

Changing also means swapping an amount for other coins or notes without the **value** changing. A 10-franc note is worth as much as five 2-franc pieces. A 100-franc note is the same as five 20-franc notes. Four 50-centime coins make 2 francs, and ten 5-centime coins make 50 centimes.

You can often make up an amount with **coins** in different ways. You can get exactly one franc, for example, with 50 centimes, two 20 centimes and 10 centimes. Good change consists of as few pieces as possible, so you start with the largest coins that fit. Because there are no more 1-centime coins, cash amounts in Switzerland are **rounded** to 5 centimes.

Count your change before you leave the till, because adults make mistakes too. With a quick **estimate** in your head you soon notice whether the amount is roughly right. If you pay the exact amount or give small coins, you help the till keep enough coins. Today many people pay by card or with apps such as TWINT, and then there is no change at all.

begriffe.erklaerung: The money you get back when you have paid too much.
Counting from the smaller amount until you reach the larger one.
Coins of low value.
Changing an amount to a simpler number, here to the nearest 5 centimes.

gewusst: In Switzerland the 2-centime piece was abolished as early as 1978, and the 1-centime piece in 2007.
The Swiss 1-franc, 2-franc and 1/2-franc coins show the standing figure of Helvetia.
Today cash registers work out the change automatically.

teile.einleitung: When comparing prices, you look at where or in which pack an item is cheapest. If you compare prices, you can buy more with your pocket money. To do this you have to read prices, put them in order and sometimes do a little arithmetic.
wichtigste: When comparing prices you look for the cheapest offer for the same item.
If an apple costs 60 centimes in shop A and 80 centimes in shop B, it is cheaper in shop A.
In Switzerland you calculate with francs and centimes (Rappen); 1 franc has 100 centimes.
You find the difference between two prices by subtracting: 9 minus 6 francs gives 3 francs.
A “special offer” (Aktion) means that something is cheaper than usual.
With packs it is best to compare the price per item or per kilo.
The cheapest price is not always the best offer; quality counts too.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland you pay with **francs** and **centimes** (Rappen). One franc is made up of 100 centimes. A price such as 3 francs 50 means three francs and fifty centimes; the price tag often shows 3.50. To compare prices, you first look at the francs and then at the centimes. That is why 3 francs 50 is more than 3 francs 05, and 1 franc 09 is less than 1 franc 90.

Comparing is easiest when it is about exactly the same item. A game costs 9 francs in the shop and 6 francs online, so in the shop it is **3 francs more expensive**. A bike costs 200 francs and only 150 francs in the sale, so it is 50 francs cheaper. You always find the difference by **subtracting** the smaller price from the bigger one. If you only have 5 francs, you can buy a book for 4 francs 80, but not one for 5 francs 20.

It gets harder with packs of different sizes. An exercise book costs 2 francs, so three single exercise books cost 6 francs. In a pack of three they cost only 5 francs, so you save **1 franc**. With food the **unit price** helps: that is the price per kilo, per litre or per 100 grams. In Switzerland the Price Display Ordinance requires shops to give this unit price for many packaged goods.

If a price tag says **“Aktion”** (special offer), the item is cheaper than usual for a certain time. In a **sale**, older goods are often sold more cheaply to make room for new ones. Supermarkets print leaflets with offers every week. If you compare the offers, you can save money, but you should only buy what you really need.

On the internet there are **comparison websites** that show the prices of many shops side by side. Adults use them, for example, to compare mobile phone contracts, insurance or electrical appliances. You should also take postage, delivery time and guarantee into account. A cheap price abroad can turn out more expensive once customs duty and VAT are added. In Switzerland there is also the **Price Supervisor** (Preisüberwacher), a federal office that checks prices that are too high.

Before shopping, a **shopping list** helps so that you do not buy too much. You should look not only at the price but also at quality and how long something lasts. A cheap item that breaks quickly often ends up more expensive. A long trip to a cheaper shop is not always worth it either. If you keep a household budget book or a pocket money list, you keep track of things.

begriffe.erklaerung: The amount of money you have to pay for an item.
The price per kilo, litre or item, so that you can compare packs.
An offer in which an item is cheaper for a short time (Aktion).
A federal office in Switzerland that checks prices that are too high.

gewusst: Many prices end in 90 or 95 centimes because that makes them seem cheaper than they are.
Switzerland is regarded as a “high-price island”, because many goods cost more here than in neighbouring countries.
The smallest coin still in circulation in Switzerland is the 5-centime piece.

teile.einleitung: The time of day tells us how late it is. We need it to be at school on time, to catch the train or to meet friends. A day has 24 hours, an hour 60 minutes and a minute 60 seconds.
wichtigste: A day has 24 hours.
An hour has 60 minutes, and a minute has 60 seconds.
Half an hour is 30 minutes, a quarter of an hour is 15 minutes.
On a clock with hands, the short hand shows the hours and the long hand the minutes.
Digital clocks show the time in digits, often from 0.00 to 23.59.
Switzerland is famous for its watches and its punctual trains.
Switzerland uses Central European Time, and summer time in summer.

abschnitte.text: On a **clock with hands** there are the numbers 1 to 12 in a circle. The short **hour hand** shows the hour, the long **minute hand** the minutes. If the long hand points to 12 and the short hand to 3, it is exactly 3 o’clock. If the long hand points to 6, it is half past, for example half past three. Some clocks also have a thin second hand that goes round once a minute.

A day has 24 hours, so the hand goes all the way round twice. An hour has 60 minutes and a minute 60 **seconds**. Half an hour is 30 minutes, a **quarter of an hour** 15 minutes and three quarters of an hour 45 minutes. In everyday life you say, for example, “quarter past eight” for 8.15 and “quarter to nine” for 8.45.

When calculating with time you have to be careful, because an hour has 60 minutes and not 100. If it is 8 o’clock, then 2 hours later it is 10 o’clock. If school starts at 8 o’clock and Lina arrives 20 minutes early, she gets there at 7.40. The time between two clock times is called a **period of time** or duration. It helps to count up to the full hour first and then carry on counting.

Because the Earth turns, it is not day everywhere at the same time. That is why the world is divided into **time zones**. Switzerland is in Central European Time, CET for short. In summer the clocks are put forward by one hour; this is **summer time**. Switzerland has had summer time since 1981.

Switzerland is known worldwide for its **watchmaking industry**, especially in the Jura and in Geneva. Places such as La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle are even UNESCO World Heritage Sites because of their watchmaking. The Zytglogge in Bern is famous too, a tower with an astronomical clock and moving figures. The Swiss **railway station clock** with its red second hand was designed in 1944 by Hans Hilfiker. Its second hand stops briefly at 12 every minute so that all the clocks run the same.

begriffe.erklaerung: The short hand that shows the hours.
The long hand that shows the minutes.
An area of the Earth in which the same clock time applies.
In summer the clock is put forward by one hour.

gewusst: The most accurate clocks in the world are atomic clocks; they lose hardly a second in millions of years.
Dividing hours and minutes into 60 parts goes back to the ancient Babylonians.
The city of Bern has, in the Zytglogge, a tower clock that has been running since the 16th century.

teile.einleitung: The Millennium Prize Problems are seven particularly difficult, unsolved questions in mathematics. The Clay Mathematics Institute presented them in the year 2000 and offered prize money of 1 million US dollars for each solution. So far only one of them has been solved.
wichtigste: The Millennium Prize Problems were presented by the Clay Mathematics Institute in the year 2000.
There are 7 problems in total.
There is 1 million US dollars for solving each problem.
So far only the Poincaré conjecture has been solved (as of 2026).
The Russian mathematician Grigori Perelman solved it and turned down the prize in 2010.
The P versus NP problem asks whether tasks that can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly.
The problems also include the Navier-Stokes equations and the Riemann hypothesis.

abschnitte.text: The **Clay Mathematics Institute** is a private foundation in the USA, set up in 1998 by the businessman Landon Clay. On 24 May 2000 it presented seven big problems in Paris. In doing so it recalled the German mathematician **David Hilbert**, who exactly 100 years earlier, in 1900, had also presented 23 important problems in Paris. Anyone who solves one of the Millennium Prize Problems receives 1 million US dollars.

The seven problems are the **P versus NP problem**, the Hodge conjecture, the Poincaré conjecture, the Riemann hypothesis, the Yang-Mills problem, the Navier-Stokes equations and the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture. They come from very different areas of mathematics and physics. The **Riemann hypothesis** from 1859 is about how the prime numbers are distributed. The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture concerns rational points on elliptic curves.

The **Poincaré conjecture** was put forward by the French mathematician Henri Poincaré in 1904. It describes what shape a certain three-dimensional space must have. The Russian mathematician **Grigori Perelman** published a proof on the internet in 2002 and 2003. After years of checking, the proof was accepted as correct. Perelman turned down the Fields Medal in 2006 and the million-dollar prize in 2010.

The **P versus NP problem** comes from computer science. It asks whether every problem whose solution can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly. One example is a large sudoku: a finished solution is quickly checked, but finding it can take a very long time. The answer would matter for computers and for encryption on the internet, for example in online banking. Most experts suspect that P and NP are different, but it has not been proved.

The **Navier-Stokes equations** describe how liquids and gases flow, such as water in a river or air around an aeroplane wing. Engineers use them all the time with computers, but it has not been proved mathematically that they always have sensible solutions. The **Yang-Mills problem** comes from the physics of the smallest particles. Both show how closely mathematics and the natural sciences are linked.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mathematical statement that is probably true but has not yet been proved.
A complete logical argument showing that a statement is true.
A number greater than 1 that can only be divided by 1 and itself.
One of the highest awards in mathematics, often compared with a Nobel Prize.

gewusst: Perelman turned down not only the prize money but also the Fields Medal, one of the most famous awards in mathematics.
Anyone who solves the P versus NP problem might even crack other Millennium Prize Problems with it, if P were equal to NP.
The Riemann hypothesis was already on David Hilbert's list of 1900, so it has been unsolved for more than 100 years.

teile.einleitung: The sieve of Eratosthenes is an ancient method for finding all the prime numbers up to a certain limit. You write down all the numbers and cross out the multiples step by step until only prime numbers are left. It is named after Eratosthenes, a Greek scholar of ancient times.
wichtigste: The sieve of Eratosthenes finds all prime numbers up to a chosen number.
First you cross out 1, because it is not a prime number.
Then you circle 2 and cross out all multiples of 2 except 2 itself.
For the numbers up to 100 you only need to sieve up to the prime number 7.
Up to 100 exactly 25 prime numbers are left, the largest being 97.
Eratosthenes was a Greek scholar who also estimated the circumference of the Earth.

abschnitte.text: **Eratosthenes** was a Greek scholar of ancient times who lived from about 276 to 194 BC. He came from Cyrene in what is now Libya. Later he ran the famous **Library of Alexandria** in Egypt. He studied mathematics, geography, astronomy and poetry.

You write all the numbers from 1 to 100 in a table and cross out 1. Then you circle 2 as the first **prime number** and cross out all its multiples, that is 4, 6, 8 and so on. The next number not crossed out is 3; you circle it and cross out 6, 9, 12 and all its other multiples. You carry on in the same way with 5 and 7, and all the numbers that are left are prime numbers.

When crossing out the multiples of 5, you can start at 25, because 10, 15 and 20 have already been crossed out as multiples of 2 or 3. In general, for each prime number you start with its **square**. For the numbers up to 100, therefore, it is enough to sieve up to 7, because 11 times 11 is already more than 100. All the remaining numbers, such as 89 or 97, stay and are prime numbers.

Eratosthenes is also famous because he estimated the **circumference of the Earth**. He knew that in Syene, today’s Aswan, the sun stood almost directly overhead at midday on a certain day. In Alexandria, further north, a stick cast a short shadow at the same time. From the angle of this shadow and the distance between the two cities he calculated the Earth’s circumference astonishingly accurately.

Prime numbers are the building blocks of all natural numbers, because every number can be written as a product of prime numbers. The sieve is one of the oldest known **algorithms**, that is step-by-step instructions. Today it is used in computer programs to find many prime numbers quickly. Prime numbers are important for encrypting data on the internet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A natural number greater than 1 that can only be divided by 1 and itself.
The result of multiplying a number by 1, 2, 3 and so on.
A precise set of instructions that leads step by step to a result.
The distance once round the Earth, about 40,000 kilometres at the equator.

gewusst: Eratosthenes is thought to be one of the first people to use the word “geography”.
2 is the only even prime number; all other prime numbers are odd.

teile.einleitung: A statistical fallacy is a mistake in thinking when dealing with numbers, chance and probabilities. It leads people to conclude something false from data, even though the numbers themselves are correct. If you know the typical traps, you are less easily fooled by surveys, graphs and games of chance.
wichtigste: A statistical fallacy is a thinking error when analysing numbers.
In the gambler’s fallacy people believe that chance has a memory.
A survey is only valid if the sample is representative.
With survivorship bias you only see the cases that made it through.
Simpson’s paradox shows that a trend can reverse when data is combined.
A correlation does not automatically mean that one thing causes the other.
Graphs with a cut-off axis make small differences look huge.

abschnitte.text: In the **gambler’s fallacy** people believe that after red five times, black must come up soon. But in roulette with 37 numbers, the chance of black stays 18/37 on every spin, whatever happened before. A famous example is an evening at the casino in Monte Carlo in 1913, when black came up very many times in a row. Many players bet more and more on red and lost a lot of money.

A survey on a sports website mainly reaches sporty people. If 80 per cent there say they do sport every day, that does not apply to the whole population. The **sample** is not **representative**, because it is not made up like the population as a whole. Serious surveys therefore choose the people they ask at random.

In the Second World War, planes returning from missions were examined, and the idea was to reinforce the places with bullet holes. The statistician Abraham Wald pointed out that it was precisely the places without bullet holes that were dangerous. Planes hit there simply did not come back. This thinking error is called **survivorship bias**.

With just 23 people in a room, it is more likely than not that two share a birthday. This is called the **birthday paradox**. In the Monty Hall problem you double your chance of winning to 2/3 if you switch after a door with a goat behind it has been opened. And in **Simpson’s paradox** a trend that holds in all the subgroups can reverse when they are combined.

For incomes the **median** is often more meaningful than the average, because a few very high incomes pull the average up a lot. After an extreme measurement, a repeat usually gives a less extreme one; this is called regression to the mean. A column chart whose axis starts at 95 instead of 0 makes small differences look exaggerated. And even if more ice cream and more sun cream are sold in summer, one does not cause the other; both depend on the warm weather.

begriffe.erklaerung: A selection of people or things that are studied instead of studying all of them.
A sample is representative if, on a small scale, it is made up like the whole.
The value in the middle when all the values are put in order of size.
A connection between two quantities that change together.

gewusst: Even many mathematicians at first believed that switching makes no difference in the Monty Hall problem.
In the birthday paradox, 70 people are enough for a probability of over 99 per cent.
A die does not know which number it showed last.

teile.einleitung: Prime numbers are numbers that can only be divided by 1 and by themselves, such as 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11. They are called the building blocks of numbers, because every other number can be made from them. Although they have been studied for more than 2000 years, they are still full of secrets.
wichtigste: A prime number is a natural number with exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
1 is not a prime number, because it has only one factor.
2 is the only even prime number.
Between 1 and 20 there are 8 prime numbers: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19.
Every number greater than 1 can be broken down into prime factors in exactly one way, such as 180 = 2² · 3² · 5.
With the sieve of Eratosthenes you can find all the prime numbers up to a limit.
Euclid proved that there are infinitely many prime numbers.

abschnitte.text: A **prime number** can only be divided without a remainder by 1 and by itself. 29 is a prime number, because no number from 2 to 28 goes into it. 15, on the other hand, is not, because 15 = 3 · 5. 1 does not count, because it has only one single factor.

Every natural number greater than 1 is either a prime number itself or a product of prime numbers. This way of writing it is called **prime factorisation** and is always unique. For example, 180 = 2 · 2 · 3 · 3 · 5 = 2² · 3² · 5. With it you can easily find the highest common factor or the lowest common multiple of two numbers.

The Greek scholar **Eratosthenes** lived in Alexandria in the 3rd century BC. His method works like this: you write down all the numbers up to a limit and first cross out all the multiples of 2, then of 3, of 5 and so on. What is left are the prime numbers. This **sieve of Eratosthenes** is still a popular method at school today.

Around 300 BC **Euclid** already proved that the prime numbers never run out. The larger the numbers get, the rarer prime numbers become, but they never stop. Sometimes two prime numbers are only 2 apart, like 11 and 13 or 17 and 19; these are **twin primes**. Whether there are infinitely many such twins, nobody knows to this day.

The largest known prime number was discovered in October 2024; it has more than 41 million digits. Such giant numbers can only be found with computers, often as part of a worldwide project. A famous unsolved puzzle is **Goldbach's conjecture** from 1742: every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two prime numbers. Christian Goldbach wrote it in a letter to the Basel mathematician Leonhard Euler.

Prime numbers protect our data on the internet. In many kinds of **encryption** you multiply two huge prime numbers, which is easy. Finding the two prime numbers again from the result, however, is extremely hard even for supercomputers. This is how online banking, emails and messages on mobile phones are protected.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that goes into another without a remainder.
A prime number that is contained in a number as a factor.
Two prime numbers that are exactly 2 apart.
Making messages unreadable for people who are not allowed to read them.

gewusst: Some cicadas in North America only emerge every 13 or 17 years, and both are prime numbers.
Printed out, the largest known prime number would fill many thousands of book pages.
The number 1 million contains only the prime factors 2 and 5.

teile.einleitung: A column chart shows numbers as vertical columns. The bigger a value is, the taller its column. This lets you see at a glance what occurs most or least often.
wichtigste: In a column chart each column stands for a category, for example a day of the week or a kind of fruit.
The height of a column shows how big the value is.
The tallest column shows the biggest value, the shortest the smallest.
You read the numbers off an axis at the edge of the chart.
Columns of the same height mean values of the same size.
If the bars are horizontal, it is called a bar chart.
The Scotsman William Playfair is regarded as the inventor of this kind of chart.

abschnitte.text: A **column chart** is a drawing that makes numbers visible. For each category there is a column that grows upwards from the bottom. All the columns are the same width; only their height is different. This lets you compare values much faster than in a long table of numbers.

A column chart has two **axes**. The categories are on the horizontal axis, for example Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. You read the values off the vertical axis. Sometimes one box does not stand for 1 but, for example, for 2 children; then a column 5 boxes high shows 10 children. You must always look at this scale first.

If a chart shows apples 6, pears 3 and bananas 8, the pears column is the shortest. If dog and cat are both 9, their columns are the same height. If the Monday column is 4 boxes high and the Tuesday column 7 boxes, the Tuesday column is 3 boxes taller. You can also add values together: if Anna has read 5 books, Ben 2 and Cem 7, that makes 14 **books** altogether.

First you collect the data, for example with a **tally chart** in class. Then you draw the two axes and label them. Next you choose a suitable scale and draw a column for each category. A title above the chart explains what it is about.

In 1786 the Scottish engineer **William Playfair** published one of the first column or bar charts, to show trade figures. Today there are many related types of chart. In a **bar chart** the bars are horizontal; in a pie chart shares are shown as slices of a pie. You come across column charts all the time in newspapers, weather reports and voting results.

begriffe.erklaerung: A drawing that shows numbers or relationships clearly.
The line at the edge of a chart on which you read off values or categories.
Tells you what value one box or one centimetre stands for.
A simple list in which you make a mark for each time something occurs.

gewusst: If the vertical axis does not start at 0, small differences in a column chart can look huge.
Climate charts often show monthly rainfall as columns and temperature as a line.
With spreadsheet programs on a computer, you can make a column chart in a few seconds.

teile.einleitung: “True or false” is about checking statements. A statement is either correct, that is true, or it is not correct, that is false. If you look carefully and check the maths, you can decide which.
wichtigste: A statement is a sentence that is either true or false.
“7 + 5 = 12” is a true statement.
“A triangle has 4 corners” is a false statement.
A week has 7 days; that is true.
A franc has 100 centimes, not 10 centimes.
To check a statement you can calculate, count or look it up.
Questions and commands are not statements; they are neither true nor false.

abschnitte.text: A **statement** is a sentence about which you can decide whether it is right or not. “10 is greater than 8” is a statement, and it is **true**. “9 is an even number” is also a statement, but it is **false**. A question such as “How old are you?”, on the other hand, is not a statement.

Many statements in mathematics are calculations. “7 + 5 = 12” is true, and so is “3 times 4 = 12”. If it said 3 times 4 = 13, the statement would be false. To be sure, you can do the calculation again or check it with an inverse sum.

You can also make true and false statements about shapes. A triangle has 3 corners, a quadrilateral 4. Even numbers can be divided by 2 without a remainder, so 2, 4 and 10 are even, but 9 is not. Half of 20 is 10; you can check this with 10 + 10 = 20.

True and false do not only exist in mathematics. “A week has 7 days” is true. “1 franc is 10 centimes” is false, because a **franc** has 100 centimes. You can check statements like these with knowledge, a calendar or a look in your purse.

Some false statements sound right at first. That is why it is important to read carefully and not to guess. On the internet and in advertising there are sometimes false statements too. If you practise checking statements, you learn **critical thinking**, and that helps far beyond mathematics.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sentence that is either true or false.
A statement is correct.
A statement is not correct.
A number that can be divided by 2 without a remainder.

gewusst: In logic people often write 1 for true and 0 for false, just as in a computer.
A sentence such as “This sentence is false” can be neither true nor false; this is called a paradox.
Questions such as “What time is it?” are neither true nor false.

teile.einleitung: Zero is the number for “nothing”. It is the smallest digit and comes directly before 1. Although it seems so unremarkable, its invention was one of the most important ideas in mathematics, because without zero our number system today would not exist.
wichtigste: Zero stands for “nothing” and is the smallest digit.
It comes directly before 1.
If you add 0 to a number, the number stays the same: 7 + 0 gives 7.
If you multiply a number by 0, the result is always 0.
If you add a zero on the right, a number becomes ten times as big: 6 becomes 60.
Roman numerals had no zero.
You must not divide by 0.

abschnitte.text: **Zero** is the number that shows that something is not there at all. If there are no apples in the basket, there are zero apples. If you work out 9 − 9, you are also left with 0. Zero is an even number, because it can be divided by 2 without a remainder. On the number line it stands between the positive and the negative numbers.

In our **place value system** the position of a digit shows how much it is worth. Zero keeps empty places free. In 100 the two zeros say that there are no tens and no units, but one hundred.
