Estimating is very handy when shopping. If things cost Fr. 4.95, Fr. 3.10 and Fr. 11.90, you work out 5 + 3 + 12 and know that it will cost about **Fr. 20**. Rough calculation also helps when travelling, with pocket money or when estimating how long a walk will take. Many adults use estimates every day without noticing.

Longer calculations can be estimated too. For 19 · 31 · 2 you work out 20 · 30 · 2 and get about 1200. If you round one number up and the other down, the errors often partly cancel out. With a **calculator** an estimate is especially worthwhile, because it is easy to mistype.

begriffe.erklaerung: A quick, approximate calculation with rounded numbers.
Replacing a number with a simpler number nearby, for example 398 with 400.
A sign for “approximately equal to”, for example 398 · 21 ≈ 8000.
Testing whether a result can be right at all.

gewusst: Engineers also often make an estimate first before big calculations.
Many mistakes with calculators come from a wrong decimal point, which an estimate shows straight away.
If you are good at estimating, you notice more quickly at the till when something has been typed in wrongly.

teile.einleitung: A pair is two things that belong together, for example two socks or two gloves. In mathematics a pair is closely linked to the number 2 and to even numbers. If you count in pairs, you get on faster and see straight away whether anything is left over.
wichtigste: A pair consists of 2 things that belong together.
A pair of socks is 2 socks.
A beetle has three pairs of legs, so 6 legs.
If a group can be split into pairs with nothing left over, its number is even.
With 7 children, one child is left over when making pairs.
In German, “ein paar” with a small p means “a few”.
In pairs (Memory) you look for pairs, that is two cards with the same picture.

abschnitte.text: A **pair** is two identical things or things that belong together. Typical examples are a pair of socks, a pair of shoes or a pair of gloves. Things like these are usually bought as a pair, because you always need them in twos. Our body also has many pairs, such as two eyes, two ears, two hands and two feet. So four children have 8 hands altogether.

If you count in pairs, you count in twos: 2, 4, 6, 8 and so on. A number of things that can be split into pairs with nothing left over is an **even number**. If one is left over, it is **odd**. With 7 children you get 3 pairs, and one child is left on their own. That is why in PE one group sometimes has to work in threes.

Many animals have their legs in pairs. **Insects** such as beetles, ants and bees have three pairs of legs, so 6 legs. Spiders have four pairs of legs, so 8. Birds and bats have one pair of wings, many insects even two pairs. Animals' bodies are often **mirror symmetrical**, which is why many body parts appear on both sides.

In **pairs** (Memory), cards lie face down on the table and you have to turn over two cards with the same picture. You may keep a pair of cards like this. The game came on the market in Germany in 1959 and is still popular today. In the card game Old Maid (Schwarzer Peter) you also put down pairs. In Jass and in poker, pairs of identical cards play a part too.

In German the word has two meanings, and the spelling shows the difference. “Ein Paar” with a capital P means exactly two things that belong together, such as “ein Paar Schuhe” (a pair of shoes). “Ein paar” with a small p means **a few**, so a small, inexact number. “Ein paar Kinder” can therefore be three, four or five children. In mathematics two numbers in a fixed order such as (2, 5) are called an **ordered pair**; they are used to describe points in a coordinate system.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two things that belong together.
A number that can be divided by 2 with no remainder.
A number that leaves one over when divided by 2.
Two numbers in a fixed order, for example for a point on a map.

gewusst: In German a pair of glasses with two lenses is not called “ein Paar Brillen” but simply “eine Brille”.
Despite its name, a millipede usually has far fewer than a thousand legs, but always an even number, because they grow in pairs.
In a group of 23 people there are already 253 different pairs.

teile.einleitung: Logic puzzles are thinking tasks that you solve not with knowledge but by thinking clearly. You have to combine clues cleverly and draw conclusions step by step. Some puzzles are more than a thousand years old and still have people scratching their heads today.
wichtigste: Logic puzzles are solved by reading carefully and thinking logically.
From “Anna is taller than Ben” and “Ben is taller than Carla” it follows that Carla is the shortest.
The puzzle with the wolf, the goat and the cabbage needs at least 7 crossings.
In the Towers of Hanoi you need at least 15 moves for 4 discs.
In knights and knaves puzzles, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie.
Sudoku is one of the best-known logic puzzles in the world.
Logic puzzles train thinking, patience and concentration.

abschnitte.text: A **logic puzzle** contains all the information you need for the solution. You only have to draw the right **conclusions**. Simple puzzles go like this: a box holds 9 balls, 4 of them red; how many are blue? You find the answer 5 by thinking instead of guessing.

Many puzzles are about orders. If today is Monday, the day after tomorrow is Wednesday. If 5 children stand in a row and Mia is exactly in the middle, there are 2 children in front of her. With **number sequences** such as 2, 6, 12, 20, 30 you look for the pattern: the gaps get 2 bigger each time, so 42 comes next.

A farmer has to take a wolf, a goat and a cabbage across a river, but there is room for only one of them in the boat. The wolf must not be left alone with the goat, nor the goat with the cabbage. The trick: the goat is brought back again in between, so it can be done in 7 crossings. This puzzle comes from a collection attributed to the scholar **Alcuin** around the year 800.

On an invented island, **knights** always tell the truth and **knaves** always lie. A says: “B is a knave.” B says: “A and I are of the same kind.” If A were a knave, B would have to be a knight, but then B's statement would be false: a contradiction. So A is a knight and B is a knave. Such puzzles were made famous by the American mathematician Raymond Smullyan.

The **Towers of Hanoi** were invented by the French mathematician Édouard Lucas in 1883. You have to move a tower of discs onto another rod, but you may never put a bigger disc on a smaller one. With 4 discs you need at least 15 moves, and with each extra disc the number roughly doubles. **Sudoku** originally comes from the USA, became popular in Japan and has been popular in Swiss newspapers too since about 2005.

It helps to draw a sketch or a table. Thinking of the **worst case** often helps too: with 10 black and 10 white socks you have to take 3 in the dark, because by then at the latest two will be the same. You can also try out an assumption and see whether it leads to a contradiction. Anyone who solves logic puzzles practises exactly the kind of thinking that programmers and detectives need.

begriffe.erklaerung: The study of correct reasoning.
Something new that you can work out for certain from known facts.
Two statements that cannot both be true at the same time.
A rule by which something repeats.

gewusst: According to a legend, monks have to move a tower of 64 golden discs, which would take more than 500 billion years even at one move per second.
The word sudoku is Japanese and means roughly “the digits must remain single”.
The so-called Einstein puzzle with five houses is often attributed to Albert Einstein, although there is no proof of this.

teile.einleitung: Multiplication is doing times sums. It is a shortcut for adding the same number again and again: 3 times 4 means 4 + 4 + 4. Anyone who knows their times tables can calculate much faster in everyday life.
wichtigste: Multiplying means adding a number several times.
3 times 4 gives 12; the result is called the product.
The order of the numbers does not matter: 2 times 6 is the same as 6 times 2.
Any number times 0 gives 0.
Any number times 1 stays the same.
The basic times tables cover all multiplications from 1 times 1 to 10 times 10.
The sign used is the multiplication dot or the cross.

abschnitte.text: In **multiplication** you add up equal groups. A box holds 6 eggs, so 3 boxes hold 6 + 6 + 6 = 18 eggs. For short you write 3 · 6 = 18. The numbers you multiply are called **factors**, and the result is called the **product**.

In Switzerland children usually learn the **times tables** in the 2nd and 3rd year of school. They include tables such as the two times table 2, 4, 6, 8 or the five times table 5, 10, 15, 20. Some results you simply have to know by heart, such as 4 · 9 = 36. Square numbers such as 5 · 5 = 25 are especially easy to remember.

You may swap the factors: 3 · 4 and 4 · 3 both give 12; this is the **commutative law**. Times 0 always gives 0, and times 1 does not change a number. Times 10 is especially easy: you add a zero, so 10 · 7 = 70. Big sums can be split up, for example 6 · 12 = 6 · 10 + 6 · 2 = 72.

You can picture every multiplication as a rectangle of dots. 3 · 4 is 3 rows of 4 dots each. If you turn the rectangle round, you see 4 rows of 3 dots each, and the number stays the same. This also explains **area**: a room 4 m by 5 m has 20 square metres.

About 4000 years ago the Babylonians already had clay tablets with multiplication tables. The multiplication cross × was introduced by the Englishman **William Oughtred** in 1631. The multiplication dot was made popular by the German scholar Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, because the cross is easily mixed up with the letter x. In the past, aids such as the **abacus** and later the slide rule helped with multiplying.

In the shop you use multiplication: if 4 bread rolls (Brötli) cost 1.50 francs each, you pay 6 francs. When baking, you double a recipe by multiplying all the ingredients by 2. A week with 7 days and 24 hours a day contains 168 hours. Computers multiply all the time too, for example to work out the pictures on the screen.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that is multiplied by another.
The result of a multiplication.
All multiplications from 1 times 1 to 10 times 10.
A number times itself, for example 5 · 5 = 25.

gewusst: The nine times table has a trick: for 9 times a number up to 10, the digit sum of the result is always 9.
You can work out the nine times table on your fingers by bending one finger down.
A computer can carry out billions of multiplications in a single second.

teile.einleitung: The average mark is the mean of all the marks in a subject or on a school report. It shows at a glance how well someone did overall. In Switzerland 6 is the best mark, and from a 4 upwards a piece of work counts as a pass.
wichtigste: For the average you add up all the marks and divide by how many there are.
In Switzerland 6 is the best and 1 the worst mark.
From the mark 4 upwards a piece of work counts as a pass.
If a mark counts double, you include it twice in the calculation.
Report marks are often rounded to half marks.
The median is the middle mark when you put them all in order of size.
In Germany the marking scale is exactly the other way round; there 1 is the best mark.

abschnitte.text: The **average mark** is the arithmetic mean of the marks. You add up all the marks and divide the sum by the number of marks. Mara, for example, has the marks 5, 4.5 and 5.5. Together that makes 15, and 15 divided by 3 is 5. So her average is exactly 5.

In most Swiss schools the scale goes from 1 to 6. **6** is the best mark, 1 the worst. From the mark **4** upwards a piece of work counts as a pass, below that as a fail. Half marks such as 4.5 or 5.5 are often given too, sometimes even tenths. In Germany it is the other way round: there 1 is very good and 6 is a fail.

Not all marks always count the same. A big **exam** sometimes counts twice as much as a small test. Leo has a 4 in the test and a 5 in the exam that counts double. You work out 4 + 5 + 5 = 14 and divide by 3, which gives about 4.67. This is called a **weighted** average.

You can also work backwards. A pupil with 4 marks and an average of 4.5 has 4 times 4.5, so 18 mark points altogether. Ana has 4.5 and 5 and wants an average of exactly 5 after three exams. For that she needs 15 points, so she still needs a 5.5. Tom has 4, 5 and 6 and still has to write a test where he gets a 3; that gives 18 divided by 4, so an average of 4.5.

On the school report the average is often rounded to the nearest **half mark**. So 4.7 becomes a 4.5, because 4.7 is closer to 4.5 than to 5. As well as the average there is the **median**, the middle number of an ordered list. For the marks 2, 5, 5.5, 6 and 6, the median is 5.5, but the average only 4.9. The median is less strongly affected by a single very bad mark.

begriffe.erklaerung: The mean you get when you add up all the values and divide by how many there are.
Deciding that some marks count more than others.
The middle value when you put all the values in order of size.
A piece of work that meets the requirements; in Switzerland from the mark 4.

gewusst: A single failing mark can lower an average more than many people think: from 5, 5 and 5, adding a 2 brings the average down to 4.25.
In Austria the marking scale only goes from 1 to 5, with 1 being the best mark.
In some countries work is graded with letters such as A to F instead of numbers.

teile.einleitung: Infinite means “without end”. No matter how big a number is, you can always add 1. Infinity is one of the most exciting and mysterious ideas in mathematics.
wichtigste: Infinite means “without end”.
There is no very biggest number, because you can add 1 to every number.
The sign for infinity ∞ looks like an 8 lying on its side.
The three dots in “1, 2, 3, ...” mean that it goes on for ever.
You can never finish counting to infinity.
There are infinitely many even numbers and infinitely many prime numbers.
Infinity is not an ordinary number but an idea for something without limits.

abschnitte.text: **Infinite** describes something that has no end. In mathematics this means, for example, that the series of numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on never stops. Infinity is bigger than any number you can write down. Even so, you do not calculate with infinity as you would with a normal number.

Imagine someone names the biggest number. Then you simply add 1 and have an even bigger one. After a million comes 1,000,001; after a billion comes a billion and one. That is why there is **no biggest number**, and even someone who counts for a whole lifetime never reaches the end.

The sign **∞** looks like an 8 lying on its side. The English mathematician **John Wallis** introduced it in 1655. The shape is also called a lemniscate. Today you find the sign in maths books, but also as jewellery or a logo.

There are infinitely many even numbers, infinitely many odd numbers and infinitely many **prime numbers**. The Greek Euclid proved more than 2000 years ago that there are infinitely many prime numbers. Between 0 and 1, too, there are infinitely many fractions, such as 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 and so on. So you can keep halving a line without ever finishing.

In the 19th century the mathematician **Georg Cantor** discovered something astonishing. There are infinities of different sizes. There are infinitely many natural numbers, but the points on a number line are even “more” infinitely many. Many mathematicians at the time were very surprised by this idea.

begriffe.erklaerung: Without end, without limits.
A curve shaped like an 8 lying on its side; this is what the sign ∞ looks like.
The counting numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on.
A number greater than 1 that can only be divided by 1 and itself.

gewusst: There are exactly as many even numbers as natural numbers, even though the even numbers are only part of them.
A famous thought experiment is “Hilbert’s Hotel”, a hotel with infinitely many rooms that can take in new guests even when it is full.
The sign ∞ is more than 350 years old.

teile.einleitung: The median is the value that stands exactly in the middle of a list put in order of size. It is also called the central value. Alongside the average, it is one of the most important figures in statistics and has a big advantage: single outliers hardly throw it off balance.
wichtigste: The median is the value in the middle of the ordered list.
First you must always put the values in order of size.
With an odd number of values, the median is the middle value, so the 5th with 9 values.
With an even number, you take the average of the two middle values.
The median of the values 2, 8, 4 and 10 is 6.
Extreme values, so-called outliers, hardly change the median.
That is why the median rather than the average is often given for wages or house prices.

abschnitte.text: The **median** divides a set of data into two halves of equal size. One half of the values is smaller or equal, the other bigger or equal. If, for example, nine children line up in order of height, the fifth child is the middle one. That child's height is the median of the group. The word comes from the Latin “medius”, which means “the middle one”.

First you put the values in order of size. For the values 12, 3, 7, 3, 20, 9 and 5 that gives 3, 3, 5, 7, 9, 12, 20. There are seven values, so in the middle is the fourth value, the **7**. With an **even number** of values there are two middle values. For 2, 4, 8, 10 these are 4 and 8, and their average, 6, is the median.

The **average**, also called the arithmetic mean, is the sum of all the values divided by how many there are. For the monthly wages 4000, 4200, 4500, 4800 and 30,000 francs, the average is 9500 francs. The median, on the other hand, is 4500 francs. The one very high wage pulls the average up a lot, but the median stays in the middle. That is why here it describes better what is “typical”.

The Federal Statistical Office gives the **median wage** for Switzerland, because a few very high wages would distort the average. The median is also often used for rents, house prices or waiting times. In sport you can use the median to show what time a typical runner needs in a race. At school you can find the median of the marks in a test.

The median is one of the **measures of central tendency**, which show where the middle of data lies. Another one is the mode, the value that occurs most often. If you divide the ordered list into four equal parts, you get the quartiles; the median is the middle quartile. In a **box plot**, the median and quartiles are drawn as a box with a line in the middle.

begriffe.erklaerung: The middle value of a list put in order of size.
The sum of all the values divided by how many there are.
A value that is much bigger or smaller than the others.
A chart that shows the median and spread of data as a box.

gewusst: If the number 20 is added to the values 4, 6 and 9, the median rises from 6 to 7.5.
In some countries, the central strip of a road is also called the “median”, for example in American English.
The median can even be found when you have no numbers, only a ranking such as “small, medium, large”.

teile.einleitung: The pigeonhole principle is a very simple but astonishingly powerful idea in mathematics. It says: if you have more things than compartments, at least one compartment must get two or more things. With this trick you can prove things without counting them one by one.
wichtigste: The pigeonhole principle says: more things than compartments means one compartment gets at least two.
It is often named after the German mathematician Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet.
In German it is called the “drawer principle”; in English the “pigeonhole principle”.
In a class of 13 children, two of them definitely have their birthday in the same month.
Among 367 people, two definitely share a birthday, even if you count 29 February.
The principle says that something definitely happens, but not in which compartment.
It is used in number theory, computer science and brain-teasers.

abschnitte.text: Imagine you have 4 socks and only 3 drawers. However you share out the socks, at least two will be in one drawer. That is the **pigeonhole principle**. In general: if you share more objects among fewer compartments, at least one compartment gets more than one object.

The German mathematician **Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet** lived from 1805 to 1859. He used this principle for proofs in number theory, which is why it is also called **Dirichlet’s box principle**. In English it is known as the “pigeonhole principle”. You imagine pigeons flying into the holes of a dovecote: if there are more pigeons than holes, two must share a hole.

A year has 12 months, which are 12 compartments. So if there are 13 children in a class, two of them definitely have their birthday in the same month. With 366 possible days including 29 February, you need 367 people for two of them to be sure to celebrate on the same day. With 30 children and 7 days of the week, at least 5 children have their birthday on the same day of the week.

The principle also works with bigger numbers. If you share 25 marbles among 6 boxes, the fullest box contains at least 5 marbles, because 6 times 4 is only 24. So you divide the number of things by the number of compartments and **round up**. This gives you the smallest possible amount in the fullest compartment.

A bag contains balls in 4 colours. If you take out 5 balls, you definitely have two of the same colour, because with 4 balls you could still have each colour once. In the same way, in the dark you are sure to find a pair of socks if you take one sock more than there are colours. In **computer science** the principle shows, for example, that different pieces of data sometimes have to be given the same short code.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small compartment, here a picture for a group or category.
A complete explanation of why a mathematical statement is always true.
Taking a number with decimals up to the next whole number.
The part of mathematics that deals with the properties of whole numbers.

gewusst: With the pigeonhole principle you can prove that in a big city there are definitely two people with exactly the same number of hairs on their heads.
The principle never says which two things end up in the same compartment; it only guarantees that such things exist.

teile.einleitung: Volume tells you how much space a solid takes up or how much fits into a container. Whether it is a milk carton, a classroom or a swimming pool: everything that has length, width and height has a volume. If you can calculate volume, you know, for example, how much water an aquarium needs.
wichtigste: Volume is the amount of space a solid takes up.
It is measured in cubic units such as cubic centimetres (cm³) or cubic metres (m³).
A cuboid has the volume length times width times height.
A cube with an edge length of 3 cm has a volume of 27 cm³.
One cubic centimetre is exactly one millilitre.
1000 litres fit into one cubic metre.
If you double all the edges of a cube, its volume becomes 8 times as big.

abschnitte.text: **Volume** is the space an object needs. It is also called the **cubic content**. A brick, a ball and a bottle all have a volume. For containers, the volume tells you how much liquid fits inside. This amount is often called the capacity.

The most important units are **cubic millimetres**, cubic centimetres, cubic decimetres and cubic metres. A cubic centimetre is a cube with an edge length of 1 cm, about the size of a sugar cube. A cubic decimetre is exactly one **litre**, and a cubic centimetre is one millilitre. Between two neighbouring cubic units there is always a factor of 1000. A cubic metre therefore holds 1000 litres, which is about as much as five full bathtubs.

For a **cuboid** you work out length times width times height. So a cuboid 5 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high has 60 cm³. In a **cube** all the edges are the same length, so you work out edge times edge times edge. A cube with an edge of 3 cm has 27 cm³. If all the edges are doubled, the volume grows by 2 times 2 times 2, that is to 8 times its size.

For a **cylinder** you multiply the circular area of the base by the height. The formula is pi times radius times radius times height. A cylinder with a radius of 2 cm and a height of 10 cm has, rounded, 125.7 cm³. A **cone** with the same base and height has exactly a third of that. For the **sphere** the formula is four thirds times pi times radius cubed.

An aquarium 50 cm long, 30 cm wide and 40 cm high holds 60,000 cm³, that is 60 litres. Drinks, medicines and petrol are sold by volume. In cooking, liquids are measured with a **measuring jug**. In the laboratory precise measuring cylinders are used for this. The engine size of a car is also given as a volume.

Irregular objects such as a stone cannot simply be measured. So you dip them in water and measure how much water is **displaced**. This idea is attributed to the Greek scholar **Archimedes**, who lived more than 2200 years ago. According to legend he cried “Eureka!”, which means “I have found it!”. The displaced water has exactly the volume of the object that was dipped in.

begriffe.erklaerung: The space that a solid takes up.
A cube with edges 1 cm long, the same as 1 millilitre.
A unit for liquids, the same as a cube with a 10 cm edge.
A solid with six rectangular faces, like a box.

gewusst: An Olympic swimming pool holds at least 2500 cubic metres of water, that is 2.5 million litres.
A cubic metre of water weighs about one tonne.
If you double the edges of a cube, you need 8 small cubes to fill it.

teile.einleitung: Surface area is the size of the whole outer skin of a solid, that is all its faces together. You need it, for example, to work out how much wrapping paper a box needs or how much paint is needed for a wall. It is given in units of area such as cm² or m².
wichtigste: Surface area is the sum of all the faces of a solid.
A cube with edge a has the surface area 6 times a times a.
A cube with an edge of 5 cm has a surface area of 150 cm².
A cuboid has three pairs of rectangles of the same size.
If you double all the edges of a cube, the surface area becomes four times as big.
The net of a solid shows all the faces side by side and helps with calculating.
Surface area is given in square units such as cm².

abschnitte.text: Imagine you want to cover a box completely with paper. The amount of paper you need at least is the **surface area**. It is the sum of all the faces that enclose a solid. Because it is about areas, it is measured in **square units** such as cm² or m². If the edges are measured in cm, the result is in cm².

A **cube** has six squares of the same size. That is why its surface area is 6 times a times a, so with an edge of 5 cm it is 6 · 25 = 150 cm². A **cuboid** has three pairs of identical rectangles. For 5 cm, 4 cm and 3 cm you work out 2 · (20 + 15 + 12) = 94 cm². A box of 10 cm by 10 cm by 5 cm has a surface area of 2 · (100 + 50 + 50) = 400 cm².

A **net** is made when you cut a solid open and spread it out flat. The net of a cube, for example, consists of six squares joined together. In the net you see all the faces side by side and do not forget any. For a pyramid with a square base of side 6 cm and side triangles of height 5 cm, you work out 36 cm² plus 4 · 15 cm². That gives a surface area of 96 cm².

A **cylinder**, such as a tin can, has a base, a top and a curved **lateral surface**. If you cut the curved surface open, it becomes a rectangle as wide as the circumference of the circle. For a sphere with radius r the formula is 4 · π · r². The Greek scholar **Archimedes** discovered in the 3rd century BC that the surface of a sphere is exactly four times as big as a circle through its middle. He was so proud of this discovery that he wanted it shown on his grave.

abschnitte.titel: Surface area in everyday life and in nature
abschnitte.text: If you double all the edges of a cube, the surface area becomes **four times** as big, but the volume eight times. That is why small things have a lot of surface compared with their volume. Fine icing sugar therefore dissolves faster than a sugar cube. Animals such as elephants give off heat through their big ears, because the ears have a lot of surface. Painters, roofers and packaging companies also calculate surface areas all the time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sum of all the faces that enclose a solid from the outside.
A solid spread out flat, with all its faces joined side by side.
The side surface of a solid; for a cylinder, the curved surface between the bottom and the lid.
The area of a square with sides of 1 cm, written cm².

gewusst: There are exactly 11 different nets of a cube.
Archimedes wanted a sphere inside a cylinder on his gravestone.
If you cut a cube into eight smaller cubes, the total surface area doubles.

teile.einleitung: A league table in sport shows how the teams in a championship are doing at the moment. It lists wins, draws, defeats, goals and points and ranks the teams by their success. Behind every table there is a lot of maths, from counting points to goal difference.
wichtigste: A sports table ranks the teams by their points.
In football there are 3 points for a win, 1 point for a draw and none for a defeat.
The goal difference is the number of goals scored minus the number of goals conceded.
In the 2025/26 season, 12 teams play in the Swiss Super League.
In Swiss ice hockey there is also 1 point for a defeat after extra time or a penalty shoot-out.
If 4 teams each play every other team once, there are 6 matches altogether.
With home and away matches in a league of 10 teams, each team plays 18 matches.

abschnitte.text: A league **table** in sport has one row for each team. The columns show the number of matches, wins, draws and defeats, the goals and the points. At the very top is the leader, at the very bottom the team in last place. After each round the table changes.

In football there are 3 points for a win and 1 point for a **draw**. So a team with 5 wins, 3 draws and 2 defeats has 15 + 3 = 18 points. If a team has 7 wins and 25 points, 21 points come from wins, so it has played 4 draws. With 30 points from 15 matches, a team takes an **average** of 2 points per match.

If two teams have the same number of points, the **goal difference** often decides. You work out the goals scored minus the goals conceded. With 25 goals scored and 18 conceded, a team has a goal difference of +7. Depending on the league, in a tie the number of goals scored or the head-to-head results may also count.

If every team in a group plays every other team once, this is called a **round robin**. With 4 teams there are then 4 times 3 divided by 2, that is 6 matches. If every team plays once at home and once away, in a league of 10 teams each team has 9 opponents and plays 18 matches. In this way you can work out before the season how long a championship will last.

In the **Super League**, the top Swiss football league, twelve teams play in the 2025/26 season. After a main round the league is split into an upper and a lower half, which play further matches. In ice hockey the top league is called the **National League**. There it is 3 points for a win in normal time, 2 points for a win after extra time or a penalty shoot-out, and 1 point for such a defeat.

begriffe.erklaerung: Goals scored minus goals conceded.
The team at the top of the table.
The period in which a championship is played.
Alternate shots at goal to find a winner after a draw.

gewusst: Because the table is recalculated after every round of matches, a team can gain or lose several places in one weekend.
The formula for a round robin is n times (n − 1) divided by 2; with 12 teams that makes 66 pairings.

teile.einleitung: In vector addition you add two or more vectors together. When drawing, you simply put the arrows one after the other; when calculating, you add the coordinates. The result shows where you end up if you carry out several movements one after another.
wichtigste: Vectors are added by adding the matching coordinates together.
When drawing, you put the tail of the second arrow at the tip of the first.
The resultant vector goes from the start of the first arrow to the tip of the last.
The order does not matter; the commutative law applies.
A vector plus its opposite vector gives the zero vector.
The length of the sum is at most as big as the sum of the lengths.

abschnitte.text: You add vectors by adding each **coordinate** separately. So (2, −1, 3) plus (4, 5, −2) gives the vector (6, 4, 1). Subtraction works in a similar way: the vector from A(1, 2, 3) to B(4, 0, 5) is B minus A, that is (3, −2, 2). You get the midpoint of a line segment by adding the position vectors of the end points and dividing by 2; for A(2, 4, −6) and B(8, 0, 2) it is (5, 2, −2).

With the **tip-to-tail method** you put the start of the second arrow at the tip of the first. The **resultant vector** then goes from the start of the first arrow to the tip of the second. You can also draw both arrows from the same point and complete them to a parallelogram. The diagonal of this parallelogram is the sum, which is why it is called the **parallelogram rule**.

The **commutative law** applies to vector addition: a + b gives the same as b + a. The associative law applies too, so when adding three vectors you may put the brackets wherever you like. Every vector a has an **opposite vector** −a, which is the same length but points the other way. If you add the two together, you get the zero vector.

The length of a sum is never greater than the sum of the individual lengths; this is called the **triangle inequality**. With |a| = 3 and |b| = 5, |a + b| can therefore be at most 8, namely when both point in the same direction. If they point in exactly opposite directions, the sum is only 2 long. If you divide a vector by its length, you get a **unit vector** of length 1; in this way (3, 0, 4) becomes (0.6, 0, 0.8).

A boat crossing a river is pushed sideways by the current. Its real movement is the sum of its own travel and the flow of the water. The Rhine ferries in Basel use exactly this: they are driven across the river by the current alone. Planes also have to take the wind into account to reach their destination.

begriffe.erklaerung: The vector that comes out when several vectors are added.
A vector of the same length that points in the opposite direction.
The vector with length zero, for example (0, 0, 0).
A vector with length 1.

gewusst: If you walk three steps east and four steps north, at the end you are only five steps from the start.
If you walk a closed loop, the sum of all the movement vectors is the zero vector.
Forces are added as vectors in exactly the same way as movements.

teile.einleitung: Thales of Miletus was a Greek scholar who lived about 2600 years ago. He is regarded as Europe’s first philosopher and as one of the first mathematicians who did not just try things out but gave reasons for them. Thales’ theorem is still named after him today.
wichtigste: Thales lived from about 624 to 546 BC in the city of Miletus.
He is often regarded as Europe’s first philosopher.
He is counted among the Seven Sages of ancient Greece.
Thales believed water was the origin of all things.
According to Thales’ theorem, a triangle in a semicircle always has a right angle.
The circle on which this corner of the triangle lies is called the Thales circle.
Other theorems are attributed to him too, for example that a diameter cuts a circle in half.

abschnitte.text: **Thales** was born around 624 BC in **Miletus**, a rich Greek trading city on the coast of present-day Turkey. He was a merchant, engineer, astronomer and thinker. None of his own writings have survived; everything we know comes from the accounts of later writers such as Herodotus and Aristotle. He is counted among the **Seven Sages**, famous wise men of ancient Greece.

Thales is often regarded as Europe’s first **philosopher**. He asked what the world is actually made of and looked for the answer in nature rather than only in stories about the gods. His answer was: everything comes from **water**. More important than the answer was the fact that he looked for natural causes; this was the beginning of natural philosophy.

The most famous theorem attributed to Thales is **Thales’ theorem**. If you draw a triangle whose one side is the diameter of a circle and whose third corner lies on the circle, it always has a **right angle** there. The semicircle over the line is therefore called the **Thales circle**. With it you can construct right angles without any set square.

Other simple but fundamental theorems are also attributed to Thales. He is said to have shown that every **diameter** cuts a circle in half. According to him, the two base angles in an **isosceles triangle** are equal. It is also attributed to him that the opposite angles where two lines cross are equal.

According to the historian Herodotus, Thales predicted a **solar eclipse**, which is usually dated to the year 585 BC. Another story tells that he measured the height of an Egyptian **pyramid** using its shadow. To do this he waited until his own shadow was as long as he was tall. He is also said to have fallen into a well while looking at the stars, which made a servant girl laugh.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who thinks about the big questions of the world and of life.
The circle over a line segment on which every point forms a right angle with the end points.
An angle of 90 degrees, like the corner of a sheet of paper.
A line through the centre that joins two points on the circle.

gewusst: Nobody knows exactly what Thales looked like; all pictures of him are later imaginary ones.
According to a story by Aristotle, Thales made a lot of money because he foresaw a good olive harvest and rented all the olive presses in advance.
A crater on the Moon is named after Thales.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss franc is the money of Switzerland and of Liechtenstein too. A franc has 100 centimes. It comes as coins and banknotes and is regarded worldwide as an especially stable currency.
wichtigste: The Swiss franc is the currency of Switzerland and Liechtenstein.
A franc is worth 100 centimes.
The smallest coin is the 5-centime piece, the largest the 5-franc piece.
There are banknotes of 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs.
Three francs and fifty centimes are written briefly as Fr. 3.50.
The international short name is CHF.
The banknotes are issued by the Swiss National Bank.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss franc** was introduced in 1850, shortly after the founding of the federal state. Before that the cantons had very different coins, which made paying difficult. A franc has 100 **centimes**. The international short name **CHF** stands for “Confoederatio Helvetica Franc”.

There are coins of 5, 10 and 20 centimes and of ½, 1, 2 and 5 francs. The smallest coin is the gold-coloured 5-centime piece; the 1- and 2-centime coins no longer exist. The franc coins show the figure of **Helvetia**, and the 5-franc piece shows the head of an Alpine herdsman. The coins are minted by **Swissmint** in Bern.

There are banknotes of 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. They are issued by the **Swiss National Bank**, which began its work in 1907. The current series appeared between 2016 and 2019 and, under the motto “The many facets of Switzerland”, shows among other things a globe and hands. Each note has its own colour; for example the 10-franc note is yellow, the 50-franc note green and the 1000-franc note purple.

In Switzerland amounts are usually written with a point, for example Fr. 3.50 for three francs and fifty centimes. Fr. 2.30 is 230 centimes. If an ice cream costs Fr. 2.80 and a water Fr. 1.20, you pay Fr. 4.00 together. Because there are no coins below 5 centimes, prices are **rounded** to 5 centimes at the till.

The franc is regarded worldwide as a very stable currency, which is why it is often called a **safe haven**. In uncertain times people from other countries like to buy francs. This makes the franc strong, which makes holidays abroad cheaper for Swiss people. For companies that sell goods abroad, however, a strong franc is difficult.

Swiss banknotes are among the hardest to forge in the world. They have many **security features**, such as pictures that change when you tilt them and a window made of transparent material. The notes are made of several layers of paper and plastic. This makes them especially durable.

begriffe.erklaerung: The money that is used in a country.
The hundredth part of a franc.
The country’s bank, which issues the banknotes and looks after the value of the money.
The federal mint in Bern.

gewusst: The 5-centime piece is made of aluminium bronze, which is why it looks golden.
The 1000-franc note is one of the highest-value banknotes in the world.
A globe is shown on every banknote of the current series.

teile.einleitung: A scale tells you how much something is reduced or enlarged on a map, a plan or a model. It is written as a ratio, for example 1 : 25,000. Without a scale, you could not tell from a hiking map how far it is to the next mountain hut.
wichtigste: The scale is a ratio between the length in the picture and the length in reality.
At 1 : 25,000, 1 cm on the map equals 25,000 cm, that is 250 m in reality.
At 1 : 50,000, 1 cm on the map equals 500 m in the real world.
The smaller the second number, the more detail a map shows.
A scale such as 5 : 1 means an enlargement: the picture is five times as big as the original.
Swiss national maps are available, among others, at the scales 1 : 25,000 and 1 : 50,000.
Building plans and model cars also have a scale, such as 1 : 100 or 1 : 43.

abschnitte.text: A scale compares two lengths with each other. The first number stands for the picture, the second for reality. **1 : 100** means: 1 cm on the plan is 100 cm, that is 1 m, in reality. A room 4.5 m long is therefore drawn 4.5 cm long on such a plan. The sign “:” is read as “to”, so “one to a hundred”.

The Federal Office of Topography, **swisstopo**, produces the official Swiss **national maps**. For hiking, the 1 : 25,000 map is especially popular, because it shows the most detail, such as individual houses and small paths. On the 1 : 50,000 map you see a larger area, but less precisely. There are also maps at a scale of 1 : 100,000 and even smaller overview maps of the whole of Switzerland.

To work out a real distance, you multiply the length on the map by the second number. 4 cm on a 1 : 25,000 map gives 100,000 cm, which is exactly **1 km**. The other way round, you divide: a hike of 3 km is 300,000 cm, so on a 1 : 50,000 map it is 6 cm. It is important to convert the units carefully, because 1 km is 1000 m and 100,000 cm.

Sometimes the picture is bigger than the original, for example in drawings of insects in a biology book. Then the bigger number comes first, for example **5 : 1**. If a beetle at this scale is drawn 2 cm long, in reality it measures only 2 cm divided by 5, that is 4 mm. Microscope pictures and photos of bacteria are also often labelled in this way.

Model cars are often built at a scale of **1 : 43**, so a model 10 cm long stands for a car 4.3 m long. Model railways in the popular H0 gauge have the scale 1 : 87. At the **Swissminiatur** park in Melide in Ticino, famous Swiss buildings stand at a scale of 1 : 25. Architects build models of houses so that people can picture a project better.

Many maps also have a **scale bar** printed on them, a small strip with distances in kilometres. With it you can measure distances without any calculating, for example with a piece of thread or a ruler. The bar has an advantage: if the map is copied larger or smaller, it is still correct. On map apps on a mobile phone, the scale bar adjusts automatically when you zoom.

begriffe.erklaerung: A comparison of two quantities, written with a colon.
An official map of Switzerland, produced by swisstopo.
A measuring strip on the map from which you read off distances directly.
A smaller or larger copy of a real object.

gewusst: Swiss national maps are regarded worldwide as especially accurate and beautifully drawn, above all because of the way they show rock.
A globe is also a scale model, often about 1 : 40 million.
A map at a scale of 1 : 1 would be exactly as big as the country itself and therefore completely impractical.

teile.einleitung: A postcode is a number that shows which place or area a letter or parcel should be sent to. In Switzerland it has four digits and comes before the name of the place in the address. Since it was introduced in 1964, it has helped the post office get items to their destination quickly and safely.
wichtigste: The postcode helps the post office deliver letters and parcels correctly.
Swiss postcodes have four digits.
Switzerland introduced postcodes in 1964.
On a letter the postcode comes before the name of the place, for example 3000 Bern.
The first digit shows the region: Zurich begins with 8, Geneva and Lausanne with 1, Ticino with 6.
Liechtenstein also uses the Swiss postcodes.
Many other countries have their own systems with four, five or more digits.

abschnitte.text: Every day Swiss Post sends millions of letters and parcels. For them to arrive correctly, every address needs a **postcode**. The number tells the sorting machines and the staff which area an item belongs to. Machines in large **sorting centres** can read the numbers automatically. That way a letter from Geneva reaches St. Gallen the very next day.

A Swiss postcode has **four digits**. The first digit stands for a large region, and the other digits get more and more precise. Larger towns often have several postcodes for different districts. Bern, for example, has the postcode 3000 and other numbers beginning with 30. In Zurich all postcodes begin with 80, such as 8001 for the old town.

The first digit tells you where a letter comes from or where it is going. **1** stands for western Switzerland with Geneva, Lausanne and Lower Valais. 2 is for Neuchâtel, the Jura and Biel, 3 for Bern and Upper Valais, 4 for Basel. 5 stands for Aargau, **6** for central Switzerland and Ticino, 7 for Graubünden. **8** is for Zurich and parts of eastern Switzerland, and 9 for St. Gallen, Appenzell and Liechtenstein.

Switzerland introduced four-digit postcodes on 26 July **1964**. This made it one of the first countries in Europe with a nationwide system. In the USA there have been ZIP codes since 1963. Germany already had two-digit codes in 1941 and changed to five-digit postcodes in 1993. The **Principality of Liechtenstein** is closely linked to Switzerland and still uses Swiss postcodes from 9485 to 9498 today.

On a letter the name comes first, then the street with the house number. In the last line the **postcode comes before the name of the place**, for example “3000 Bern”. For letters abroad you write the country in capital letters underneath. A wrong postcode can mean that a letter travels to the wrong town. Many places have similar names, so the right number is especially important.

Today postcodes are used for many other things too. Online shops use them to work out delivery times and postage costs. Insurance companies and public offices use them to divide up areas. In **satnavs** you can often enter the postcode first to find a place quickly. Statistics, for example about the population, are also sometimes arranged by postcode.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that shows which area an item of post belongs to.
A large building in which machines sort letters and parcels by destination.
The details of where an item is sent: name, street, postcode and place.
A larger area of a country.

gewusst: The German municipality of Büsingen on the Upper Rhine is completely surrounded by Switzerland and has a Swiss postcode as well as a German one.
Lausanne has postcodes beginning with 10, Geneva ones beginning with 12.
The postcode 3000 for Bern is easy to remember because it is such a round number.

teile.einleitung: Orthogonality is the technical word for two lines or surfaces being perpendicular to each other, that is forming a right angle. The word comes from Greek and means roughly right-angled. Right angles are all around us: on the walls of houses, the edges of tables, the pages of exercise books and at road junctions.
wichtigste: Two straight lines that cross at a right angle are perpendicular to each other.
A right angle measures exactly 90 degrees.
That two lines are perpendicular is written with the sign ⊥.
The perpendicular you drop from a point onto a line is called the perpendicular from the point.
The shortest distance from a point to a line is measured along this perpendicular.
If g is perpendicular to h and h is perpendicular to k in the same plane, then g and k are parallel.
With a set square (Geodreieck) you can draw and check right angles.

abschnitte.text: The word **orthogonal** is made from the Greek words for right or straight and for angle. Two lines are orthogonal if they cross at a **right angle**. A right angle measures 90 degrees, which is exactly a quarter of a full turn. At school people usually just say the lines are perpendicular to each other. It is written as g ⊥ h.

If you want to draw a line from a point P that meets a line at a right angle, you **drop a perpendicular**. The point where it meets the line is called the foot of the perpendicular. The segment from the point to the foot of the perpendicular is the shortest way to the line. That is why the **distance** from a point to a line is always measured along this perpendicular. Any slanting route to the line would be longer.

Perpendicular and **parallel** are closely linked. If, in a plane, g is perpendicular to h and h is perpendicular to k, then g and k run parallel side by side. You can see this well on the lines of squared paper. A **coordinate system** also consists of two axes that are perpendicular to each other. That way you can describe every point exactly with two numbers.

In maths lessons you check and draw right angles with a **set square** (Geodreieck), whose centre line is perpendicular to the long edge. On building sites, experts use a square, a spirit level and a **plumb line**, a weight on a string. The plumb line always hangs straight down, perpendicular to the ground. The ancient Egyptians already marked out right angles with a string with twelve knots, which they stretched into a triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5. Today lasers help with this too.

abschnitte.titel: In everyday life and in science
abschnitte.text: Walls stand orthogonal to the floor so that houses are stable. Many cities, such as Manhattan or La Chaux-de-Fonds in the Jura, have streets that cross at right angles. Windows, books, screens and the squares on a chessboard have right angles. In higher mathematics, orthogonality is also used for arrows, called vectors. In physics, gravity, for example, acts perpendicular to level ground.

begriffe.erklaerung: An angle of exactly 90 degrees, like the corner of a sheet of paper.
A line drawn from a point onto another line at a right angle.
Two lines that are the same distance apart everywhere and never cross.
A see-through triangle (Geodreieck) for drawing and measuring angles and lines.

gewusst: A triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 always has a right angle.
The watchmaking town of La Chaux-de-Fonds was rebuilt in a chessboard pattern after a fire and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A plumb line always points towards the centre of the Earth.

teile.einleitung: Matchstick puzzles are brain-teasers in which you lay out shapes, numbers or sums with matchsticks. Usually you have to move, take away or add a few matches to make a new shape or a correct sum. You do not need formulas for them, just good ideas and a sharp eye.
wichtigste: In matchstick puzzles you use matches to lay out shapes, numbers or sums.
Often you may only move a few matches to solve the puzzle.
You need 4 matches for a square and 3 for a triangle.
If shapes share a side, you need fewer matches.
Roman numerals are also easy to lay out with matchsticks.
The puzzles train spatial thinking and patience.
Instead of real matches you can also use toothpicks or lolly sticks.

abschnitte.text: In a **matchstick puzzle** there is a shape or a sum made of matchsticks on the table. The task might be: move two matches so that you get three squares. Sometimes a wrong sum is laid out, which you have to correct with a single match. Such puzzles have been popular in puzzle books and magazines for more than a hundred years.

For a **square** you need 4 matchsticks, for a triangle 3 and for a hexagon 6. If you lay two squares side by side, they share a side, so you need only 7 matches instead of 8. Three squares in a row need 10 matches. With 12 matches you can lay out three separate squares that do not touch.

**Roman numerals** are made of straight strokes and are therefore good for matchsticks. The number VI needs 3 matches, two for the V and one for the I. If you move the I in IV from the left to the right of the V, the 4 becomes a 6. In this way many sums can be changed with a single move.

First you should count carefully how many matches there are and how many sides the shapes you are looking for need. It often helps to place sides so that two shapes share them. Sometimes you have to **think outside the box**, for example by turning a number upside down or looking at the shape from the other side. If you keep trying and do not give up, you will often find a surprising solution.

Matches, called **Zündhölzli** in Switzerland, are made for lighting fires. For puzzles you can use burnt matches, toothpicks or lolly sticks. Children should only strike real matches together with adults. The modern **safety match**, which only lights on the striking surface of the box, was developed in Sweden in the 19th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: A quadrilateral with four sides of equal length and four right angles.
A shape with six sides and six corners, like a honeycomb cell.
The Swiss German word for match.
The number symbols of the ancient Romans, for example I, V and X.

gewusst: Some matchstick puzzles have several correct solutions.
With just 6 matches you can build four triangles of the same size if you build upwards and make a pyramid.
In Jönköping in Sweden there is a museum about matches.

teile.einleitung: Powers are a short way of writing repeated multiplication of the same number, so 2 to the power 3 equals 2 · 2 · 2 = 8. The laws of indices are rules with which you can rearrange powers quickly and cleverly. They help when calculating with very large and very small numbers, for example in science and computer science.
wichtigste: A power a to the power n means that a is multiplied by itself n times.
With the same base, the exponents are added when multiplying: 3⁴ · 3⁻² is 3² = 9.
With the same exponent you can multiply the bases: 5³ · 2³ is 10³ = 1000.
Any number except 0 to the power 0 gives 1.
A negative exponent means a reciprocal: 2⁻³ is 1/8.
A fraction in the exponent means a root: 8 to the power 2/3 is 4.
In -2⁴ the minus does not belong to the power, and the result is -16.

abschnitte.text: A **power** consists of a **base** and an **exponent**. In 2⁵, 2 is the base and 5 the exponent, and you work out 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 = 32. You read it as “2 to the power 5”. Instead of 10 · 10 · 10 you write 10³ = 1000 for short. A square with sides of 4 cm has an area of 4² = 16 cm², which is where the term “square number” comes from.

If you multiply powers with the same base, you add the exponents: a to the power m times a to the power n is a to the power (m + n). When dividing, the exponents are subtracted. If you raise a power to a power, you multiply the exponents, so (x²y³)² equals x⁴y⁶. With the same exponent you may combine the bases: 5³ · 2³ = 10³ = 1000. For fractions, too, (a/b)³ = a³/b³.

From the laws it follows that a⁰ = 1, as long as a is not 0. That is because a³ divided by a³ is 1 on the one hand and a to the power 0 on the other. A **negative exponent** means the reciprocal: 2⁻³ is 1 divided by 2³, so 1/8. So 3⁴ · 3⁻² = 3², which is 9. Fractional exponents stand for **roots**: 8 to the power 1/3 is the cube root of 8, so 2, and 8 to the power 2/3 is 2² = 4.

In -2⁴ the exponent only applies to the 2; the minus comes afterwards, and the result is -16. If you want to raise the negative number to a power, you need brackets: (-2)⁴ gives +16. Another common mistake is to work out (a + b)² as a² + b². The correct answer is a² + 2ab + b², because the laws of indices apply to products, not to sums. If you know the rules well, you avoid mistakes like these.

In science, large numbers are written with powers of ten; this is called **scientific notation**. The Earth is about 1.5 · 10⁸ km from the Sun. Small numbers are written with negative exponents: a millimetre is 10⁻³ m. Prefixes such as kilo, mega and giga stand for 10³, 10⁶ and 10⁹. In computer science people often count in powers of two: 2¹⁰ gives 1024.

An old legend from India tells of the inventor of chess. As a reward he asked for one grain of rice or wheat on the first square, two on the second, four on the third and always twice as many. On the last square there would be 2⁶³ grains. Altogether that makes more than 18 quintillion grains (18 followed by 18 zeros), far more than has ever been harvested on the whole Earth. The story shows how fast powers grow; this is called **exponential growth**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number that is multiplied by itself several times.
The raised number that shows how many times you multiply.
A number with the numerator and denominator swapped; the reciprocal of 8 is 1/8.
Growth in which a quantity keeps multiplying.

gewusst: If you folded a sheet of paper 10 times, it would be 2¹⁰ = 1024 layers thick, but in practice you can hardly manage more than 7 folds.
In the 17th century the French philosopher René Descartes made today's way of writing raised exponents popular.
A one with a hundred zeros, that is 10¹⁰⁰, is called a googol.

teile.einleitung: A percentage point is the unit for the difference between two percentages. If an interest rate rises from 2% to 3%, it has risen by 1 percentage point, but by 50 per cent. If you know this difference, you understand news about elections, interest rates and taxes much better.
wichtigste: A percentage point describes the simple gap between two percentages.
If a value rises from 20% to 25%, that is 5 percentage points.
The change in per cent, on the other hand, measures how much the value has changed in relation to the starting value.
From 2% to 3% is plus 1 percentage point or plus 50%.
The standard rate of Swiss VAT rose in 2024 by 0.4 percentage points, from 7.7% to 8.1%.
100 basis points equal 1 percentage point.
Percentage points and per cent are often mixed up in the media.

abschnitte.text: A **percentage point** is the difference between two percentages. You simply take the new value minus the old value. If turnout rises from 45% to 48%, the difference is 3 percentage points. So percentage points tell you how far apart two values are on the percentage scale.

The **relative change** in per cent asks: by what share of the old value has something changed? If an unemployment rate rises from 4% to 5%, that is 1 percentage point, but 25% more, because 1 is a quarter of 4. If an interest rate rises from 3% to 6%, it has doubled, so it has increased by 100%. For turnout going from 45% to 48%, that gives 6.7% when rounded.

It works in just the same way when values fall. If a share falls from 10% to 8%, it drops by 2 percentage points. In relation to the starting value, however, that is a fall of 20%, because 2 is a fifth of 10. Anyone who just says “fell by 2 per cent” is therefore describing the situation wrongly.

After elections the media report how many percentage points a party has gained or lost. If a **share of the vote** rises from 20% to 25%, the party has gained 5 percentage points. For VAT, the standard rate rose on 1 January 2024 from 7.7% to 8.1%, so by 0.4 percentage points. The Swiss National Bank also gives changes to its key interest rate in this way.

For interest rates, experts often use even smaller units, **basis points**. One basis point is a hundredth of a percentage point. If a central bank raises its key interest rate by 50 basis points, that is 0.5 percentage points. This way even tiny changes in interest rates can be described precisely.

begriffe.erklaerung: The gap between two percentages; for example, from 3% to 5% is 2 percentage points.
How much a value changes compared with its starting value, given in per cent.
A hundredth of a percentage point, so 0.01 percentage points.
The most important interest rate of a central bank, which other interest rates follow.

gewusst: An increase of only 1 percentage point can mean a doubling if the starting value was 1%.
The abbreviation for percentage points is often “pp”, especially in business texts.
Even experts sometimes mix up per cent and percentage points, which is why newspapers keep printing corrections about it.

teile.einleitung: A quadrilateral is a flat shape with four corners and four sides. Squares, rectangles, rhombuses, trapeziums and kites are special quadrilaterals. You find quadrilaterals everywhere, from windows to exercise books to football pitches.
wichtigste: A quadrilateral has four corners, four sides and four angles.
The angles in every quadrilateral add up to 360°.
A trapezium has one pair of parallel sides.
In a parallelogram opposite sides are parallel.
In a rectangle the two diagonals are the same length.
In a rhombus the diagonals are perpendicular to each other.
The square is the most regular quadrilateral; it is both a rectangle and a rhombus.

abschnitte.text: A **quadrilateral** is a polygon with exactly four corners. Between the corners there are four sides, and at each corner there is an angle. A triangle is not a quadrilateral, and neither is a pentagon. The lines joining opposite corners are called **diagonals**.

In every quadrilateral the four interior angles add up to **360°**. This is easy to show: a diagonal divides the quadrilateral into two triangles of 180° each. In a parallelogram two neighbouring angles add up to 180°. So if one angle measures 70°, the neighbouring angle measures 110°.

The **trapezium** has one pair of parallel sides. In a **parallelogram** both pairs of opposite sides are parallel. The rhombus has four sides of equal length, the rectangle four right angles. The square has both: sides of equal length and right angles.

The **kite** consists of two pairs of neighbouring sides of equal length. It looks like a paper kite that you fly in autumn. One of its diagonals is a line of symmetry. The rhombus is also a special kind of kite.

We come across quadrilaterals everywhere: doors, windows, books, mobile phone screens and chessboards are rectangles or squares. Many road signs have the shape of a rhombus or a rectangle. Football pitches and tennis courts are rectangles. Architects often design houses from rectangular rooms, because they are easy to furnish.

begriffe.erklaerung: A line joining two opposite corners.
Two lines that are the same distance apart everywhere and never meet.
A quadrilateral with one pair of parallel sides.
A quadrilateral with four sides of equal length, also called a diamond.

gewusst: A chessboard is made up of 64 small squares.
The flag of Switzerland is one of the few square national flags in the world.
Every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square.

teile.einleitung: The Mandelbrot set is a famous figure from mathematics which, because of its shape, is also called the “Apfelmännchen” (little apple man) in German-speaking countries. It is made from a very simple calculation rule that a computer applies again and again. The result is an infinitely finely branched picture in which you keep discovering new patterns as you zoom in.
wichtigste: The Mandelbrot set is produced with the rule “new z equals z² + c”, starting with z = 0.
A number c belongs to the set if the numbers do not grow to infinity.
As soon as the modulus of z is greater than 2, you know for certain that the sequence will run away.
The set is drawn in the complex plane, the plane of complex numbers.
On the real axis, the range from -2 to 1/4 belongs to the set.
It is named after Benoît Mandelbrot, who studied fractals with computers at the company IBM.
The Mandelbrot set is the best-known example of a fractal.

abschnitte.text: You choose a number c and start with z = 0. Then you work out **new z = z² + c** again and again. This repetition is called **iteration**. For c = 1 you get the sequence 0, 1, 2, 5, 26 and so on, so the numbers keep getting bigger. For c = -1, on the other hand, the sequence jumps back and forth between 0 and -1 for ever and stays small, so -1 belongs to the Mandelbrot set.

The Mandelbrot set consists of **complex numbers**. These are numbers with two parts that can be shown as points on a plane, the **complex plane**. So every point in the picture is a number c of its own, for which the computer tests the calculation rule. If the sequence stays bounded, the point is usually coloured black. If it runs away, it gets a colour depending on how quickly it goes past the modulus 2.

The shape is reminiscent of a little man made of a fat apple with a smaller head next to it. Countless smaller buds sit on the edge, and smaller ones again on these. If you zoom in, you find spirals, seahorse shapes and even tiny copies of the whole figure. This property is called **self-similarity** and is typical of fractals. The whole figure lies inside a circle with radius 2 around zero.

**Benoît Mandelbrot** lived from 1924 to 2010 and was born in Warsaw. For many years he worked as a researcher at the computer company **IBM** in the USA. In 1975 he coined the word “fractal”, which comes from the Latin word for “broken”. Around 1980 he had computers draw the first pictures of the set. French mathematicians such as Gaston Julia had already studied similar questions around 1918, but without computers they could not see the pictures.

The Mandelbrot set shows how incredibly complicated shapes can arise from a very simple rule. Fractals help to describe things in nature, such as coastlines, clouds, lightning, ferns or cauliflower. In **computer graphics** fractal methods are used to create mountains and landscapes for films and games. Many people also program the Mandelbrot set simply because the pictures are so beautiful.

begriffe.erklaerung: A shape in which similar patterns repeat again and again on a small scale.
A calculation is repeated again and again with its own result.
A number with two parts that can be drawn as a point on a plane.
A part looks roughly like the whole.

gewusst: However far you zoom into the edge of the Mandelbrot set, you always find new patterns, because the edge is infinitely finely branched.
Although the figure fits into a circle with radius 2, its edge is infinitely long.
The number c = -2 is the point of the Mandelbrot set that lies furthest to the left.

teile.einleitung: The logarithm answers the question of which exponent you must raise a base to in order to get a particular number. So log₂(8) = 3, because 2 to the power 3 is 8. Logarithms turn multiplications into additions and were therefore an important calculating aid for centuries.
wichtigste: The logarithm is the reverse of raising to a power.
log₂(8) = 3, because 2³ = 8.
log₁₀(0.01) = -2, because 10⁻² = 0.01.
For every allowed base, log_b(1) = 0.
log(a · b) = log(a) + log(b).
The natural logarithm ln has Euler's number e as its base.
Jost Bürgi from Lichtensteig in the Toggenburg developed tables of logarithms independently of John Napier.

abschnitte.text: When raising to a power, you ask: what is 2 to the power 5? Answer: 32. The **logarithm** asks the other way round: 2 to the power of what gives 32? Answer: 5, written log₂(32) = 5. The small lowered number is called the **base**. That is why logarithms are used to solve equations such as 2ˣ = 32, in which the unknown is in the exponent.

The most important rule is: log(a · b) = log(a) + log(b). In this way a difficult multiplication becomes a simple addition. In addition, log(aⁿ) = n · log(a), so log₂(4⁵) = 5 · 2 = 10. Because every number to the power 0 is 1, log_b(1) = 0 for every allowed base. These **laws of logarithms** used to make laborious calculations much quicker.

At the beginning of the 17th century, two men developed tables of logarithms independently of each other. The Scotsman **John Napier** published his tables in 1614. The clockmaker and instrument maker **Jost Bürgi** from Lichtensteig in the Toggenburg had calculated similar tables even earlier but only published them in Prague in 1620. Bürgi worked at the imperial court and also helped the astronomer Johannes Kepler there.

The **common logarithm** has the base 10, so log₁₀(1000) = 3 and log₁₀(0.01) = -2. The Englishman Henry Briggs made it popular for tables in the 17th century. The **natural logarithm** ln has Euler's number e, about 2.718, as its base and is especially important in science and engineering. In computer science people often calculate with the logarithm to base 2.

Many measuring scales are logarithmic, because they make huge differences manageable. Loudness in **decibels** goes up by 10 dB when the sound power increases tenfold. On the Richter scale for earthquakes, one step more means a ten times bigger swing on the measuring instrument. The pH value, which tells you how acidic a liquid is, is also based on the common logarithm. Until the 1970s engineers calculated with the slide rule, which is based on logarithms.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number that is multiplied by itself several times when raising to a power.
The raised number that says how many times the base is multiplied by itself.
A book with long tables in which you could look up logarithms.
A calculating device with sliding scales, used for multiplying before the calculator.

gewusst: Jost Bürgi also built artistic celestial globes and clocks that can be admired in museums today.
The Apollo astronauts also had slide rules with them on their flight to the Moon.
A sound that is 20 decibels louder has a hundred times the sound power.

teile.einleitung: Proportionality is a special relationship between two quantities: if one becomes twice as big, the other also becomes twice as big. You come across relationships like this all the time, for example when shopping, filling up with petrol or cooking. If you recognise them, you can solve many problems in your head in a flash.
wichtigste: In a proportional relationship, double x goes with double y, and triple x with triple y.
The quotient y divided by x is the same for all pairs of values and is called the constant of proportionality.
Every proportional relationship can be described with the formula y = k · x.
The graph of a proportional relationship is a straight line through the origin.
With a fixed price per kilo, the amount of minced meat and the price are proportional to each other.
If there is a basic charge, as with a taxi, the relationship is no longer proportional.
With the rule of three, proportional problems can be solved step by step.

abschnitte.text: Two quantities are **proportional** if they grow or shrink in the same ratio. If you triple x, y is tripled too. If you halve x, y is halved too. If x = 0 goes with y = 0, that is a first sign of a proportional relationship.

If you divide y by x in a proportional relationship, the same number always comes out. This number is called the **constant of proportionality** and is often shortened to k. For the pairs of values (1|4), (2|8) and (3|12), k = 4, because 4 : 1 = 8 : 2 = 12 : 3 = 4. If y = 2.5 · x, then x = 8 goes with y = 20. Tables like these are also said to have **equal quotients**.

If you plot the pairs of values in a coordinate system, they all lie on a **straight line**. This line always passes through the **origin** (0|0). The bigger the constant of proportionality, the more steeply the line rises. This lets you recognise a proportional relationship at a glance.

If a kilogram of minced meat costs 20 francs, 2 kilograms cost 40 francs and half a kilogram 10 francs. The amount of petrol and the price at the pump are proportional too. When cycling at the same speed, the distance is proportional to the time. A taxi with a basic charge of 6 francs and 3 francs per kilometre, on the other hand, is not proportional, because the ride already costs something at 0 kilometres.

The **rule of three** is a popular method for proportional problems. If, in a table, x = 4 goes with y = 10, you first work back to x = 1 and get 2.5. Then you multiply by 10 and get y = 25. That way you reach the answer safely in three steps.

There are also relationships in which one quantity gets smaller when the other grows. If twice as many people work on a task, they need only half as long. Relationships like these are called **inversely proportional**. Here it is not the quotient but the product x · y that always stays the same.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rule that gives each value of one quantity a value of another quantity.
The fixed number by which you multiply x to get y.
A method in three steps for finding an unknown value with proportional quantities.
When one quantity becomes twice as big, the other becomes half as big.

gewusst: The word proportion comes from Latin and means roughly “ratio”.
A town map with a scale is proportional too: distances twice as long on the map are also twice as long in reality.
Many calculation mistakes when shopping happen because people overlook a basic charge or a bulk discount and wrongly calculate proportionally.

teile.einleitung: In an optimisation problem you look for the best of many possible solutions, for example the largest area, the least material used or the highest profit. Tasks like this come up all the time at school, in technology and in business. The derivative from differential calculus often helps.
wichtigste: An optimisation problem looks for the largest or smallest value of a quantity.
The quantity to be optimised is called the objective function.
A constraint links two variables so that you can replace one of them.
You often find the optimum where the derivative is zero.
You must also check the edges of the domain, because the optimum can lie there.
For positive x, x + 1/x is smallest at x = 1.
A cylindrical tin needs the least metal when its height equals its diameter.

abschnitte.text: In an **optimisation problem** there are many possible solutions, and you are looking for the best one. What “best” means is set by the **objective function**, such as an area, a volume, costs or a profit. Usually there are restrictions, for example a fixed length of fence or a fixed volume. These restrictions are called **constraints**. The best value is called the optimum, that is a maximum or a minimum.

First you write down the objective function, which usually depends on two variables. Using the constraint, you replace one variable so that only one is left. Then you find the **derivative** and set it equal to zero, because at a high or low point the curve is horizontal. Finally you check whether it really is a maximum or a minimum. It is also important to look at the edges, because the optimum can lie there without the derivative being zero.

A rectangle is to be fenced off against a wall with 60 m of fence. The best solution has two sides of 15 m and one side of 30 m, which gives **450 m²**. From a square piece of card with sides of 12 cm you fold a box that is open at the top. You get the largest volume if you cut squares of 2 cm out of the corners. For a rectangle under the parabola y = 12 − x², the largest possible area is 32.

A drinks can or tin with a fixed volume needs the least metal when its height equals its diameter. Many real tins differ from this because they are meant to sit well in the hand. **Honeycombs** are made of hexagons, which give a lot of space for little wax. Engineers optimise bridges, aeroplane wings and cars so that they are strong and light at the same time. Of all shapes with the same perimeter, the **circle** encloses the largest area.

Companies want to maximise their profit. For the profit function G(x) = −2x² + 80x − 300, the highest profit comes at 20 items sold and is 500 francs. Navigation apps look for the fastest or shortest route; that is also an optimisation problem. In the famous **travelling salesman problem**, someone has to visit many cities by the shortest route. With many cities this is extremely difficult even for computers.

The ancient Greeks already knew optimisation questions, such as which shape has the largest area for a given perimeter. With the **differential calculus** of Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in the 17th century, such problems could be solved systematically. In the 20th century **linear optimisation** was developed, used for example to plan transport or production. Today optimisation is a large field of its own in mathematics and computer science.

begriffe.erklaerung: The quantity that is to be as large or as small as possible.
A restriction that the solution must keep to.
Shows how steep a curve is at a certain point.
The largest value a quantity can take.
The smallest value a quantity can take.

gewusst: Soap bubbles are round because, for a given volume, the sphere has the smallest surface.
Bees build their honeycombs from hexagons, a shape that creates a lot of space with little wax.
Even for 20 cities, the travelling salesman problem has more possible routes than a person could ever try out.

teile.einleitung: A linear equation is an equation in which the unknown x appears only simply, that is not as x² or x³. Such equations are the most common at school and in everyday life. If you draw them, you always get a straight line.
wichtigste: In a linear equation the variable appears only to the first power.
The solution of 3x + 7 = 22 is x = 5.
You solve them with equivalent transformations, that is the same steps on both sides.
A linear function such as y = mx + q gives a straight line in a coordinate system.
Two linear equations with two variables form a system of equations.
A system of equations can have one, no or infinitely many solutions.
Many price calculations, for example taxi fares, lead to linear equations.

abschnitte.text: The word **linear** comes from the Latin linea, the line. In a linear equation x appears only “simply”, at most multiplied by a number, as in 5x − 3 = 12. Expressions such as x² or 1/x do not appear. That is why a linear equation with one variable usually has exactly one solution.

You rearrange the equation so that x is on its own. For 5(x − 2) = 3x + 4 you first multiply out: 5x − 10 = 3x + 4. Then you bring all the x terms to the left and all the numbers to the right and get 2x = 14, so x = 7. With fractions such as 2x/3 − 4 = 6 you first add 4, then multiply by 3 and divide by 2, giving x = 15. Such steps are called **equivalent transformations**.

In Switzerland a linear function is often written as y = mx + q. The number m is the **gradient**; it says how steep the line is. The number q tells you where the line crosses the y-axis. Solving a linear equation means, as a picture, finding the point where the line reaches a particular height.

If you have two unknowns, you need two equations, a **system of equations**. From x + y = 10 and x − y = 4, adding gives 2x = 14, so x = 7 and y = 3.
