Lengths are measured in millimetres, centimetres, decimetres, metres and kilometres.
Masses are measured in milligrams, grams, kilograms and tonnes.
Prefixes such as kilo, centi and milli show how big a unit is.
Centi means a hundredth, milli a thousandth and kilo a thousand times.
The International System of Units has seven base units.
Before converting, you often have to put everything into the same unit.

abschnitte.titel: What is a unit of measurement?
abschnitte.text: If you say a table is 2 metres long, the **metre** is the unit and 2 is the number. Together they make a **quantity**. Units of measurement are agreements so that everyone measures in the same way. There are separate units for each kind of quantity: the metre for lengths, the kilogram for masses and the second for time. Without a unit, a number like 5 does not tell you much.

Many units get **prefixes** that change their size. **Kilo** means a thousand times, so 3.5 km is exactly 3500 m. **Centi** means a hundredth and **milli** a thousandth. Deci stands for a tenth, which is why a metre has 10 decimetres. These prefixes work the same way for many units, for example for the kilogram, the millilitre or the kilowatt.

For lengths: 1 cm is 10 mm, so 45 mm is exactly 4.5 cm. For masses, 1000 mg are a gram, 1000 g a kilogram and 1000 kg a tonne. So a tonne has 1,000,000 g, and 2.4 tonnes are 2400 kg. 750 g is 0.75 kg. If you want to add values, you must first convert them into the **same unit**: 5 dm and 30 cm are 50 cm plus 30 cm, that is 80 cm.

The **International System of Units**, SI for short, has seven base units. They include the metre, the kilogram, the second, the ampere for current, the kelvin for temperature, the mole for the amount of substance and the candela for luminous intensity. Today the metre is defined using the speed of light, that is the distance light travels in a certain tiny time. Since 2019 the kilogram has also been defined using a **constant of nature** and no longer by a piece of metal in Paris. That way the units are equally precise everywhere in the world.

In the past almost every town had its own measures such as the **ell**, the foot or the pound. A foot was a different length in Zurich from one in Bern, which made trade difficult. In France, after the Revolution around 1790, the **metric system** with the metre came into being. Switzerland introduced it nationwide in the 19th century. Today the Federal Institute of Metrology, METAS, in Bern-Wabern makes sure that scales and measuring devices in Switzerland measure correctly.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number in front of the unit, for example the 2 in 2 metres.
A word part such as kilo or milli that says how much bigger or smaller a unit is.
The International System of Units, used almost everywhere in the world.
The science of precise measurement.

gewusst: An ell was originally about the length of a forearm and so differed from place to place.
In the USA people still often measure in inches, feet and miles in everyday life instead of metres.
A litre of water weighs about one kilogram.

teile.einleitung: A pyramid is a geometric solid with a polygon as its base and triangular side faces that meet at a point. The best known are the pyramids in Egypt, which were built more than 4500 years ago as tombs for kings. In maths you learn how to calculate their volume and surface area.
wichtigste: A pyramid has a base and side faces made of triangles that meet at an apex.
The volume is one third times base area times height.
A square pyramid with a base edge of 6 cm and a height of 10 cm has a volume of 120 cm³.
A pyramid with a hexagon as its base has 12 edges.
With a base edge of 6 cm and a height of 4 cm, the lateral surface of a square pyramid is 60 cm².
The Great Pyramid of Giza was originally about 146.6 m high and had a volume of about 2.6 million m³.
A pyramid with a triangle as its base is called a tetrahedron.

abschnitte.text: A **pyramid** has a polygon as its **base** and a point above it, the **apex**. If you join each corner of the base to the apex, you get triangular side faces, which together form the lateral surface. Depending on the base, we speak of triangular, square or hexagonal pyramids. A pyramid with a triangle as its base is called a **tetrahedron**. If the apex lies exactly above the centre of the base, the pyramid is a right pyramid.

If the base has n corners, the pyramid has n plus 1 vertices, namely those of the base and the apex. It has 2n edges: n edges around the base and n edges leading to the apex. So a pyramid with a hexagonal base has 12 edges and 7 vertices. The number of faces is also n plus 1. A square pyramid therefore has 5 vertices, 8 edges and 5 faces.

The **volume** of a pyramid is exactly one third of the volume of a prism with the same base and height. The formula is V equals one third times G times h. For a square pyramid with a base edge of 6 cm and a height of 10 cm, the base area is 36 cm². One third of 36 times 10 gives 120 cm³. You can remember that three identical pyramids together take up as much space as a matching cube or cuboid.

The lateral surface of a square pyramid consists of four identical triangles. To work out their area you need the height of a side triangle, the **slant height**. It can be calculated using Pythagoras’ theorem from half the base edge and the height of the solid. With a base edge of 6 cm and a height of 4 cm, this gives the square root of 3² plus 4², which is 5 cm. One triangle then has 6 times 5 divided by 2, which is 15 cm², and the whole lateral surface 60 cm².

The Egyptian pyramids were built around 4500 years ago as tombs for the kings, the **pharaohs**. The largest is the **Great Pyramid of Khufu** at Giza near Cairo; it was originally about 146.6 m high. Its square base has a side length of about 230.3 m. Its volume is roughly 230.3 times 230.3 times 146.6 divided by 3, which is about 2.6 million m³. For more than 3800 years it was the tallest building in the world.

The Maya and Aztecs in Central America also built pyramids, often with steps and a temple on top. In Paris a modern pyramid made of glass and steel has stood in front of the Louvre museum since 1989. Small pyramid shapes can be found in tents, church spires and some packaging. The shape is very stable because the weight from above is spread over a wide area. That is why the ancient pyramids have survived for thousands of years.

begriffe.erklaerung: The highest point of a pyramid, where all the side edges meet.
A pyramid made of four equilateral triangles.
The height of a side triangle of a pyramid.
A king in ancient Egypt.

gewusst: The Great Pyramid of Giza is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that is still standing today.
Because the outer casing and the tip are missing, the Great Pyramid is now only about 138 m high.

teile.einleitung: A mathematical proof shows beyond any doubt that a statement is always true. It is not enough to try out a few examples. You have to show with logical steps, starting from secure foundations, that it cannot be otherwise.
wichtigste: A proof shows that a mathematical statement is true in all cases.
Examples alone prove nothing, but a single counterexample can disprove a statement.
The number 2 disproves the statement “All prime numbers are odd”.
With a proof by contradiction you show that √2 is not a fraction.
In proof by induction you prove a starting case and a step from n to n + 1.
More than 2000 years ago Euclid proved that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
In the 1990s Andrew Wiles proved Fermat's Last Theorem.

abschnitte.text: In the natural sciences, ideas are tested with experiments. In mathematics that is not enough: a **proof** must show that a statement holds for all cases, even for infinitely many numbers. You start with basic assumptions, the **axioms**, and reason onwards step by step. Once a theorem has been proved, it holds for ever.

To disprove a statement, a single **counterexample** is enough. The claim “All prime numbers are odd” is not true, because 2 is a prime number and even. On the other hand, even a thousand examples that fit do not prove a statement. There could always be a very large number for which it suddenly stops working.

In a **direct proof** you reason step by step from what is known. In a **proof by contradiction** you assume the opposite and show that something impossible then follows; this is the classic way of proving that √2 is irrational. Instead of “If A, then B” you can also prove the contrapositive “If not B, then not A”, which is equivalent. In **proof by induction** you show that a statement holds for the start and always carries over from n to n + 1, like a row of falling dominoes.

Around 300 BC the Greek mathematician **Euclid** wrote the “Elements”, one of the most influential books in history. In it he proved that there are infinitely many prime numbers. Another well-known proof shows that 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n always gives n(n + 1)/2. The story goes that the young Carl Friedrich Gauss calculated the sum of the numbers from 1 to 100 at lightning speed at school in this way: 5050.

In 1637 the Frenchman **Pierre de Fermat** wrote in the margin of a book that he had found a wonderful proof of a theorem, but the margin was too narrow. For more than 350 years mathematicians tried in vain to prove this Fermat's Last Theorem. Only the Englishman **Andrew Wiles** managed it in 1994, after years of secret work. His proof is more than 100 pages long.

Some proofs are so long that computers have to help. The **four colour theorem**, which says that every map can be coloured with four colours, was proved in 1976 with the help of a computer. Today there are programs that check proofs step by step. But many big questions in mathematics, such as Goldbach's conjecture, are still unproved today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic assumption that is taken as true without proof.
A mathematical statement that has been proved.
A statement believed to be true that has not yet been proved.
A case that shows that a claim is false.
The equivalent reversed form “If not B, then not A”.

gewusst: At the end of a proof people often write q.e.d., Latin for “which was to be proved”.
Several hundred different proofs of Pythagoras' theorem are known.
In the 18th century Leonhard Euler from Basel proved so many theorems that his collected works fill more than 70 volumes.

teile.einleitung: A recipe is a set of instructions for cooking or baking that tells you exactly which ingredients you need and how much of each. It gets interesting when you want to cook for more or fewer people: then you have to convert the quantities. That turns the kitchen into a maths room.
wichtigste: A recipe consists of a list of ingredients with quantities and a set of instructions.
Quantities are given, for example, in grams (g), kilograms (kg), decilitres (dl) or litres (l).
tsp stands for teaspoon and tbsp for tablespoon.
If you double a recipe, all the quantities double: 200 g of flour becomes 400 g.
If you halve a recipe, all the quantities are halved: instead of 600 g of pasta you need 300 g.
The amount of ingredients and the number of people are proportional to each other.
Baking and cooking times usually do not change by the same amount when you double a recipe.

abschnitte.text: A **recipe** describes how to prepare a dish. At the top it usually says how many people it is meant for. Then comes the **list of ingredients** with exact quantities. Finally there are the instructions, step by step, often with the oven temperature and times.

Solid ingredients such as flour, sugar or butter are usually weighed in **grams**; 1000 g is 1 kg. Liquids such as milk are measured in decilitres or litres; in Switzerland the decilitre is especially popular. Small quantities are given in spoons: **tsp** stands for teaspoon and tbsp for tablespoon. A tablespoon holds about 15 millilitres, a teaspoon about 5 millilitres, and a pinch is as much as you can hold between two fingers.

If you want to cook for twice as many people, you multiply all the quantities by 2. If a cake needs 2 eggs, 2 cakes need 4 eggs, and 3 tablespoons of sugar become 6. A recipe for 4 people with 1 litre of milk needs 2 litres for 8 people. This relationship is called **proportional**, because all the quantities grow in the same ratio.

For awkward numbers of people the **rule of three** helps. If a recipe for 6 people needs 600 g of pasta, you first work out 600 : 6 = 100 g per person. For 3 people it is then 300 g, for 5 people 500 g. It only gets tricky with ingredients such as eggs that cannot easily be divided; then you round sensibly.

Not everything in the kitchen behaves proportionally. A cake twice as big does not need twice as long in the oven, only a little longer. You should also be careful with spices when multiplying and rather add more later. The right **baking tin** must also suit the new amount of mixture.

In Switzerland many young people learn to cook in home economics lessons with the well-known school cookbook “Tiptopf”. Popular Swiss recipes include Bircher muesli, rösti, plaited bread (Zopf) and fondue. Bircher muesli was invented by the doctor Maximilian **Bircher-Benner** around 1900 in Zurich. Today there are also countless recipes on the internet and in apps.

begriffe.erklaerung: A food you need for a dish.
A unit of weight; 1000 grams are 1 kilogram.
A tenth of a litre, that is 100 millilitres.
A tiny amount, for example of salt, that you take between two fingers.

gewusst: The word recipe comes from the Latin “recipe”, which means “take”.
In the past “Rp.” for “recipe” also appeared on doctors’ orders, which is why a doctor’s prescription is also called a “Rezept” in German.
In baking, weighing exactly is much more important than in cooking, because even small differences change the mixture.

teile.einleitung: The litre is a unit of volume, that is of how much fits into a container. Milk, water, petrol or squash are measured in litres. A litre is exactly as much as fits into a cube with an edge length of 10 cm.
wichtigste: A litre has 10 decilitres.
A litre has 1000 millilitres.
The abbreviation for decilitre is dl.
Half a litre is 5 decilitres, 3 litres are 30 decilitres.
An ordinary drinking glass holds about 2 decilitres.
A bath holds much more than 10 litres.
A litre of water weighs about 1 kilogram.

abschnitte.text: The **litre** measures **volume**, that is how much space a liquid or another substance takes up. Its abbreviation is l or L. A litre corresponds exactly to a cubic decimetre, that is a cube of 10 cm by 10 cm by 10 cm. A typical carton of milk or a large bottle of water contains one litre or a little more.

A litre can be divided into smaller parts. 1 litre is 10 **decilitres** (dl), 100 centilitres (cl) or 1000 **millilitres** (ml). In Switzerland people very often calculate with decilitres in everyday life, for example in recipes or in restaurants. Half a litre is 5 dl, 3 litres are 30 dl. Medicines and perfume are measured in millilitres.

An ordinary **drinking glass** holds about 2 dl, and a cup about the same. A bucket often holds 10 litres. A full bath needs well over 100 litres of water. For large amounts such as wine, or milk on a farm, the **hectolitre** is used, which is 100 litres.

A litre of water weighs about 1 **kilogram**. That is no coincidence: at the end of the 18th century in France, the kilogram was defined by the mass of a litre of water. Other liquids are lighter or heavier; a litre of cooking oil, for example, weighs less than a kilogram. That is why oil floats on water.

The litre was introduced in France in 1795 as part of the new **metric system**. Before that, almost every region had its own units of capacity, for example the Mass or the Eimer, which were different sizes everywhere. Switzerland also introduced metric units in the 19th century. Today the litre is used worldwide; only in a few countries such as the USA do people still often calculate with gallons in everyday life.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much space something takes up or how much fits into a container.
A tenth of a litre, shortened to dl.
A thousandth of a litre, shortened to ml.
100 litres, shortened to hl.

gewusst: A person should drink about 1.5 litres a day, and more on hot days and when doing sport.
A teaspoon holds about 5 millilitres, so you would need about 200 teaspoons for a litre.
The capital letter L is allowed as the abbreviation, so that the small l is not confused with the digit 1.

teile.einleitung: The perpendicular bisector of a line segment is a straight line that cuts the segment exactly in the middle at a right angle. Every point on it is the same distance from both ends of the segment. With compasses and a ruler you can construct it without any measuring.
wichtigste: The perpendicular bisector is the perpendicular line through the midpoint of a segment.
All points on the perpendicular bisector of AB are the same distance from A and B.
You construct it with two arcs of the same size around A and B.
The radius of the compasses must be greater than half the length of the segment.
A triangle has 3 perpendicular bisectors, which meet in one point.
This meeting point is the centre of the circumcircle.
If you reflect a point P in a line g, then g is the perpendicular bisector of the segment PP'.

abschnitte.text: A **line segment** is a straight connection between two points A and B. Its **midpoint** M lies exactly in the middle, so with a segment 9 cm long it is 4.5 cm from A. The perpendicular bisector passes through M and stands at a right angle, that is at 90 degrees, to the segment. Unlike the segment, it is a straight line and so infinitely long.

Every point on the perpendicular bisector is exactly the same distance from A and from B. The other way round, every point that is the same distance from A and B lies on the perpendicular bisector. That is why it is called the **locus** of all points at the same distance from A and B. This property makes it very useful in many problems.

You put the point of the **compasses** on A and draw an arc above and below the segment. With the same radius you do the same around B. The two arcs cross at two points, which you join with the ruler. It is important that the radius is greater than half the segment. With a segment 6 cm long, a radius of 2 cm is not enough, because then the arcs do not meet at all.

A triangle has three sides and so three perpendicular bisectors. These three always meet at a single point, the **circumcentre**. Around this point you can draw a circle that passes through all three corners, the circumcircle. To find the point, 2 perpendicular bisectors are enough, because the third one passes through the same meeting point anyway. In a right-angled triangle this point lies exactly in the middle of the longest side.

The perpendicular bisector helps with practical questions. Two villages, for example, want a shared bus stop on a road that is the same distance from both. Then you look for the point where the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them crosses the road. It is also important in **reflection**: the mirror line is always the perpendicular bisector between a point and its mirror image. With perpendicular bisectors you can also divide a map into areas that are each closest to a school or a hospital.

begriffe.erklaerung: The shortest straight connection between two points.
At a right angle, that is at 90 degrees, to a line.
A circle that passes through all the corners of a triangle.
A drawing instrument used to draw circles and arcs.

gewusst: More than 2000 years ago the Greek mathematician Euclid described how to halve a line segment with compasses and a ruler.
In an obtuse-angled triangle the circumcentre lies outside the triangle.
If you fold a sheet of paper so that two points lie on top of each other, the fold line is exactly their perpendicular bisector.

teile.einleitung: Per cent means “out of a hundred”. Percentages make it easy to compare shares, no matter how big the whole is. Whether it is a discount in a shop, interest on a savings account or the result of a vote, percentages are everywhere.
wichtigste: One per cent is one hundredth, 1 % = 1/100.
The word comes from the Italian “per cento”, meaning “out of a hundred”.
Percentage calculations involve three quantities: the base value, the percentage value and the percentage rate.
If a jumper costing 120 francs is reduced by 20 %, it then costs 96 francs.
If a price rises by 10 % and then falls by 10 %, it ends up lower than at the start.
Since 2024, VAT in Switzerland has normally been 8.1 %.

abschnitte.text: The sign **%** stands for hundredths. 50 % means half, 25 % a quarter and 12.5 % an eighth. 100 % is the whole. This lets you compare shares: if Nino scores 18 out of 24 points, that is 75 %, exactly the same as 3 out of 4 points.

Every percentage calculation has three parts. The **base value** is the whole, that is 100 %. The **percentage value** is the part of it, and the **percentage rate** tells you how many per cent it is. In “15 % of 240 is 36”, 240 is the base value, 15 % the percentage rate and 36 the percentage value.

Many people work via one per cent: 1 % of 240 is 2.4, so 15 % is exactly 15 · 2.4 = 36. If you are looking for the base value, you work backwards: if 30 % of a number is 45, then 1 % is 1.5 and 100 % is 150. For discounts you often calculate directly with what is left: 20 % off means paying 80 %, and 80 % of 120 francs is 96 francs. The **rule of three** in three lines is also helpful.

In the sales, signs show discounts such as “minus 30 %”. A savings account pays **interest**: if 5000 francs earn 2 % interest, you receive 100 francs after one year. When shopping in Switzerland you pay **value added tax (VAT)**; since 2024 it has normally been 8.1 %, and 2.6 % for food and books. In votes, too, the yes votes are given as a percentage.

Percentages always refer to a particular base value, and that can change. If a price of 200 francs rises by 10 %, it costs 220 francs. If it then falls by 10 %, you calculate 10 % of 220 francs, which is 22 francs, leaving a price of 198 francs. That is why an increase and an equally large decrease do not cancel each other out.

Even in ancient Rome taxes were calculated in hundredths. In the Middle Ages Italian merchants calculated “per cento”, which became the word **per cent**. Over time the abbreviation turned into today’s sign %. There is also the per mille sign ‰, which means thousandths.

begriffe.erklaerung: The whole you start from; it corresponds to 100 %.
How many hundredths you take, for example 20 %.
The part that corresponds to the percentage rate.
Money you receive for savings or pay for a loan.
A price reduction, often given as a percentage.

gewusst: More than 100 % is possible when something grows: if a price doubles, it has risen by 100 %.
The human body is about 60 % water.
About 71 % of the Earth’s surface is covered by water.

teile.einleitung: Hiking signposts are the yellow signs that show the way to destinations such as mountain huts, lakes or villages in Switzerland. Next to each destination is the walking time in hours and minutes. If you can read them, you can calculate with times and plan a hike well.
wichtigste: Swiss hiking signposts are yellow.
Next to the destination is the walking time, not the distance in kilometres.
“h” means hours, “min” means minutes.
1 h 30 min is 90 minutes.
Mountain trails are marked white-red-white.
With the times given you can work out arrival times and return journeys.
The Swiss network of hiking trails is one of the densest in the world.

abschnitte.text: All over Switzerland the **hiking signposts** look the same: yellow signs with black writing and a point in the direction of the path. They list several destinations, one below the other, usually with the nearest at the top. Often a white field gives the name of the place and its height above sea level. Between the signposts, small yellow diamonds show that you are still on the right path.

Unlike road signs, the **walking time** is shown next to the destination. “Hut 2 h” means that it takes about 2 hours to reach the hut. The time is worked out for an average hiker without breaks, and climbs are already included. Children and families often need a little longer.

You can do plenty of maths with the information. 1 h 30 min is 60 + 30 = 90 minutes. If the signpost shows “Lake 45 min” and “Village 1 h 15 min”, you walk 30 minutes longer to the village. If you set off at 10 o’clock and read “Summit 2 h”, you will be at the top at about 12 o’clock, and for 20 minutes there and back you need **40 minutes**.

The colour of the marking shows how demanding a path is. Yellow stands for ordinary **hiking trails**, which you can usually walk in good shoes. **Mountain trails** are marked white-red-white and can be steep, narrow and exposed. White-blue-white means an alpine trail; for these you need experience and often special equipment.

The Swiss network of hiking trails is about 65,000 kilometres long (as of around 2024), which is more than one and a half times round the Earth. The signposting is looked after by the cantonal hiking trail organisations and the association **Swiss Hiking Trails** (Schweizer Wanderwege). Many volunteers help to check and replace signposts. Hiking is one of the most popular leisure activities in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: The approximate time you need to reach a destination without breaks.
A more demanding path in the mountains, marked white-red-white.
All the signs and markings that show a path.
A small yellow sign between the signposts that confirms the path.

gewusst: The Earth’s circumference is about 40,000 kilometres; the Swiss network of hiking trails is considerably longer.
The walking time on the way back can be quite different, because going downhill is often faster.
The yellow colour of the signposts is the same throughout Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: In a balance puzzle there are different things on a pair of scales, and you have to work out how heavy something is. If the scales are balanced, both sides weigh exactly the same. Balance puzzles are a playful preparation for solving equations.
wichtigste: A balance is level when both sides are equally heavy.
The heavier side goes down.
You may take the same away from both sides, and it stays balanced.
If 3 identical balls balance 12 kilograms, one ball weighs 4 kilograms.
Balance puzzles work like equations with one unknown.
You can compare weights over several steps, for example a pear, a plum and a cherry.
Such puzzles train logical thinking.

abschnitte.text: A **balance** has a beam with two pans. If both sides are equally heavy, the beam is horizontal and the scales are **balanced**. If there are 4 kilograms on the left and 7 kilograms on the right, the right side sinks. If you take an apple away from the left of a balanced pair of scales, the right side sinks too.

If there are 2 identical cubes on the left and 10 grams on the right, one cube weighs 5 grams. So you share the weight out fairly. If there are 3 identical balls on the left and 12 kilograms on the right, one ball weighs 4 kilograms. And if 1 apple weighs as much as 3 nuts, then 2 apples weigh as much as 6 nuts.

If there are 3 kilograms and a parcel on the left and 8 kilograms on the right, you imagine taking 3 kilograms away from both sides. Then only the parcel is left on the left and 5 kilograms on the right. So the parcel weighs **5 kilograms**. In the same way a banana weighs 7 grams if a banana and 2 grams on the left balance 9 grams on the right.

Some puzzles link several balances. A pear weighs as much as 2 plums, and a plum as much as 3 cherries. Then the pear weighs as much as 2 · 3 = **6 cherries**. So you replace one object with another step by step.

A balance puzzle is really an **equation**. “A parcel and 3 kg weigh 8 kg” becomes x + 3 = 8. What you do on the balance, taking the same away from both sides, you also do when calculating. That is why teachers like to use the picture of the balance to explain equations.

begriffe.erklaerung: A pair of scales with a beam and two pans for comparing weights.
The state in which both sides are equally heavy.
A mathematical statement that two sides are equal.
The number you are looking for in an equation, often called x.

gewusst: Balances already existed in ancient Egypt several thousand years ago.
The balance is still a symbol of justice today, because both sides are treated equally.
The equals sign = looks a little like a balance that is level.

teile.einleitung: A table arranges information in rows and columns so that you can find and compare it quickly. We come across tables everywhere: in the school timetable, in the train timetable, in the times tables or in the sports pages. If you can read a table, you find what you are looking for in seconds.
wichtigste: A table consists of rows and columns.
Rows run horizontally side by side, columns vertically one below the other.
Where a row and a column cross, there is a cell.
In the times table, the number 12 is in row 3 and column 4.
Tables let you compare values, for example heights or temperatures.
Train timetables and school timetables are tables too.
On the computer you work with spreadsheets.

abschnitte.text: A **table** is a grid of boxes. The boxes lying side by side horizontally form a **row**. The boxes lying one below the other vertically form a **column**. At the very top or on the far left there are often headings that tell you what is in the row or column.

To find a value, you look for the right row and the right column and see where they cross. In the times table you find the number 12 at row 3 and column 4. In the school timetable you can see that German comes in the 2nd lesson on Monday. The box where a row and a column meet is called a **cell**.

Tables help with comparing. If a table shows Lia at 120 cm, Noah at 128 cm and Ella at 115 cm, you can see at once that Noah is the tallest. With temperatures of 15, 18 and 12 degrees, Wednesday, at 12 degrees, was the coldest. If class 1a has 18 children and 1b has 21, 1b has 3 more children.

The **train timetable** is an important table, especially in Switzerland with its many trains, buses and boats. If it says departure 9.15 and arrival 9.40, the journey takes 25 minutes. Nutrition information on food, weather reports and rankings in sport are tables too. In chemistry the **periodic table** arranges all the known elements in one big table.

On the computer you create tables with a **spreadsheet**, for example with Excel or LibreOffice Calc. There the columns have letters and the rows numbers, so cell B3 is in column B and row 3. The program can calculate totals and averages automatically. A lot of data on the internet is stored in big tables called databases.

begriffe.erklaerung: The boxes of a table that lie side by side horizontally.
The boxes of a table that lie one below the other vertically.
A single box where a row and a column cross.
A computer program with which you create tables and calculate in them.

gewusst: The periodic table of the elements was drawn up as a table in 1869 by the Russian Dmitri Mendeleev, and he left gaps in it for elements that were not yet known.
The ancient Babylonians were already writing calculation tables on clay tablets around 4000 years ago.

teile.einleitung: A missing number problem is a sum in which one number is missing and has been replaced by a gap, a line or a box. The task is to find the missing number, for example in 5 + __ = 12. Problems like this are a first step towards the equations with x that come later at school.
wichtigste: In a missing number problem one number in the sum is missing.
The gap can be a line, a box or a symbol.
You find the missing number with the inverse calculation.
For 5 + __ = 12 you work out 12 − 5 and get 7.
For 3 times __ = 15 you work out 15 divided by 3 and get 5.
With a check you test whether the answer is right.
Later you write a letter such as x instead of a gap.

abschnitte.titel: What is a missing number problem?
abschnitte.text: In a **missing number problem** part of the sum is empty. Instead of a number there is a line, a box or sometimes a question mark. This sign is called a **placeholder**, because it keeps the place free for the number you are looking for. One example is 5 + __ = 12. You have to think about which number fits in the gap so that the sum is right.

The easiest way to solve such problems is with the **inverse calculation**. Plus and minus undo each other, and so do times and divided by. For 5 + __ = 12 you work out 12 − 5 and get 7. For __ + 4 = 10 you work out 10 − 4 and get 6. For 3 times __ = 15 you work out 15 divided by 3, which gives 5.

With minus sums you have to look carefully at where the gap is. For 15 − __ = 9 you ask: how much do I have to take away from 15 to get 9? The answer is 15 − 9, so 6. If the gap is at the front, as in __ − 3 = 8, you add: 8 + 3 = 11. In the same way, __ − 5 = 10 gives the number 15.

After calculating you should do a **check**. To do this, you put the number you found into the gap and work through the whole sum. For __ times 2 = 18 the answer is 9, and 9 times 2 really does give 18. Sometimes the answer is 0, as in 7 + __ = 7. For 20 + __ = 50 it helps to think in tens: 2 tens plus 3 tens are 5 tens, so 30 is missing.

Missing number problems are the first step towards **equations**. At secondary school you write a letter instead of the gap, usually **x**. So 5 + __ = 12 becomes 5 + x = 12, and you solve it in the same way. Letters like these that stand for unknown numbers are called variables. Anyone who can solve missing number problems confidently will therefore find algebra easier later on.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sign that keeps the place free for a missing number.
A calculation that undoes another one, for example minus instead of plus.
Putting the answer back in to test whether the sum is right.
A letter such as x that stands for an unknown number.

gewusst: Even an ancient Egyptian papyrus from more than 3500 years ago contains problems in which an unknown quantity has to be found.
The letter x for an unknown number became common mainly through the French philosopher René Descartes.
A sudoku is also a kind of missing number problem, just with many gaps at once.

teile.einleitung: A thermometer is a measuring instrument that shows the temperature. If you can read a thermometer, you are working with a number line and with negative numbers along the way. In Switzerland temperature is measured in degrees Celsius.
wichtigste: A thermometer measures temperature.
In Switzerland temperature is measured in degrees Celsius, abbreviated °C.
A healthy person is about 37 °C warm.
On a hot summer’s day the thermometer in Switzerland shows about 30 °C.
Minus 5 °C means it is colder than 0 °C.
If the temperature rises from 8 °C to 15 °C, it has become 7 degrees warmer.
Water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.

abschnitte.text: A **thermometer** shows how warm or cold something is. The word comes from Greek and means heat measurer. In the classic liquid thermometer there is a coloured liquid in a thin glass tube. When it gets warmer, the liquid expands and rises; when it gets colder, it sinks. You read the value off a **scale** next to the tube.

In 1742 the Swedish scientist Anders **Celsius** proposed a temperature scale with 100 steps. Today: water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C, both at sea level. Everything below zero degrees is written with a minus, for example minus 5 °C. In the USA temperature is mostly measured in degrees Fahrenheit, and in science also in **kelvin**. The lowest possible temperature, absolute zero, is minus 273.15 °C.

A thermometer is like a vertical **number line**, with the warm values at the top and the cold ones at the bottom. If the temperature rises from 8 °C in the morning to 15 °C at midday, you work out 15 minus 8 and get 7 degrees. It gets harder with **negative numbers**: from minus 3 °C to plus 4 °C is 7 degrees, because you count 3 steps to zero and 4 steps above it. The lower a value is on the scale, the colder it is. That is why minus 10 °C is colder than minus 2 °C.

A **clinical thermometer** measures body temperature, which in healthy people is about 37 °C. From about 38 °C people speak of a fever. Today most clinical thermometers are digital or measure with infrared in the ear or on the forehead. In the past many thermometers contained poisonous mercury; today coloured alcohol or electronic sensors are used. There are also thermometers for the oven, the aquarium, the fridge or the bath.

On a hot summer’s day the thermometer on the Swiss Plateau shows about 30 °C. In winter the values fall, especially in the mountains, often far below zero. The weather service MeteoSwiss measures the air temperature in a white, ventilated hut two metres above the ground, so that the sun does not heat the thermometer directly. Switzerland’s heat record is 41.5 °C in Grono, and its cold record minus 41.8 °C in La Brévine. If you hang a thermometer by a window, you should therefore hang it in the shade.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of how warm or cold something is.
The unit in which temperature is given in Switzerland.
A row of lines with numbers from which you read off a measurement.
A number smaller than zero, written with a minus.

gewusst: Around 1600 Galileo Galilei built one of the first devices that could make heat visible.
Anders Celsius originally had his scale the other way round: water boiled at 0 and froze at 100 degrees.
At minus 40 degrees a Celsius and a Fahrenheit thermometer show exactly the same number.

teile.einleitung: An antiderivative is a function whose derivative gives a given function. So you are searching backwards, as it were: which function must I differentiate to get f(x)? Antiderivatives are the most important tool for calculating areas under curves and integrals.
wichtigste: A function F is called an antiderivative of f if the derivative of F equals f.
An antiderivative of x³ is x⁴/4, and one of sin(x) is -cos(x).
Two antiderivatives of the same function differ only by an added constant.
With a given point you can choose exactly one matching antiderivative.
The fundamental theorem of calculus links antiderivatives with areas.
Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed this kind of calculation in the 17th century.

abschnitte.text: When **differentiating** you find the gradient of a function. With the **antiderivative** you go the other way: you look for a function F whose derivative F' is exactly the given function f. This process is also called indefinite integration. For example, F(x) = x² is an antiderivative of f(x) = 2x, because the derivative of x² is 2x.

For powers the **power rule** applies: you increase the exponent by 1 and divide by the new exponent. So x³ becomes the antiderivative x⁴/4, and √x, that is x to the power of 1/2, becomes (2/3) · x^(3/2). For 1/x³, that is x to the power of -3, you get -1/(2x²). A sum is integrated term by term, which is why 2x³ − 2x² is an antiderivative of 6x² − 4x.

The derivative of a number is zero, so x² + 1 or x² + 4 are also antiderivatives of 2x. Two antiderivatives of the same function therefore differ only by an **added constant**, often called C. On a graph, all the antiderivatives are identical curves that are just shifted up or down. If the antiderivative of 2x is to pass through the point (1|5), then 1 + C = 5, so F(x) = x² + 4.

An antiderivative of sin(x) is -cos(x), because the derivative of -cos(x) is sin(x). For the **exponential function** e^(3x), e^(3x)/3 is an antiderivative. Dividing by 3 makes up for the factor that the chain rule produces when differentiating. Some functions do have an antiderivative, but it cannot be written down with simple formulas.

The **fundamental theorem of calculus** says: the area under a curve between a and b is F(b) minus F(a). This makes it easy to calculate areas, volumes and distances travelled. In the 17th century Isaac Newton in England and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in Germany developed this calculation independently of each other. In physics, for example, the antiderivative of speed gives the distance travelled.

begriffe.erklaerung: A function that tells you how steep a curve is at every point.
A measure of the area between a curve and the x-axis.
A fixed number that does not change.
The small raised number in a power, for example the 3 in x³.

gewusst: The curly integral sign ∫ comes from Leibniz and is a stretched S for “summa”, meaning sum.
Newton and Leibniz argued for years about who had invented the calculation first.

teile.einleitung: Set theory is a branch of mathematics that deals with collections of things, called sets. What sounds simple now forms the foundation of almost the whole of mathematics. It was founded by the mathematician Georg Cantor in the 19th century.
wichtigste: A set is a collection of distinct objects, the elements.
Georg Cantor is regarded as the founder of set theory.
The intersection A ∩ B contains all elements that are in both A and B.
The set of all subsets of a set is called the power set.
Russell's paradox showed that you may not form sets in just any way.
Today Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory is the usual foundation.
With Venn diagrams you can draw sets clearly as circles.

abschnitte.text: A **set** is a collection of things, for example the set of all the children in a class or the set {1, 2, 3}. The things in a set are called **elements**. Sets are written with curly brackets. The order does not matter, and each element counts only once. There is also the empty set ∅, which contains no elements at all.

You can calculate with sets. The **intersection** A ∩ B contains everything that is in both sets: for A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5} it is {3, 4}. The union A ∪ B contains everything that is in at least one of the sets, here {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. The **Cartesian product** A × B consists of all pairs; if A has 3 and B 4 elements, there are 12 pairs. The power set of a set with n elements has 2 to the power n elements.

Around 1880 the English mathematician John Venn drew sets as overlapping circles. Such **Venn diagrams** help with puzzles: in a class of 25 pupils, 15 play football, 12 play floorball and 5 play both. So altogether 15 + 12 − 5 = 22 play at least one of the sports. That means 3 pupils play neither. The 5 are subtracted because otherwise they would be counted twice.

**Georg Cantor** lived from 1845 to 1918 and taught at the University of Halle in Germany. From about 1874 he published his work on sets. He proved amazing things about infinity: there are infinities of different sizes. The real numbers, for example, are “more” than the natural numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on. Many colleagues rejected his ideas at first; today they are regarded as groundbreaking.

Around 1901 the British philosopher **Bertrand Russell** discovered a problem. He asked about the set of all sets that do not contain themselves as an element. If this set contains itself, it is not allowed to, and if it does not contain itself, it would have to. This contradiction is called **Russell's paradox**. That is why Ernst Zermelo and Abraham Fraenkel developed precise rules, the axioms of today's Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory.

Children meet the language of sets early on, for example when sorting shapes and colours. Later, number ranges such as the natural numbers ℕ or the integers ℤ are described as sets. Databases and search engines also work with intersections and unions, for example when you search for two search words at the same time. In logic and computer science, set theory is an essential tool.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single thing that belongs to a set.
All the elements that two sets have in common.
The set of all subsets of a set.
A contradiction in which two conclusions rule each other out.
A basic rule that is accepted as true without proof.

gewusst: The set {∅, {∅}} has 2 elements, although it seems to consist only of “nothing”.
In set theory you can build up all the natural numbers from the empty set alone.
A well-known puzzle about Russell's paradox is the barber who shaves everyone who does not shave themselves.

teile.einleitung: Subtraction means taking away, or doing minus sums. If you give away 7 of your 15 marbles, you have 8 left, and that is exactly what subtraction works out. Together with addition, multiplication and division, it is one of the four basic operations of arithmetic.
wichtigste: Subtraction is one of the four basic operations of arithmetic.
Its sign is the minus sign.
The result of a subtraction is called the difference.
Subtraction is the inverse of addition.
In subtraction you cannot simply swap the numbers.
If you subtract a larger number from a smaller one, you get a negative number.
You can check any result with an addition.

abschnitte.text: Subtracting means taking something away. The number you take away from is called the **minuend**, and the number you take away is called the **subtrahend**. The result is called the **difference**. In the sum 15 minus 7 equals 8, 15 is the minuend, 7 the subtrahend and 8 the difference. The sign is read as “minus” or “take away”.

Subtraction is the **inverse operation** of addition. Because 8 plus 5 equals 13, you know straight away that 13 minus 5 equals 8. That is why you can check every subtraction with an addition. Unlike addition, swapping does not work. 7 minus 3 is 4, but 3 minus 7 gives minus 4.

For 60 minus 20 you simply work out 6 tens minus 2 tens, so 40. For 42 minus 18 you can first take away 20 and then add 2 back on, which gives 24. This trick is called **compensating** or rounding. For 80 minus 35 you work out 80 minus 30 equals 50 and then minus 5 equals 45. Counting on helps too: from 18 to 42 there are 24 steps.

With large numbers you write the numbers underneath each other, units under units and tens under tens. Then you work from right to left, place by place. If a digit at the top is not big enough, you need a **carry**: you borrow a ten from the next place, so to speak. In Switzerland children often learn the counting-on method for this. With a little practice it works with six-digit numbers too.

We subtract all the time, often without noticing. If there are 20 passengers on the bus and 6 get off, 14 stay on the bus. When shopping you work out the **change**, that is the amount paid minus the price. Differences in temperature, differences in age and the minutes left until break are also differences. When the temperature drops below zero, **negative numbers** come into play.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number you take something away from.
The number that is taken away.
The result of a subtraction.
A number smaller than zero, for example minus 4.

gewusst: The word subtract comes from Latin and means roughly “to pull away from underneath”.
Today’s minus sign became common in German arithmetic books from the 15th century onwards.
100 minus 1 is 99, the largest two-digit number.

teile.einleitung: An inverse sum is a calculation that undoes another calculation. The inverse sum of 6 + 3 = 9 is 9 − 3 = 6. With inverse sums you can check results and find missing numbers.
wichtigste: An inverse sum undoes a calculation.
Minus is the inverse of plus.
Divided by is the inverse of times.
With the inverse sum you can check whether a result is correct.
In problems with a missing number, the inverse sum helps to fill the gap.
The inverse sum of 4 · 5 = 20 is 20 : 5 = 4.
Inverse sums are the basis for solving equations later on.

abschnitte.text: An **inverse sum** goes along the path of a calculation backwards. You start at the result and arrive back at the starting number. 6 + 3 = 9 becomes 9 − 3 = 6. This shows that calculations are like a path that you can walk there and back.

**Addition** and **subtraction** are opposite operations. If you add 3, you can undo it again with minus 3. With 9 + 6 = 15 you check whether 15 − 6 = 9 is right. This is a simple and reliable checking trick.

**Multiplication** and **division** also belong together. 4 · 5 = 20 goes with 20 : 5 = 4. The other way round, 32 : 4 = 8 has the inverse sum 8 · 4 = 32. That is why anyone who knows their times tables well is also good at dividing.

Often there is a question mark in a problem, for example ? + 7 = 12. With the inverse sum 12 − 7 you find the missing number 5. For ? · 6 = 42 you work out 42 : 6 and get 7. Such problems are also called **missing number problems**.

Inverse sums train your understanding of how the operations are connected. Later, in secondary school, exactly this idea is used to solve **equations**. It helps in everyday life too: if you pay 20 francs and get 7 francs back, you can work backwards to find out how much the shopping cost. That is why teachers recommend the inverse sum as a check after every calculation.

begriffe.erklaerung: A calculation that undoes another calculation.
Testing whether a result really is correct.
A sign such as ? or an empty box for a missing number.
The operation that cancels out another, such as minus for plus.

gewusst: If you add 5 to a number and then subtract 5, you always end up back at the starting number.
You cannot divide by zero, which is why the calculation “times 0” has no inverse sum.
Computers also check some calculations by working backwards.

teile.einleitung: Probability tells you how certain or uncertain it is that something will happen. It is a number between 0 and 1, which can also be written as a fraction or a percentage. With it you can predict how often a 6 comes up when rolling a die or how big the chance of winning is.
wichtigste: Probability always lies between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).
An impossible event has the probability 0.
The probability of rolling a 6 is 1/6.
You roll an even number with a probability of 1/2.
Not rolling a 6 has the probability 5/6.
When tossing a coin three times, heads three times has a probability of only 1/8.
Three children can stand in a row in 6 different ways.

abschnitte.text: Many things in life are **random**, for example a roll of a die or the weather. **Probability** describes with a number how good the chances are. 0 means that something never happens, and 1 means that it is completely certain to happen. A probability of 1/2 corresponds to 50 per cent. That is like tossing a coin, where heads and tails have equally good chances.

If all outcomes are equally likely, you divide the **favourable outcomes** by the possible outcomes. A die has 6 possible outcomes, but only one of them is the 6. So the probability is 1 divided by 6, that is 1/6. For an even number there are three favourable outcomes, namely 2, 4 and 6, which gives 3/6 or 1/2. This rule is also called the **Laplace rule**, after the Frenchman Pierre-Simon Laplace.

A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green balls, 10 altogether. If you draw a ball without looking, the chance of red is 5 out of 10, that is 1/2. For green it is only 2/10 or 1/5. Examples like this are called the **urn model** in mathematics. They can be used to act out many random experiments.

If you toss a coin three times, there are 2 times 2 times 2, that is 8 possible outcomes. Only one of them is heads, heads, heads, so the probability is 1/8. With two dice there are 36 combinations, and 6 of them give a **total score** of 7. That is why 7 comes up most often, with 1/6. The probability that something does not happen is called the **complementary probability**; for the 6 it is 5/6.

Often you have to count how many possibilities there are. Three children can line up in 3 times 2 times 1, that is 6 ways. With four children there are already 24 ways. This kind of counting is called **combinatorics**. It helps with calculating probabilities in games and puzzles.

The weather forecast might give a **chance of rain** of 70 per cent, for example. In board games such as “Eile mit Weile”, the die decides your luck. Insurance companies calculate how likely accidents are. In lotteries such as the Swiss Lotto, the chances of winning the jackpot are very small. If you understand probabilities, you can judge risks better.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something whose outcome you do not know for certain beforehand.
A possible outcome of a random experiment, for example “rolling a 6”.
The chance that an event does not happen.
The mathematics of cleverly counting possibilities.

gewusst: Even after five sixes in a row, the chance of another 6 is again exactly 1/6, because the die has no memory.
With two dice the total 7 is the most common, and 2 and 12 are the rarest.
Probability theory began in the 17th century with questions about games of chance.

teile.einleitung: The normal distribution is the most important probability distribution in statistics. Its picture is the famous bell curve, often called the Gaussian bell curve after Carl Friedrich Gauss. Many measurements from nature and everyday life, such as people's heights, are spread out roughly like this.
wichtigste: The normal distribution has the shape of a symmetrical bell.
After Carl Friedrich Gauss it is often called the Gaussian bell curve.
It is fixed by the mean and the standard deviation.
About 68% of the values lie at most one standard deviation from the mean.
About 95% lie within two and about 99.7% within three standard deviations.
The standard normal distribution has the mean 0 and the standard deviation 1.
The points of inflection of the curve lie at the mean plus or minus one standard deviation.

abschnitte.text: If you draw how often certain values occur, normally distributed data produce a **bell curve**. In the middle, at the **mean**, it is highest. To the left and right it falls away evenly, so it is symmetrical. Far out at the edges, values occur only very rarely. The curve never quite touches the axis.

The **standard deviation** shows how widely the values are spread around the mean. If it is small, the bell is narrow and tall; if it is large, the bell is wide and flat. At the mean plus or minus one standard deviation lie the **points of inflection**, where the curve changes the way it bends. For heights with a mean of 170 cm and a standard deviation of 8 cm, a height of 180 cm has the **z-score** 1.25, because 10 divided by 8 gives 1.25.

For every normal distribution there is a simple rule of thumb. About 68% of all values lie within one standard deviation of the mean. About 95% lie within two and about 99.7% within three standard deviations. In IQ tests with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15, roughly 68% therefore have a score between 85 and 115. About 16% each lie above or below that.

The French mathematician **Abraham de Moivre** described the curve as early as 1733. It was made famous by **Carl Friedrich Gauss**, who used it at the beginning of the 19th century to calculate measurement errors in astronomy and land surveying. That is why it is often called the Gaussian bell curve. Gauss and the bell curve were pictured on the German 10-mark note until the euro arrived in 2002.

Roughly normally distributed are, for example, the heights of adults, the weight of apples of one variety or measurement errors in experiments. Factories use it for **quality control**, for example so that screws almost always have the right length. A **Galton board** shows the normal distribution clearly: balls fall through many rows of nails and collect at the bottom in the shape of a bell. The reason is that many small, random influences add up.

begriffe.erklaerung: The average of all the values; in the normal distribution it lies exactly in the middle.
A measure of how far, on average, the values are from the mean.
Shows how many standard deviations a value is from the mean.
A board with nails through which balls fall and form a bell curve.

gewusst: Values more than three standard deviations from the mean occur in only about 3 out of 1000 cases.
The area under the whole bell curve is always exactly 1, that is 100 per cent.
The English scientist Francis Galton built the Galton board in the 19th century to make chance visible.

teile.einleitung: A prism is a geometric solid with two identical, parallel polygons as its base and top. The side faces in between are rectangles or parallelograms. A well-known example is the triangular box of Toblerone chocolate, and every cuboid is a prism too.
wichtigste: A prism has a base and a parallel top of the same size.
The base can be a triangle, quadrilateral, hexagon or another polygon.
The volume of a prism is base area times height.
A prism with a right-angled triangle as base (shorter sides 3 cm and 4 cm) and a height of 10 cm has 60 cm³.
A cuboid with edges of 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm has a surface area of 52 cm².
According to Cavalieri's principle, a slanting prism has the same volume as an upright one with the same base area and height.
Cuboids and cubes are special prisms.

abschnitte.text: A **prism** is made when you move a polygon straight upwards and join all its corners to their copies. At the bottom is the **base**, at the top the exactly identical **top face**. The side faces together form the **lateral surface**. Depending on the shape of the base, you speak of a triangular, quadrilateral or hexagonal prism. A prism with n corners in its base has 2n corners, 3n edges and n plus 2 faces.

If the side edges are perpendicular to the base, the prism is a **right prism**, and all the side faces are rectangles. If the side edges lean, it is called an oblique prism, and its side faces are parallelograms. If the base is a regular polygon and the prism is right, it is called regular. A **cuboid** is a right prism with a rectangle as its base. A cube is a cuboid whose edges are all the same length.

The volume of every prism is worked out with V equals base area times height. If the prism has a right-angled triangle with shorter sides of 3 cm and 4 cm as its base, the base area is 3 times 4 divided by 2, so 6 cm². With a height of 10 cm that gives 60 cm³. A regular hexagon with sides of 2 cm has an area of about 10.4 cm²; with a height of 5 cm that gives about 52.0 cm³. **Cavalieri's principle** shows that an oblique prism with the same base area and height has the same volume, much like a stack of beer mats pushed sideways.

The **surface area** of a prism consists of the base, the top face and the lateral surface. The lateral surface of a right prism is worked out as the perimeter of the base times the height. A cuboid with edges of 2 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm has two faces each of 6 cm², 8 cm² and 12 cm². Together that gives 2 times 26, so 52 cm². The **net** of a prism is its unfolded surface, from which you can cut out and fold the solid.

Prism shapes are found in boxes, building blocks, pencils with a hexagonal cross-section and roofs of houses. The box of **Toblerone**, which has been made in Bern since 1908, is a triangular prism. Honeycombs consist of many small hexagonal prisms. In physics, glass blocks with a triangular base are also called prisms. They split white light into the colours of the rainbow, which Isaac Newton studied in the 17th century.

The word prism comes from Greek and means “something sawn off”. The Greek mathematician Euclid already described prisms in his work “Elements”. In the 17th century the Italian **Bonaventura Cavalieri** formulated the principle named after him. Prisms are the basis for understanding cylinders and other solids later on. A cylinder, after all, is something like a prism with a circle as its base.

begriffe.erklaerung: The face on which a solid stands.
All the side faces of a solid together.
A prism with a rectangle as its base, for example a shoebox.
The unfolded surface of a solid laid out flat.
A rule saying that solids with equal cross-sections at every height have the same volume.

gewusst: Bees build their honeycombs from hexagonal prisms, because this shape gives a lot of space for little wax.
A glass prism bends violet light more strongly than red light, which is why a band of colours appears.

teile.einleitung: The standard deviation is a number from statistics that shows how widely measurements are spread around their mean. If it is small, the values lie close together; if it is large, they are widely spread. It helps you understand marks, heights or weather data better, for example.
wichtigste: The standard deviation describes how widely the values are spread around the mean.
It is the square root of the variance.
If all the values are the same, as in 5, 5, 5, 5, the standard deviation is 0.
If you add the same number to all the values, the standard deviation stays the same.
If you double all the values, the standard deviation doubles too.
It has the same unit as the measurements, for example centimetres.
It is often written with the Greek letter sigma, σ.

abschnitte.text: Two classes can have the same **mean** mark and still be very different. In one, everyone has a 4.5; in the other there are lots of 6s and lots of 3s. The **standard deviation** measures exactly this difference, that is the **spread** of the values. The larger it is, the further the values lie from the average.

First you calculate the mean of all the values. Then for each value you work out its distance from the mean, square it and take the average of these squares; that is the **variance**. Finally you take the square root and get the standard deviation. For the values 10 and 20 the mean is 15 and each value differs by 5, so the standard deviation of the whole population is 5.

If you add 10 to all the values, only the mean shifts; the spread stays the same. If you double all the values, all the distances double too, and so does the standard deviation. Because you take the square root at the end, it has the same **unit** as the data, so centimetres for heights. The variance, on the other hand, would have the unit square centimetres.

Many measurements in nature follow the **normal distribution**, which looks like a bell. Then about two thirds of all the values lie at most one standard deviation from the mean, and about 95 per cent at most two. If you toss a fair coin 100 times, you expect heads 50 times, and the standard deviation is 5. So results between 45 and 55 are perfectly normal.

In the 19th century the mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss studied the normal distribution, to which the standard deviation is closely linked. The name “standard deviation” was coined towards the end of the 19th century by the Englishman Karl Pearson. Today it is used in **quality control**, for example to make sure that screws or bars of chocolate weigh the same. It is also essential in medicine, weather forecasting and science.

begriffe.erklaerung: The average, that is the sum of all the values divided by how many there are.
The average of the squared distances from the mean.
How far apart values lie.
A common distribution of measurements with the shape of a bell.

gewusst: Germany’s last 10-mark banknote showed Carl Friedrich Gauss and his bell curve.
In factories people talk about “Six Sigma” when faults should be so rare that they only occur six standard deviations away from the mean.

teile.einleitung: The intercept theorems are important rules in geometry. They say that line segments in a figure made of two rays and two parallel lines are in the same ratio. With them you can calculate lengths that cannot be measured directly, such as the height of a tree or a pyramid.
wichtigste: The intercept theorems apply when two rays from a point Z are cut by two parallel lines.
The segments on the rays are then in the same ratio.
The parallel segments are also in the same ratio as the segments measured from the vertex.
The figure can look like a V or like an X.
With a stick and its shadow you can work out the height of trees or towers.
Thales of Miletus is said to have found the height of an Egyptian pyramid in this way.
The pinhole camera and dividing a line segment are also based on the intercept theorem.

abschnitte.text: Two **rays** start from a common point Z, the vertex. Two parallel lines cut these rays at the points A and B and at A’ and B’. The most important condition is that the cutting lines really are **parallel**. Otherwise the intercept theorems do not apply.

The **first intercept theorem** says: the segments on one ray are in the same ratio as those on the other. If ZA = 4 cm, ZA’ = 10 cm and ZB = 6 cm, then ZB’ = 15 cm, because everything is enlarged by 2.5. The **second intercept theorem** compares the parallel segments with the segments from the vertex. With ZA = 3 cm, ZA’ = 9 cm and AB = 5 cm, A’B’ is three times as long, so 15 cm.

The vertex Z can also lie between the two parallel lines; then the figure looks like an X. The intercept theorems apply here in exactly the same way. If ZA = 2 cm, ZA’ = 5 cm and AB = 3 cm, then A’B’ = 3 cm times 5/2 = 7.5 cm. This is exactly how the upside-down image forms in a **pinhole camera**: a tower 30 m high at a distance of 100 m gives an image 3 cm high 10 cm behind the hole.

When the sun shines, its rays arrive parallel. If a stick 2 m high casts a shadow 1.5 m long and a tree casts one 12 m long, the tree is 8 times as tall as the stick, so 16 m. According to tradition, the Greek scholar **Thales of Miletus**, who lived in the 6th century BC, found the height of an Egyptian pyramid in this way. That is why in French the intercept theorem is called “théorème de Thalès”, Thales’ theorem.

Thanks to the intercept theorem, you can divide a line segment into equal parts with compasses and a ruler, even if the length is awkward to divide. With the **thumb jump** method you estimate distances by sighting over your outstretched thumb with one eye and then the other. Maps, enlargements on a photocopier and cameras also work with the same ratios. The intercept theorems are closely linked to the **similarity** of shapes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A straight line that starts at a point and goes on for ever.
Two lines that are the same distance apart everywhere and never meet.
The common starting point of the two rays.
A comparison of two quantities by dividing, for example 4 to 10.

gewusst: The Great Pyramid of Giza was originally almost 147 metres high and was for a long time the tallest building in the world.
In the human eye, too, an upside-down image forms on the same principle as the pinhole camera.
